Regarding the ritual for reciting the sutra:
if there is anyone who upholds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, they must first wash their hands, burn incense, and open the scroll.
With a sincere mind, they should recite the Mantra for Purifying Oral Karma and the Mantra for Purifying the Dharma Realm three times each. Thereafter, they should invoke the Eight Vajras.
The names of the four bodhisattvas and the mantra for purifying verbal karma: *śūli śūli mahāśūli śūśūli svāhā*.
The Mantra of the Pure Dharma Realm: Oṃ laṃ.
Request the Eight Vajras.
I invoke the Vajra of Blue Disaster-Dispelling; I invoke the Vajra of Poison-Averting;
I invoke the Vajra of Yellow Wish-Fulfilling; I invoke the Vajra of White Pure Water;
I invoke the Vajra of Red Sound-Fire; I invoke the Vajra of Sustaining Stability Against Disaster.
I respectfully invoke the Vajra of Purple Wisdom; I respectfully invoke the Great Deity Vajra;
I respectfully invoke the Four Bodhisattvas;
I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; I respectfully invoke the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa.
Invitation to Bodhisattva Vajrarāga and Invitation to Bodhisattva Vajravākya Aspiration Prayer:
I prostrate to the Honored One of the Three Realms; I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions. Now I make this great vow.
By upholding this Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, may we repay the four profound debts of gratitude above, and relieve the sufferings of the three miserable realms below.
May all who see or hear it resolve to attain Bodhicitta; at the end of this present life, may they be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Verse for Opening the Sutra:
The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma Is difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas;
Now that I have seen, heard, received, and upheld it, I pray that I may understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.
Preface to the Record of Experiences from Upholding the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*.
The *Buddhabhāṣita Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of six hundred fascicles; the *Vajracchedikā* is the five hundred and seventy-seventh among them.
Zhongfeng said: "The six hundred fascicles provide an extensive exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, specifically intended for those of the Hīnayāna, to harmonize and refine their understanding."
Desiring to purify the vessel of the mind, one may thereafter store within it the flavor of the sublime, sudden nectar of the Mahāyāna.

Thus, the great purport of this sutra takes non-characteristic (*animitta*), non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) as its central tenet. Through repeated inversions and turnings, establishing and then immediately sweeping away [all positions], it most thoroughly discusses emptiness;
yet, in its ultimate sense, it does not discuss emptiness. This is what is meant by the Tathāgata being one who speaks words of truth.
Regarding "not speaking deceptively," it is further said: when the mind of faith is pure, one immediately gives birth to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is like the case of "tortoise hair" and "rabbit horns. One simply says that the tortoise has no hair and the rabbit has no horns; these words are most capable of shattering worldly conventions.

If one looks only at the four characters "neither real nor false" in the middle [of the phrase], the World-Honored One has already himself provided the commentary for the entire sutra. Where there is reality, all is empty; where there is emptiness...

Abiding in ultimate reality, neither arising nor ceasing, one completely severs the dharmic marks of worldly afflictions—wherein cessation gives rise to cessation and birth gives rise to birth—with a single stroke.
With courageous and resolute liberation, one directly seeks the original source; this is called the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.
This is what is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Yet within this sūtra, on one hand it speaks of abiding and subduing, while on the other it speaks of faith and pure confidence;
on one hand it explains the meaning of the sūtra, while on the other it describes its karmic rewards.
With a single heart of compassionate concern and a thousandfold weary tongue, he desires to deliver good men and women, urgently protecting and mindful of them through his entrustment.
It is entrusted to all Bodhisattvas. Those who wish to deliver all sentient beings do so with even greater urgency than they would deliver good men and women;
therefore, all the characteristics of dharmas they speak of are like clouds reflected in a deep pool, like nail-marks upon snow, or the ethereal and spontaneous transformations of space.

It is said that there is nothing that can be spoken. Yet, it is stated that if in a future age there should be someone who receives, upholds, and expounds this sutra—even so much as a single four-line verse—they shall immediately be highly commended and entrusted with the burden [of the Dharma], praised for their rarity, and extolled with the utmost words as possessing immeasurable and boundless merit.
This statement appears some ten times throughout the preceding and following sections; every instance is intended to inspire those living after the five hundred years.
By instantly shattering all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and personally realizing *prajñā*, this sutra is the book in which the World-Honored One tirelessly instructs humanity.
He uses sentient beings to deliver sentient beings, and he uses those who are not sentient beings to deliver sentient beings;
yet in reality, each sentient being delivers themselves. I do not deliver sentient beings, nor do sentient beings perceive that I am delivering them. Therefore...
Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha; the Buddha is himself sentient beings. There is no characteristic of separation, nor is there any characteristic of union.

Some may say that the doctrine of karmic retribution is taught exclusively for those of the third grade. This seems like the masters following the Sixth Patriarch who occupy a high position and claim this as their own record.
Should one not, however, regard those of the first and second grades with the same expectation for future lives? As it was said of old: "Full..."
The streets are sacred; thus, one may say that the entire realm of dust is Buddha. Since it is said to be Buddha, why differentiate three grades?
Those who speak thus [claim] that the ordinary person’s view of self is merely the failure to empty the four marks.
The Buddha has previously taught that for those who are to be saved by a particular body, he manifests that very body to preach the Dharma to them.

I shall not now distinguish between first, second, or third classes of people; rather, wherever there are thousands of millions of billions of beings in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system who uphold this sutra, it is not difficult for [the Buddha] to manifest before those thousands of millions of billions in the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
He preaches the Dharma through the bodies of billions of Buddhas, merely to enable them to hear this teaching, so that they may joyfully practice it.
Thus, the wisdom-life of all these Buddhas remains unbroken. Spontaneously, empty space falls to the earth; iron trees bloom at night.

One may search and compile at will, resulting in voluminous words and numerous volumes, yet from the time of figures such as Du Jiangu onwards, none have done more than use the Buddha’s words to verify the Buddha’s words.
This is not merely an addition of common parlance. The Buddha further said: "If I were to explain this in full detail, people might become deranged or harbor doubts and fail to believe it.
However, if today there are those with pure faith and no doubt, the Buddha will explain it in full detail according to their desire."

With joy, he poured out his heart and confessed it all to that person. Since the Buddha is indeed one who speaks the truth and never utters falsehood, how much more so regarding these recorded accounts that verify the facts from antiquity to the present? What room, then, is there for madness or doubt?
Nevertheless, a Bodhisattva should have no dwelling-place in phenomena; how could one dwell upon the marks of merit in such a manner? One must know that they are signless and non-existent.
I then understood that one should not be greedily attached to merit. This was not spoken by the Buddha solely for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Please allow me to offer a further explanation for those who uphold this teaching: "The Tathāgata says that the retribution of karmic fruit is itself no retribution;
it is called 'retribution. The Tathāgata says that one does not receive merit; it is itself no non-reception of merit; it is called 'non-reception of merit.'"
Exhortation to Circulate the Diamond Sūtra:

The Diamond Sūtra is regarded as the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle. Among the six hundred fascicles of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Fifth Patriarch uniquely recommended this sūtra as the essential gateway for realizing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
He universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople to receive and uphold it. From the various Dharma masters of the Qin and Wei dynasties...
After its translation, from emperors, dukes, and officials down to scholars and commoners, there were none who did not practice it through recitation and propagation.
The miraculous responses and spiritual efficacy of its observance have been clearly attested by evidence throughout the ages. In the Tang dynasty, there was Duan Taichang’s *Juyi*;

in the Song dynasty, Emperor Taizong compiled the *Taiping Guangji*. In recent times, there are Tang Yizhi’s *Jinyucheng* and Wang Zaisheng’s *Xinyilu*, as well as Mao Zongqi’s *Shou...* [text truncated].
Those who uphold these various collections of karmic fruits have all exerted their utmost strength to proclaim the sacred bell, widely ferrying those lost at the ford of delusion.
By propagating the gift of the Dharma, they sustain the life of wisdom; their merit is indeed imperishable. Within this compendium, the accounts of cause and effect are detailed:
fire can be made to turn back, water can be made to flow out, the sick can be restored, misfortune can be escaped, and one’s lifespan can be prolonged. One’s fame...

It shall cause [the deceased] to attain completion; it shall enable their lineage to continue; it shall cause blessings to accumulate; it shall cause shackles and manacles to open of their own accord; it shall cause knives and saws to fall away of their own accord.
Above, it can deliver the deceased ancestors; below, it can dissolve past grudges. The officers of the underworld and the ghost-messengers will not dare approach;
the divine lord of Mount Tai will not dare to record them. The various heavens shall provide precious canopies and stūpas to cover and enshrine them. Yama...
It is provided with golden couches and silver beds for its veneration; furthermore, it can liberate one from worldly afflictions and lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.
In the underworld, it is called the "Sutra for Extending Life" and the "Sutra of Merit. It is evident that its honor among both the unseen and the seen reaches the highest degree.
If the merit of copying and reciting it is already inconceivable in this way, how much more so when one is able to illuminate the ground of the mind!

How diligent are those who receive and uphold [this teaching]! These are the various deities who protect the Dharma. Having protected the treasure of the Dharma, they themselves protect those who propagate it;

their commitment to those who carry this treasure is indeed absolute. (Kefu) When I first resolved to compile these records, I fortunately encountered like-minded virtuous friends who together gave rise to the Bodhicitta.
They contributed funds to assist in the carving of the blocks, collating ancient and modern sources and synthesizing what has been heard and seen, exerting themselves to the utmost.
My eyes have not yet been able to claim this as a great achievement; however, compared to previous versions, it may be considered a superior edition.

I reflect that while most prior editions were produced within the region of Wu, they have rarely been disseminated to other provinces. Thus, those born within the adorned Buddha-lands have failed to witness the excellence of the circulation of these Dharma teachings.
Is this not, indeed, a deficiency in the world? I respectfully inform my fellow practitioners of this matter.
With faith, I have come to witness this record. I shall not begrudge the effort of carving it for wide distribution—whether following the original text or revising it into a new compilation.

I especially hope that those who have encountered or heard of accounts related to the efficacy of upholding [the name] will continue to compile them, so as to provide sufficient encouragement for the future and ensure they remain an imperishable refuge.
In the past, there were sages who created "pitted-mold" diagrams (*pikē tú*) to exhort people to recite the Buddha’s name; ultimately, through the recitation of others...

The Buddha often attains rebirth in the Pure Land; thus, he attributes this merit to those who provide the illustrations, so that they too shall be born in the Pure Land. Furthermore, the *Shanguoge* (Excellence of Transmissions) states:

"One who can bestow the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle upon others, causing them to achieve awakening through these words, shall receive the merit of ten good deeds for every person they transmit it to.
For ten such persons, the merit is equivalent to a hundred good deeds. If one transmits it to a person of great nobility, great power, or great heroism, the merit is even greater."
To collect, edit, carve the woodblocks, and print this scroll to bestow upon others constitutes a thousandfold merit.

To propagate this present *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*, the unsurpassed secret truth, truly acting as its wings to spread it so that one awakens oneself and awakens others, will ensure that the light of wisdom remains uninterrupted and that all achieve the perfection of wholesome fruits together.
May the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, jointly protect the scrolls within these precious cases; may the fire-houses of the six sense-objects [be extinguished].
To open the flower of the *tambula* [lotus], I respectfully compose this brief preface to exhort my fellow practitioners.
Written with humble earnestness by the Dharma-fellow Kefu,
according to the eight rules of protocol.
This sutra has been transmitted for a long time, undergoing a total of six translations over its history; consequently, there are slight differences in the wording and phrasing.
Herein, I have strictly followed the original translation by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin dynasty, whereby all doubts may be resolved.
This sutra consists of thirty-two sections. It is traditionally said that these were divided by Prince Zhaoming.

The edition carved at Shouchun during the fifth year of the Baoda era of the Southern Tang dynasty followed the original canon version and did not mark the number of sections; it was truly comprehensive and integrated. Recently, many have followed this precedent.
However, as the division into sections has been widely circulated for a long time, even Zhongfeng’s *Brief Meaning* (Lüyi) maintains those divisions for the sake of convenient recitation.
This is the retention [of the text]. Regarding the phonetic transcriptions of characters in the sutra, the Sanskrit and Chinese differ; a single character may be read with several pronunciations.
For those cases where the original character has a distinct reading, as well as occasional difficult characters, all have been clearly annotated for the convenience of beginners.

The historical record begins with a chronological account of successive dynasties, starting from the Later Wei and extending to the present era. By listing ancient and modern periods side by side, one may gain confidence that the narrative is grounded in evidence.
However, while the events of the Tang and Ming dynasties are relatively detailed, those of the Song and Yuan are regrettably sparse.

This is because there were no scholars such as the Grand Music Master Duan or the Vice Minister of Justice Tang to preserve them; thus, virtuous deeds have been lost to oblivion and illustrious names have failed to shine.
The merit of undertaking this compilation later on—how could it be slight?
First are recorded the good men and good women; next are the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs. Previously, when carving [the scriptures], the monastic community was extensively listed.

As disciples of the Empty Gate who revere and believe in the Buddhist canon, it is naturally fitting that they should be categorized thus. Only those from secular families... [who study... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
The Way is like the true blue lotus, which emerges from the mud yet remains unstained; it is especially lamented as rare and marvelous, and is therefore compiled in detail within this collection.

Works by minor officials and unofficial histories are for the most part absurd, consisting of hearsay and idle talk that cannot be relied upon for transmission of truth; thus, this collection has been examined [for authenticity].
Adhering to the strictest standard, any accounts that even slightly involve suspicion have been eliminated;

the endeavor has been to ensure that what is presented is authentic, sufficient to provide inspiration and encouragement. Under each entry, the source is annotated in detail to demonstrate its credibility.

The purpose of this commentary is to elucidate the essential meaning of the present case. By tracing the sequence of events and awakening the reader at every point, those who read it will have their mental eye suddenly opened;
they will naturally feel a keen sense of personal concern, and thus avoid the reproach of being like a cup of wine whose words are inappropriate.

May this serve as a means to avoid [calamity]. Written with one hundred prostrations by the son Shi, respectfully recording the accounts of the Vajradhara’s spiritual efficacy throughout successive dynasties.
Compiled by Zhou Kefu of Jingxi (Chonglang), and edited by the son Zhou Shi.
Chen Jisheng (style name Huangshi) of Wumen visited Lu Jingyu (style name Zhongru) of the Later Wei dynasty after his ordination.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Jiemin, Lu served as a State Academy (Guozijian) Doctor and was a devoted believer in the teachings of Śākyamuni.
He annotated the *Zhouyi* and the *Lunyu*. His cousin Shenli, relying on a plot by local people, coerced Fayu into joining forces to respond to the Western Wei.
Fayu was imprisoned in the Jinyang jail; there, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with single-minded devotion, and his shackles and fetters fell off of their own accord.

When Shenwu of the Qi dynasty became Chancellor, he specifically granted him amnesty. Alas! People may be subjected to the shackles, fetters, and manacles of both the world of the living and the underworld.

And yet they do not seek liberation? Thus, the shackles of affection and love before one's eyes, the fetters of pleasure—how can these be taken as one's very life-force, such that one knows not how to escape them?
Furthermore, becoming entangled in layers upon layers, they refuse to be free; this is truly a great delusion and a matter of profound pity.
If one could, for even a moment, receive and uphold [the teachings] like Jingyu, then regarding both past causes and future limits, [one would realize the truth].
All [obstacles] were severed at once, and he attained great mastery (from the *Baoying ji*).
During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, there was a Dharma Master named Yan who resided at Zhaoti Monastery in Chang’an. He entered the monastic order at the age of eleven.
Once, while accompanying a monk from the same monastery to the home of a physiognomist, the physiognomist said to Yan: "It is a pity that your brilliance will last for no more than eighteen years."

When Yan heard this, he was displeased. He returned to the Scripture Treasury Hall, where he burned incense and paid homage to the Buddha, vowing that the Buddha would grant him one scroll of scripture to uphold for the remainder of his life.
Upon finishing his prayer, he reached into a case within the treasury and drew out a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. From then on, he recited it day and night.
Suddenly, one evening after midnight, a five-colored radiance appeared in his room. In a short while, a Brahman monk appeared, standing fifteen feet tall.
[The deity] granted this. He said to Yan, "Your life was to end at eighteen, but through the power of upholding the Mahāyāna sūtras with sincerity and truthfulness, it has been extended.
Having spoken, he vanished. When Yan was over nineteen years old, she again encountered a physiognomist, who looked at her in astonishment and said, "Master, your life-span has completely vanished;
how could you have reached such a state? Yan replied, "I have focused my mind exclusively on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The physiognomist said, "Master..."
His life was destined to reach ninety-two years. When that time arrived, he sat in meditation and passed away, with a wondrous fragrance filling the room (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).

During the early Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenruo died of illness. After seven days had passed and his family was about to prepare him for burial, he suddenly withdrew one leg, whereupon they halted the proceedings.
Having revived, he said: "I was pursued by a man into the City of Darkness. The King asked what meritorious deeds I had performed during my lifetime."

He replied, "I have merely upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King said, "This is the foremost merit; even if one's lifespan were to be exhausted by calculation, it may yet be extended.
He added further, "Among all sins, those of killing are most grave. You regularly provide pigs and sheep for the kitchen; dispatch a messenger to lead you to the place of suffering.
Traveling two or three li northward, beneath a high wall there is a hole just large enough for a body to pass through. Exit through this hole and ascend..."
There was a high mound from which the four directions appeared vast and wide. A city stood extremely high and steep; its smoke and fire reached the heavens, and black vapors overflowed the earth.

One heard the sounds of wailing and lamentation everywhere, so intense that they seemed to block the ears and eyes. [The man] knelt with his head to the ground, seeking release, feeling as though his heart were being torn apart and blood flowing from his mouth.
The messenger led him back to see the King, saying: "You took great pleasure in eating flesh; you cannot escape even a light punishment. He then demanded a long [tongue].
Five nails were driven into his head and both his hands and feet; the pain was extraordinary. From then on, he abstained from meat and devoted himself to reciting the sutras.
Later, while traveling to a post station on official business, he suddenly dreamed of a girl in green clothing begging for help.
He asked the station attendant what food was available, and was told there was a very fat and tender sheep. Upon seeing it, he realized it was a blue cow. Wenruo said, "I do not eat [meat]."
He then ransomed and released them. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Those who eat sheep will become sheep when they die; those who are human will become human when they die.

Thus, through death after death and birth after birth, they prey upon one another. Although Zhao Wenruo upheld this scripture and extended his lifespan, he ultimately suffered from long nails due to his fondness for meat.
Had he not possessed this merit, the cycle of retribution for killing would have continued without end.

(From the *Tàipíng guǎngjì*). In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Zhao Wenchang, an assistant director of the Grand Court of the Imperial Guard, died suddenly. Only his heart remained warm, and he was restored to life.
He reported that at the time of his death, someone led him to an audience with King Yama. The King asked whether he had ever performed meritorious deeds; Wenchang—
He replied that his family was poor and lacked the means to perform meritorious deeds; he could only focus his mind on reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King joined his palms in praise, saying, "Excellent! The karmic fruit of your practice is truly vast. He then ordered attendants to lead him into the treasury to retrieve the scriptures.
Having traveled five or six li westward, Chang saw dozens of buildings, most magnificent and ornate, filled with sacred texts. He reached out his hand and drew one at random.

He took one scroll; it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Holding it up, he went to where the king was. One man held the scroll on the west side while Wenchang stood on the east and recited it toward him, omitting not a single character.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately released Wenchang, ordering him to lead the way out through the southern gate.
There he saw Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou in a room by the gate, his body bound with three layers of shackles and chains. The Emperor called out to Wenchang, saying, "You..."
"I am a native of this country. Do you recognize me? Changwen said, "Your servant formerly served as a guard to Your Majesty.

The Emperor said, "You are an old minister. Return home and tell the Emperor of Sui: 'My various offenses have been adjudicated; only the sin of destroying the Buddha-dharma is grave and difficult to escape.
I hope you will perform meritorious deeds on my behalf so that I may be released from hell. Changwen took his leave and departed through the south gate, where he saw...
A man was found inside a large pit of excrement with his hair protruding from it. Someone pointed him out, saying, "This is Bai Qi, the General of Qin, who has been imprisoned here;
his retribution is not yet finished. Once Chang had revived, he reported this to the throne. An imperial edict was issued to the entire empire regarding the household registration tax.

He translated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for Emperor Wu and recorded the circumstances of these events in the *History of the Sui*. According to the records, when Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty destroyed bronze Buddhist statues, he said:
"In Buddhism, if the head, eyes, marrow, or brain can benefit sentient beings, one does not begrudge them;
how much less would one cherish a bronze image? He then struck down the Great Compassion Image of Zhenzhou, which was renowned for its spiritual efficacy, using an axe to destroy it.
The axe pierced through his chest from the front. Later, when Emperor Shizong campaigned northward, a carbuncle broke out and perforated his chest.
How bitter indeed is the retribution! (From the Fayuan zhulin).

Xu Xiaokē, the Sui Dynasty’s National Academy Doctor, had admired and placed his faith in the Buddhist scriptures since his youth. He provided commentaries on many sutras and śāstras. During the Tiānjiā era of the Chen dynasty, he was appointed as the Magistrate of Shàn.
In the fourth year of the Dàjiàn era, he was summoned to serve as the Secretariat Vice-Director but did not accept the appointment.

Amidst the chaos caused by Hóu Jǐng, he sold his wife to support his mother; he maintained a vegetarian diet, observed perpetual fasting, and upheld the Bodhisattva precepts. The imperial palace was frequently plagued by ghosts and strange phenomena, yet Xu...
He occupied the position [of Administrator of the Southern Capital]. Malevolent omens and transformations all ceased. After the fall of the Chen dynasty, he entered Chang’an.

Emperor Wen, having heard of his reputation and conduct, summoned him to the Hall of the Ministry of Personnel (*Shangshu Dutang*) to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This was in the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era. He passed away at the age of seventy-three.

At the time of his death, he recited the Buddha’s name; a wondrous fragrance filled the room, leaving neighbors and villagers in awe. The histories record that Xu Xiaokeng was a man of filial piety. [This was written by] Xu Ling.
His younger brother was naturally filial. He left the household life and changed his name to Fazheng (as recorded in the *Shouchi guobao*).
According to the *Sui Shu*, he was born into the Xun family and resided in Wangli Village, forty li west of Xinpan County in Yizhou. His conduct was always humble and reclusive;
no one knew of his inner qualities. Once, on a vacant plot of land to the east of the village, he gazed into the distance toward the void and wrote characters in the air with his hand.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Consequently, various devas, nāgas, and spirits manifested their protection over a space of about one *zhang* at this site;
even when it rained, the ground remained dry, as if covered by a roof. Several cowherd boys used this spot to take shelter from the rain.

During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a strange monk said to the villagers: "In the air above this place, someone has written the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The various devas have established..."
A jeweled canopy was placed above it; it must not be defiled or treated with irreverence. From then on, a railing was erected to surround it for the worship of the Buddha image.
On every fast day, people from near and far set out offerings and recited the sutras, constantly hearing the sound of celestial music that resounded throughout the region.

According to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, its essence is identical to empty space. When people of the world transcribe the sutra, they mostly do so because their thoughts are moved by the prospect of meritorious retribution. Xunzi once wrote upon the air.
The Sūtra clarifies that this is a model for understanding emptiness: writing without writing, which is what is meant by "writing without abiding in signs.
Realization comes from the inconceivable realm of empty space, evoking precious canopies and celestial music;
such merit is likewise inconceivable (from the *Sanbao gantong ji*).
During the Sui dynasty, Mu Yan-tong served as the magistrate of Wulao County. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten scrolls daily.

When Li Mi’s rebellion broke out, people wished to kill him so that he might join the righteous banners. Yan-tong then threw himself down from the city wall; the rebels drew their blades and pressed him toward execution.
There was a deep ravine ahead, so he leaped into it. In the air, he saw the Vajra Deity, who caught Yan-tong’s arm with his hand and placed him upon a stone platter.
Upon the stone, there was not a single mark of injury. He called out, "I have been moved by your recitation of the sutras; therefore, I have come to save you.
Yan Tong returned home, and a wondrous fragrance emanated from his right arm for several days without fading. Later, he rose to the rank of Fangbo (a high provincial official).

One day, while free from illness, he requested a brush to write a verse and passed away after bathing. The verse said: "Eighty-nine years spent in this world, I have performed my daily work with my own body."
I reckon that today one must let go and proceed; then the bright moon and clear wind are at one's disposal. Maogong Qi said: "Today the stroke of death continues in succession;
human life is like a single thread. Both I and Yizhi are merely playing with a blade of grass atop the tip of an arrow."
At this time, those who hear of these causes and effects should swiftly make vows and engage in recitation;

they should take the hell of weapons and warfare as a bridge to liberation, lest they reach a state where there is no recourse, crying out in bitter pain and grievance (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Du Zhiliang of the Sui dynasty served as a military aide in the retinue of Prince Liang of Han during the Renshou era.

Later, when Liang raised troops in Bingzhou and was defeated in rebellion, Zhiliang and his subordinates were all imprisoned. Weeping and wailing day and night, he suddenly dreamed one night of a monk who said:
"You need only recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; this calamity can be overcome. At dawn, he took the sūtra and practiced its recitation with single-minded devotion.

When the executioner led the crowd to the place of execution and the executioner called out their names, everyone was to die except for Wuliang’s name; consequently, the executioner was held accountable and punished.
Soon thereafter, he was pardoned. During the Xianqing era, he died while serving as the Prefect of Huangzhou. How extraordinary!
When Sengliang was about to be executed by decapitation, his name suddenly vanished, and he transformed from a headless ghost into an indestructible body.
This was because his single-minded sincerity surpassed mere verbal recitation. To witness his shackles and chains fall away of their own accord is even more marvelous (from the *Taiping guangji*).

Xiao Yu of the Sui dynasty was the great-grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang. Having entered the service of the Sui, he served as Grand Secretary of the Chancellery and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Song. His daughter became the Empress Dowager.

Xiao Yu was a devout believer in the Buddha-dharma and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Consequently, due to his opposition to the Emperor’s plan to invade Goguryeo, he incurred the sovereign’s displeasure.
He was confined together with He Ruo-bi and Gao Jing, and [the Emperor] intended to place him under the law. For eight days, Yu recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven hundred times.
On the following day, his shackles suddenly fell off by themselves. The guards turned pale with fear;

when he was led back to be bound again before the Hall, Yu alone received pardon, while Bi and Jing were both severely punished. Consequently, Yu composed the "Eighteen Accounts of the Miraculous Efficacy of the *Prajñā*" and built [a shrine].

A three-foot sandalwood stupa was used to store the scriptures. According to the records, Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, knowing that Yu was fond of Buddhism, once presented him with a single embroidered Buddha image, with an embroidered portrait of Yu placed at its side.

He also bestowed upon him the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* transcribed by Wang Biao, along with a monastic robe for use in lecturing and recitation. Furthermore, the Emperor once remarked of Yu: "He cannot be enticed by profit, nor can he be coerced by death."
This is the power of the Vajra-samādhi (from the *Baoying ji*).
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the śramaṇa Fazang resided at Baoshi Monastery in Fuzhou.

Pure by nature and ancient in his conduct, while he was in Luochuan County, he constructed monastic buildings; having sold his robes and alms bowl, he erected two halls and transcribed eight [volumes of] scriptures.
[His collection] comprised over one hundred fascicles. In the second month of the second year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, he fell ill.

During a state of deep sleep, he saw a Vajra deity holding a single fascicle of a sutra, who said: "Because you built a temple and transcribed scriptures, you have incurred the sin of 'interchanging' [resources].

I now bestow upon you this one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. If you can indeed copy it with a sincere heart and circulate, read, and recite it, the sin of interchanging will be entirely extinguished."
Soon his illness was cured. He then sold all his possessions to copy one hundred scrolls of sutras and cultivate various meritorious deeds, never again entangling himself in worldly affairs.
Reaching the age of ninety-nine, on the fifteenth day of the first month, he invited the assembly to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, each for seven volumes.
Sitting upright, he wrote a verse and addressed the great assembly, saying: "This year I am ninety-nine; look, there is nothing at all."

Do not ask further how it was; it was as if performing a somersault through empty space. At once, both monastics and laypeople alike beheld the emanation of Amitābha Buddha receiving them and leading them to rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

According to the account, when Zhang Andao had finished copying the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and deposited it at Mount Jinshan, he was reborn in a later generation and perceived it as having been his own writing.
When Dongpo requested that Gong complete the transcription, he preserved it as a family treasure. Dongpo himself wrote one scroll.

They were hidden within the mountains. Such was the power of aspiration of the ancients who transcribed the scriptures. Furthermore, the law of cause and effect within the Buddha-dharma is even more rigorous than that of worldly laws;
as it is said, "one may not purchase tiles with money earned from bricks. Since these are all wholesome dharmas, one must not err regarding them.
How much more so for unwholesome dharmas! Formerly, the monk Baoming of Lingjue Monastery claimed that before he left the household life, he had served as the Governor of Longxi.

Upon completing the construction of Lingjue Monastery, he immediately abandoned his office to enter the Way. Although he did not engage in meditation or recitation, he was never remiss in his prostrations.
After his death, the King of the Netherworld rebuked him, saying: "When you served as governor, you perverted justice and violated the law, plundering from the people."

Wealth. Although you have built Buddhist temples, it was not by your own power. Examining this case together, there are many in the world who claim their own acts are meritorious, yet ultimately they become evil karmic results.
This is certainly not limited to building temples or copying scriptures; there is the sin of misappropriating funds (as recorded in the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*).

During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, Su Renqin, a wealthy man of Chang’an, indulged his whims in slaughtering and roasting living beings. Those who were killed filed complaints with the underworld authorities, who then summoned his soul and imprisoned it.
Renqin suffered from a severe illness for many years and died prematurely as his allotted lifespan was diminished. The King of the Netherworld spoke thus:

"Because you cultivated merit in your previous life, you enjoyed wealth and abundance in this present existence. However, because you have now committed the grave karma of unrestrained slaughter, you shall receive this retribution."
"You must repay [your debt]. He was immediately driven to the Mountain of Knives and the Forest of Swords. In his terror and distress, he pleaded for mercy, saying:

"In my life, although I have not performed any good deeds, I once requested a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. I gave it to the late monk Shenjing of Anguo Temple, who received and upheld it."

Although the monk had passed away, he could be taken as a witness. After a short while, a fragrant incense scent wafted through the air, and a monk appeared holding a scripture and arrived at the hall.
He said, "I have long practiced the recitation and upholding of this with you; it possesses the merit of Prajñā. The King then joined his palms and released him, whereby he was able to be reborn.

Because he had sponsored the printing and distribution of one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and one thousand fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and had performed the Great Water-Land Repentance (*shuilu daizhai*) to deliver sentient beings, his deceased father, Wenzhong, suddenly appeared to him in a dream one night and said: "I was wealthy but lacked benevolence; I killed living beings and took their lives.

In my old age, I fell into a latrine, and upon death, I was cast into hell. Because you have cultivated merit on my behalf, I have been reborn in the celestial realms" (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, Chen Zhao, a native of Jiangling, observed the fasts and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, accumulating merit through his practice.
A large python would appear daily by his side; once the recitation was finished, it would withdraw. A neighbor, Li Chang, was known for his fierce and violent nature.

He suspected it was a demon and struck it down, killing it. The snake appealed to the underworld authorities, who summoned Li Chang to suffer the punishment of having his body entwined by snakes that bit him.
Thereupon, he appeared in a dream to his wife and said, "The snake wished to hear one hundred scrolls of the sutras so that it might ascend to heaven; it lacked only seven scrolls.
I killed it by mistake, and now I am suffering this calamity. Quickly invite a monk to transcribe seven scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for me to perform repentance."

"Save me! My wife is so impoverished she cannot do it. She had a five-year-old son named Saṃgharakṣita, who saw his mother weeping in sorrow and said to her, "Why not sell the child to save your father?
The mother then took the boy out to the market and sold him to a traveler from Shu for two strings of cash.

She requested that a monk copy a scripture and offered prayers to the Triple Gem, making two vows: first, that her deceased husband’s sins might be extinguished; second, that she and her son might be reunited.

Feng then became blind from missing his son. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* daily while begging for alms in the marketplace. His son had followed a traveler to Shu, where he remained for thirty years;
subsequently, both his adoptive parents passed away. Suddenly remembering his birth mother, he returned to Jiangling to search for her, but she was nowhere to be seen.
He purchased a house for temporary residence. Coinciding with the winter solstice festival, he performed ancestral rites, praying: "I was unfortunate to lose my father in childhood;
my mother sold me to offer sacrifices for him. Now that I seek my mother, she has left no trace. I pray that both parents may together transcend the Three Realms.

Just then, his mother arrived at the hall seeking alms. Hearing these words, she cried out loudly, "I am your mother! The deed of sale from those years is still in my possession at my current dwelling. She pointed toward a basket.

Internally, he embraced his mother and wept bitterly; he burned incense and prostrated before Heaven; he drew water to rinse his mouth and licked his mother’s eyes with it, whereupon both her left and right sides became clear (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
Ren Yifang of Le'an, who served as the Prefectural Governor of Kuozhou during the Tang dynasty, died several days ago and subsequently revived.
He stated that he was led into an audience with the King (Yama), who ordered him to be escorted to observe the hells; these were no different from those described in the Buddhist scriptures.
The underground was pitch black throughout the night, as if one were walking through a mist. Because Yifang had maintained a sense of righteousness and integrity, there was a warm breath in the air;
he immediately requested a monk to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. From beneath the ground, Yifang heard the sound of the sutra recitation faintly. The King inspected his case.

He said to the official, "His lifespan has not yet expired; why did you mistakenly pursue him? He was then released and sent back home. His escort said, "Just follow the sound of the sutras and you will arrive at your house.
Suddenly, they saw a great pit in the middle of the road. Intending to leap over it, he fell into the pit. At that very moment, he rose up again.
Having returned to life, he spoke about the hells and drew a map of them on the ground. All the stipends and emoluments he received...
He commissioned the production of scriptures and images and invited monks to transcribe more than one thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Maozong Qi said:

"If the sound of the scriptures issues from the mouths of the monks, one will immediately pass through the Ghost Gate Barrier; if the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is taken up by the faithful mind, the seeds of birth and death will be forever severed" (from the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Zhao Wenxin, a native of Suzhou during the Tang dynasty, died suddenly in the first year of the Zhenguan era. After three days, he revived and said:
"When I first died, I was driven along by others. Ten companions followed me as we went to the abode of King Yama. Among them was one monk."
The King first asked, "What meritorious deeds did you practice while in the world? He replied, "I did nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King rose, joined his palms, and said, "Master, you were destined for heaven; why have you come here by mistake? Before he had finished speaking, a celestial robe suddenly descended from above.
The guide led him upward into the heavens. The King called Wenxin back and questioned him. He replied, "In my life, I have never read Buddhist scriptures;
I only took pleasure in the writings of Yu Xin. The King said, "Yu Xin is a person of great sin who is currently undergoing punishment here.
Do you recognize him? Wenxin answered that although he had read his writings, he did not know the man himself. The King then ordered that Xin be brought out. Thereupon—
It was a tortoise. Following the command, it was led away. After a short while, it returned in human form and said: "In my previous life, I delighted in composing literary works.
I falsely cited Buddhist scriptures and intermingled them with secular texts. Furthermore, I slandered the Buddha-dharma, claiming it did not equal the teachings of Confucius and Laozi.
Because of this evil retribution, I am unable to escape this state; I have been reborn as a tortoise. I shall relate this in detail for you. He recounted it all for the man.
Regarding this matter: Tian Ji, the Magistrate of Fugou during the Tang dynasty, had been deceased for over a year when he appeared in a dream to his wife and said:

"During my lifetime, I was fortunate enough to pass the imperial examinations. Relying on my own talent and brilliance, I recklessly criticized and refuted the writings of the sages and philosophers of antiquity.
When I encountered the renowned scholars of my time, they pointed out my shortcomings. Now that I am beneath the earth, every day two snakes and three centipedes come and go [to torment me]."
Passing through the agonizing pains of the seven apertures, one must wait a full three hundred and sixty days before finally attaining rebirth.
Thus, if one does not eliminate the karma of the mouth, what benefit is there in reciting the sutras? (From the Fayuan zhulin).

Sima Qiaoqing, a *sishizhi* of the Ministry of Justice during the Tang dynasty, was by nature pure and prudent and possessed noble character and conduct. During the Yonghui era, he served as the *sihu cao* (Accountant) of Yangzhou.
When his mother passed away, he emaciated himself through mourning until he was reduced to a mere skeleton. He drew blood to transcribe two fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Just as he finished, he suddenly saw two *zhicao* (fungus/herb) growing beside the grave; on the ninth day, they had grown to one chi and eight cun in height, with green stalks and crimson caps.
One *sheng* of its juice was distilled daily; its flavor was as sweet as honey, and once taken, it would grow back again (*from the Fayuan zhulin*).

Chen Wenda of the Tang dynasty was a native of Qi County. He constantly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it eighty-four thousand times for the sake of his deceased parents, during which he frequently witnessed auspicious omens.
When he recited the sutra on behalf of others, all their illnesses and calamities were averted. There was also Chen Yue of Tongshan.
He once followed [the deceased] to the underworld and saw a platform built beneath the earth, which was labeled: "This is the Prajñā Platform, awaiting Chen Wenda.
Such was the reverence he received from the offices of the netherworld. In the *Zhuchuang suibi* (Random Notes from the Bamboo Window) of Yunqi, it is said: "I was born late;

I had only just begun to hear the Buddha-dharma when the sorrow of the wind-blown tree and the withered wood [the death of my parents] already arrived. Though I wished to follow after them, there was no way to do so. I offer this exhortation."

Worldly people, while their parents are still living at home, should early on encourage them to recite the Buddha’s name; when their parents pass away, they should recite the sutras to repay their kindness (from the Fayuan zhulin).
During the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, Bai Renzhe served as the Magistrate of Zhuyang in Guozhou. While transporting rice to Liaodong, he encountered a violent gale at sea;
the four quarters became pitch black. Renzhe burned incense and urgently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

After only a few recitations, he suddenly felt as if he were dreaming and saw a monk from India in the sky who said to him, "Because you have recited the true scripture, I have come to save you. You must..."
The wind suddenly subsided, and more than eighty people were all saved (from the *Baoying ji*).

Chen Libin of Huiji during the Tang dynasty was a man who passed the examinations at the age of twenty. He was skilled in composing poetry and prose. Upon shedding his plain clothes, he was appointed as the Magistrate of Changcheng.

In his youth, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Whenever he encountered misfortune, he frequently received its protection. During the Kaiyuan era, Bin was traveling from the River of Kuaiji to Dongyang.
It had rained heavily for a long time, and the river waters were overflowing. More than twenty boats were traveling together, catching the wind and hoisting their sails.
In an instant, the sky grew dark and the wind grew fierce; they reached the Jieshi Cavern, where the current flowed violently upstream and downstream, and the waves crashed against them. Not...
They managed to reach the mooring. The twenty-odd boats ahead had all been wrecked at the mouth of the Ditch. The sailors were terrified and at their wits' end.

Li Bin hurriedly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the swift current, a creature resembling a red dragon suddenly emerged and propped up the boat, enabling them to get ashore.
Everyone attributed this to the merit of his recitation (from the *Guang yi ji*).
Tang Yuanchu was a native of Jiujiang. He sold firewood in the market and was seventy years old. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

One evening, as he was returning from the north bank of the river, a great storm of wind and waves arose in midstream. Everyone on the same boat perished, yet Yuanchu alone floated upon the water and drifted to the south bank.
Those who had moored their boats there were all prominent merchants; seeing a light several feet high emanating from Yuanchu’s back, they suspected he was a person of noble station.
They vied with one another to leave him their clothing and food, only then realizing he was a village elder.

They questioned him about his origins, and he said, "I have been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for fifty years. That which was on his back was the scripture itself (from the *Tàipíng guǎngjì*).

Tang Wangling was a man of noble reputation who, from his youth, had maintained the practice of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. While returning to Linxi in Qiongzhou, he encountered a path of extreme danger and obstruction.
Suddenly, he was confronted by a fierce beast; he hurriedly recited this sūtra, whereupon the beast stared at him intently and then slithered away with its tail trailing.

He later served as a subordinate magistrate in Anzhou. Once, while crossing the Yangtze River, a violent storm arose at night. Although hundreds of ships were moored side-by-side, they all sank; only Wangling’s vessel remained afloat.

Complete. Later, he served as the Magistrate of Qiao in Bozhou. Having read this, he realized that the gale winds could not destroy him, the great floods could not submerge him, and the fierce beasts could not harm him;
thus he beheld the reality of being neither startled nor terrified (from the *Baoying ji*).
Wei Xun of the Tang dynasty was the son of Shangde, the Left Attendant-in-Ordinary. He upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At the beginning of the Shengong era, he served as a General of the Jianmen Guard. At that time, there was a man in the capital named Cai Ce who died suddenly and only revived after several days.

He said that when he first arrived at the Office of the Netherworld, the officials could not find those they were pursuing and were about to flog their messengers. The messengers replied, "General Wei upholds..."

The Diamond Sutra was protected by benevolent deities; though they pursued him, they could not catch him. The officials then dispatched messengers separately to pursue him again, but upon their return a moment later, the report was identical.
The underworld official said, "Cease the pursuit for now. When Xuun heard this, he redoubled his diligent practice (from the *Guang yiji*).

Tang Wangtu served as a *guoyi* (commander) of the Eagle-Flight Command (*Yingyang Fu*). Due to illness, he abstained from meat and wine and resolved to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* five times daily.
Later, when he contracted a malarial fever, he saw a host of ghosts approaching; upon hearing the sound of Wangtu reciting the sutra, they retreated, calling out from afar:
The King ordered that you be pursued and commanded you to cease reciting the sutras. Da-xie, all the ghosts moved forward toward him; he then fell into a stupor, nearly losing consciousness.
After a short while, another ghost arrived and said, "O reciter of the sutras, the King has granted you a temporary reprieve for six months.

Upon regaining his senses, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation, never ceasing from dawn until dusk. When the six months had passed, the ghosts became silent. At night, he heard voices in the air.
A voice called out, saying: "By virtue of your recitation of this sutra, you shall live for ninety years. In the end, it accorded exactly with that number (*from the Taiping Guangji*).
During the Tianbao era, at the beginning of the Tang dynasty, the Military Commissioner of Yizhou, Tian, was habituated to keeping hawks and dogs and made hunting his primary pursuit.
While releasing a hawk in the forests and thorn thickets of Yizhou, he saw a single scroll of a book, which was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He then resolved to take up its recitation.
Several years passed, and he had recited [the scripture] more than two thousand times. Yet he continued to hunt as before. Later, he fell ill and died suddenly.

Upon arriving at the Underworld (Difù), he saw various birds and beasts circling an area of several mu, clamoring for his life. The King asked why his transgressions were so numerous. Tian was unable to answer.
Consequently, he was sent to the Bureau of Officials for interrogation. There were ten of his companions there; the officials ordered them to open their mouths and gave each a pill of medicine.
He threw it into his mouth, whereupon a fierce fire immediately arose, burning his entire body until he was charred and mangled. In an instant, he was reduced to ashes;

yet, in a moment, he was restored to human form. This occurred six or seven times. When it came to Tian Shi, however, although he swallowed three pellets, no sign of fire appeared. The official found this strange and led him again before the King.
He related in detail how he had previously enjoyed hunting and how he had once obtained a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from atop a thorn tree in Yizhou, and had recited it twice.
He recited it more than a thousand times. The King said, "This alone shall extinguish all sins. He ordered his attendants to examine the registers of merit, and indeed it was as had been reported.
Consequently, the King commanded him to recite it again. When he had only finished three sheets of the scripture, the birds and beasts in the courtyard suddenly vanished.

He was then released and returned home; furthermore, his life span was extended by fifteen years. This shows that even if a worldly person observes the precept against killing for but a single day, they will obtain the merit of that very day.
There is nothing to do but wait for karma to exhaust itself; yet the resentment of past deeds remains as it was before.
Only by upholding the sutras can one bring enmity to rest in the past and plant seeds of wholesome fruit for the future—this brings great benefit (as recorded in the *Guang yi ji*).
Li Qiuyi of the Tang dynasty was fond of hawks, dogs, and hunting. In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, while serving as the Assistant Magistrate of Gaoyou, he suddenly died a violent death.
He saw two men come to pursue him; one said his surname was Duan. Among those being pursued together with him were over a hundred men and women.
Once Qiu was placed in shackles and led forward, they traveled for some ten li before seeing several dozen large locust trees with horse troughs beneath them.
Duan said, "The Great Deity of the Five Paths inspects the good and evil of the human world; he stops his horse here. At this, Qiu finally realized that he was dead.
Upon reaching the gate of the King, Duan pointed to an official and said, "This man is surnamed Jiao and named Ce; he is the one commissioned to carry out the public duties."

The matter was thus brought before the King for an audience. The King said, "You have committed the karma of killing; now you suddenly see the birds and beasts you slaughtered all speaking in human voices, begging for an early judgment.
Qiu Jin replied, "I am not yet fit to die; I once produced one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King said, "In the underworld, the *Vajracchedikā* is known as the supreme merit. He immediately ordered him led toward the scripture repository.
He personally verified this. Upon arriving at a palace hall filled with various scriptures, Qiu reached out with one hand and drew forth a single scroll; it was indeed the text he had composed.

When he turned back and saw the King, [he saw] the living beings who had been killed seeking to perform meritorious deeds. Qiu made a single vow: "Transcribe one hundred scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Everyone rejoiced and dispersed. The King said, "Release them. As Ce led them out of the city, he remarked, "If such is the result of his utmost effort, what more could be expected?"
He repaid him by saying, "I have already granted you three hundred thousand coins. [The monk] would not accept them, saying, "I shall use them to produce twenty copies of the scriptures.
When they reached a pit, Jiao Ce pushed him; he was subsequently revived. He had been inside the coffin for three days, hearing only the sound of wailing.

Startled, he called out for people to come, and they broke open the coffin so he could emerge. Within ten days, he had transcribed twenty scrolls of scripture. Jiao Ce came again to express his gratitude. Shortly thereafter—

The hundred fascicles were also completed. The Regional Inspector of Yangzhou memorialized the matter to the throne. By imperial decree, Qiu was granted the rank of the fifth grade and appointed as the Commissioner for the Pacification of Jia Prefecture (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
During the Xuantian era of the Tang dynasty, Cui Wenjian served as the Sima of Fangzhou. At that time, the Tufan suddenly arrived and he was among those driven off and plundered.
His shackles were very secure, yet after he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with single-minded devotion for three days, the locks suddenly opened of their own accord.

The Tufan suspected treachery and beat him severely, but when he related the facts exactly as they were, they re-shackled him. Before his recitation was even finished, the locks opened again, leaving everyone in awe and wonder.
He was subsequently sent out of the country. Formerly, Mr. Liu Anshi once took up the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and said to his disciple Ma Yongqing:
"The Great Being Avalokiteśvara’s nature of sound is perfectly penetrating; by turning the faculties of hearing and seeing back upon themselves, he is free from all defilements and delusions.

He can cause sentient beings to be such that fetters, shackles, and locks cannot adhere to them. This means that when a person attains the power of fearlessness, then fetters and locks cannot [bind them]."
This is harmful. My friend may use this principle to instruct others, so that future generations do not come to slander the Buddha.
Yuancheng was a disciple who studied under Sima Wen Gong; his words were such as these, which can open the eyes of those with conventional learning.
(From the *Taiping Guangji*).

During the reign of Empress Wu, Wu Sixuan of the Tang dynasty served as a *boshi* (lecturer) at the Imperial Academy. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twice daily and experienced many miraculous responses.
While he was ill in the capital, there was a sorcerer named Chu Xier who prayed under the stars; his pronouncements were as accurate as those of a god.
Sīxuán went to visit him, and the young boy was startled, saying, "What arts do you possess? When ghosts see you, they all flee.

Sīxuán realized this was due to the power of the scripture and redoubled his diligent practice, reciting it five times every day. When the boy’s illness proved incurable by physicians, Sīxuán arrived;
after three days of mental recitation of the scripture, the boy recovered. Furthermore, he once saw an old man at the Weiqiao Bridge whose beard and hair were white, wearing coarse...
Wearing mourning clothes, he asked him about this in astonishment. He replied, "It was for my biological mother.
He then related that when his mother was forty-three years old, a strange monk instructed her, saying, "Do you wish for long life? Simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

His mother resolved her mind accordingly and recited it twice daily until she reached the age of one hundred and seven. Her maternal aunt and a neighbor’s mother also recited it and both exceeded one hundred years of age. I have followed my mother’s instruction.
He was already ninety years of age (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

Lü Wenzhan of the Tang dynasty served as the County Vice-Magistrate of Langzhong during the third year of the Kaiyuan era. He had a refined appreciation for Buddhist scriptures and devoted his mind particularly to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reaching more than thirty thousand recitations.
His spiritual responses were extraordinary and miraculous. As he grew old and his vigor declined, three fangs [appeared on his upper lip].
His teeth fell out, yet suddenly grew back as they were before. While he was in Langzhong, it was a time of severe drought;

the Prefect Liu Jun ordered him to pray for rain, and after reciting [the scripture] only once, a copious downpour was obtained. Later, during a period of heavy rains and flooding, the Vice-Governor again ordered him to chant the sutras to pray for clear weather, and the skies cleared immediately.
Such verifications of his efficacy occurred both before and after, and cannot be cited in their entirety (from the *Taiping guangji*).

During the Tang dynasty, while Liu Yihuai was in Bianzhou, Han Hong served as the Right Chamber Commander-in-Chief (youxiang yuhou), and Wang Shi served as the Left Chamber Commander-in-Chief (zuoxiang yuhou).
The two were on very good terms. Some people remarked that the two men were seizing military influence and would eventually act against Liu’s interests. Liu became greatly incensed.
He summoned them for interrogation. Hong was indeed Liu’s nephew. He struck the ground and smashed his head, shouting with great intensity; Liu’s suspicions were somewhat dispelled.

Wang, being elderly, trembled in his thighs and could not defend himself. Liu shouted at him and struck him thirty times with a staff. At that time, new red clubs had been manufactured, with heads several inches in diameter.
The staff was firmly bound with sinews and lacquer; had he received it, he would have surely died. Daohong went to his house in the dark to investigate, but there was no sound of weeping.
He further remarked that the man must have been afraid and did not dare to cry. Daohong entered straight into the inner chamber, yet Wang remained entirely unharmed.

He said, "I have read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for forty years, and only now do I truly derive its power. When I was first struck by the staff, I saw a giant hand, as large as a winnowing basket, suddenly expand and shield my back."
He bared his chest to show it to Han; there were no marks from the lash at all. Although Senghong was not fond of Buddhism, from that time on he associated with monks.

Every day he personally transcribed ten sheets of scripture, accumulating a total of several hundred fascicles. Later, while serving in the Secretariat during the height of summer, an official of the Censorate came to visit him on business.

Senghong was then perspiring profusely as he transcribed scriptures. The official asked him about this in surprise, whereupon Senghong related the matter concerning Wang Shao in detail. (Source: *Guang Hongming Ji*)

The Case of Chen Zhe of Lin’an during the Tang Dynasty. Chen Zhe was a resident of Yuhang who refined his conduct through single-minded devotion and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At the beginning of the Guǎngdé era, the Wukang rebel Song Tan raided Yuhang. Chen Zhe was wealthy and intended to move his household to avoid the danger, but the rebels soon arrived.
Zhe thought these were government troops and asked how near or far the rebels were. The rebels became enraged and cried, "What kind of old slave dares to insult us?

They vied with one another to stab him with their swords. Yet, with every stroke of a sword, a five-colored circular light, five or six feet in diameter, shielded Zhe’s body so that they could not strike him.
The rebels were struck with wonder, lamented their shame, and departed (from the *Guang yiji*).
During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Su Lang, a vice magistrate of Wugong in Jingzhao, upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
For many years, his entire household of over fifty members had maintained a vegetarian diet. His wife, Lady Cui, also recited this sūtra.

A relative, seeing that she had reduced her food intake due to illness, urged her to temporarily lift her prohibition against meat. She consequently purchased mutton and ate it; however, as soon as a single slice had entered her mouth, it suddenly transformed into—
The bones became stuck in her throat; she could neither swallow them nor expel them. At dusk, her breath ceased, but because her body remained warm, she was not yet encoffined.

On the sixth day, she revived and said: "The King of the Netherworld declared, 'Your husband is a great Bodhisattva. Because you ate meat, the Vajra-Devas transformed the flesh into bones to admonish you.
You were destined to live to the age of seventy, but because you have upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, [your life has been extended]."

Now [the number] increased to ninety, and he was released and returned home. The man consequently felt remorse and repentance, never committing the offense again. When the Emperor heard of this, he personally annotated the scriptural text and circulated it throughout the world.
According to records, in the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Emperor Xuanzong, he personally annotated the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Zhang Jiuling, the Chief Secretary of the Secretariat, and others requested that an imperial preface be issued for circulation both within and outside the palace. The Emperor replied in a handwritten edict: "Coincidentally..."
Being deeply moved, he recorded what he had witnessed. He now requests that this be distributed;

yet, fearing it may not yet be entirely satisfactory, he has requested that the monk-in-charge Enyou prepare banners and flowers to welcome [the image] at Jing’ai Temple, so as to demonstrate it to the world and entrust it to the Historiographic Office. This was granted.
Could this not have been due to the incident involving Su Wugong? (From *The Retribution of Upholding [the Sūtras]*).
In the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued that all Buddhist halls throughout the realm that were small should be demolished;

their religious merit (puṇya) was to be transferred to nearby monasteries. At once, officials looked to the wind of the decree and sought its favor; even large buildings and great statues suffered destruction.

When the edict reached Yuzhou, Li Xu, the Magistrate of Xinxixian, was addicted to wine and stubbornly intoxicated. Upon the arrival of the provincial mandate, he was ordered to complete the task within three days.

On that day, Xu Jian was greatly enraged; he immediately summoned the local officials and decreed that anyone who demolished [the structure] would be put to death. Thus, the entire boundary remained intact. Over a year later, Xu Jian died of illness during the hot season.
He was encoffined overnight, and on the following day, when they were about to carry him to the burial site, his mother and son circled the coffin wailing.

After a long time had passed, they heard a sound like fingernails or claws scratching against the coffin from within. It grew increasingly intense for a moment, whereupon the wife and son fled in terror, while the mother remained alone.
He did not go. He immediately ordered the coffin to be opened. His attendants said, "It is the height of the humid summer; we fear it will be ruined.
His mother grew angry and urged him to open it, and he was found empty. His body was quite mangled and festering. After bathing and nursing him for over a month, Xu said:

"When I was first seized and brought before the King, the King was not present. I saw an official at the foot of the steps; he was the magistrate of Xinxi, though he had been dead for years. Seeing me, he bowed."

He asked the official, "How did you come to be here? Xu replied, "I was summoned. The officer said, "The official has long been prone to killing and harm; you were unaware of the retribution for sin and merit.
Now that you receive this retribution, what can be done? Xu, filled with panic and fear, begged for rescue.

The officer said, "Within your jurisdiction, the Buddhist hall alone remains intact. Because of this great merit, although you are dead, it is not appropriate for you to be apprehended here. In a short while, simply—"
While Xu was thus confronted and beginning to recall past events, the official led him before the King. The King ordered that the registers of good and evil deeds be brought forth.
Immediately, someone arrived carrying a large case, as thick as the trunk of a tree. The King commanded the document to be opened and the offenses to be proclaimed.

A court clerk read from it: "He was particularly fond of cutting off the hooves of sheep. The clerk stated, "He deserves one hundred strokes of the cane, and furthermore, his [feet] shall be cut off."
"One hundred jin of my own flesh. The King said, "Agreed. Xu said, "Last year there was an imperial edict to demolish Buddhist halls and Buddha images;
within my jurisdiction alone, they remain intact. Can this be counted as an offense? The King asked in surprise, "Is it truly so? An official from Xinxi stepped forward and said:

There is a register of merit in heaven. The King ordered his officials to ascend to the southern tower of the palace courtyard to retrieve it, but they had not yet returned when two monks arrived before the hall.
The King asked the masters what they possessed. One replied, "I have often recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The other replied, "I have often read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King rose, joined his palms, and invited the Dharma Master to ascend the steps. Behind the King’s throne, to the right, was [a golden...].
[The two monks] sat down; the one on the left sat upon a silver seat. The King requested that the reciter sit upon a golden seat and the reader sit upon a silver seat.
As they were about to finish reciting and reading the sutra, suddenly clouds of five colors appeared before the golden seat, and purple clouds appeared before the silver seat.

The two monks mounted the clouds and flew away into the sky, whereupon they vanished. The King said to those below the steps, "Did you see the two monks? They have all been reborn in heaven. At that time...

The officials brought forth the registers of merit. There was but a single sheet, which they read aloud: "By imperial decree, the Buddhist halls were to be destroyed fifteen years ago; yet the entire county of Xinxi alone remained intact.
This shall cancel the sins of one lifetime and extend your life by thirty years, and you shall be reborn in a realm of goodness.

As soon as he finished speaking, fire issued from within the register of sins and consumed it entirely. The King commanded two officials to escort him back. As they exited through the south city gate, they saw that both sides of the road were filled with...

There were tall buildings and large mansions where men and women sat together, drinking and singing to the accompaniment of flutes and songs; they enjoyed the empty splendor of string and wind instruments and took pleasure in them.

An official said to him, "Pass by this quickly and do not look back; if you look back, you will surely suffer harm. He stood there for a while gazing at them, when a person inside the shop called out:
The official said, "This is no pleasant place. Since you do not believe me, let him go as he pleases. Xu, still unawakened, reached the drinking hall;
when everyone rose and took their seats, music was played on string and wind instruments. When the wine was served, it turned out to be a cup of excrement, foul and loathsome beyond measure.
Xu refused to drink it, whereupon a bull-headed hell-warden emerged from beneath the bed and impaled him through the chest with a fork.
Xu drank several cups and then departed. An official led him southward into a small path through a desolate field.
From afar, he saw a lamp glowing brightly; beside it was a great pit, pitch-black and bottomless. The official pushed him into it, whereupon he revived.

Originally, Li Xu had been by nature fierce and obstinate, ignorant of both sin and merit; yet because he had violated propriety while intoxicated, he instead preserved the Buddha hall. This is the origin of the story.

This was not because they had conceived views regarding the Buddha; nevertheless, they were still reborn in heaven and their registers of sins were consumed by fire. Is this not the retribution for protecting the Dharma?

If one can diligently perform prostrations and recitations day and night, upholding the monastic discipline while simultaneously performing Buddhist services, yet fail to escape birth and death, such a thing has never occurred.
As for why these two monks were reborn in heaven—was it not because their recitation of the sutras surpassed that of those who merely read them?
"Reciting" means on one's back; there is no scripture before one’s eyes, and the mind becomes increasingly tranquil (from the *Jiwen*).

During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Wu Kui, a man from Yixing in Changzhou, would daily at the fifth watch recite the seven fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before a Buddha image, prostrating and reciting the Buddha’s name.
He had a poem that said: "When the bell strikes at the fifth watch, do not greedily linger in sleep; shake yourself awake..."

With his spirit directed toward the Buddha, he performed one prostration for each recitation of "Namu Amitābha Buddha. He had already planted a single lotus in the Flower Pond. When he reached the age of ninety-two, he passed away without illness.

Summoned to appear before the King of the Underworld, he recounted his life from youth to old age, specifically how he had devoted himself to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The King joined his palms and bade him sit. Kui then recited the entire scroll aloud; when he reached the passage concerning the Kingdom of Śrāvastī, his mouth— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
From within [the stupa], a wondrous fragrance immediately issued forth, and the Buddha was seen manifesting. The king rejoiced and said, "You possess the power of *prajñā*.

He issued an edict to send him to live in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. There he served as a high-ranking official; he enjoyed wealth and nobility, and his blessings extended to his descendants. When Dui passed by his former house, he announced to his children from the air:
"By the power of this sutra, I have been reborn in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. You all should receive and uphold the Vajra Dharma."
Flowers. The underworld authorities deeply revere these two sutras. If you are unable to receive and uphold them, you may instead offer them respectful worship with various flowers and incense;
thus you shall obtain immeasurable merit. Furthermore, be most careful not to kill living beings; by being able to release captive creatures, you will receive the reward of longevity.
When his children heard this, they wept bitterly, saying, "Do not be so distressed. In the world of men, there is at least one good deed upon which one can rely when life comes to an end."
"It is like one who has slept through the night and sees the sun and moon at dawn; having proceeded exclusively along the path of evil, one will surely enter the darkness.
Strive! Having spoken these words, he vanished (from the *Vajrasiddhi*).
When the Tang Wang Daizhi’s boat reached the Han River, a violent storm arose; the masts tilted and the oars broke, leaving everyone in a state of terror.
With no other recourse, Daizhi cast the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—which he had habitually recited—into the river. Immediately, the wind subsided and the waves became calm.
Daizhi was deeply moved by this experience with the sutra and remained despondent and unhappy for over two months. Upon arriving at Zhenjiang, he saw a boat...
About a hundred paces downstream, there was an object resembling a ball that appeared and disappeared at no fixed time; the assembly marveled at this.
