The Waitzhi ordered fishermen to cast a net and catch it, finding it to be a cluster of snails joined together into a mass. When they cut it open, the exterior was damp while the interior was dry; the sutra he had cast into the Han River was found therein.
The Waitzhi sighed and said, "The waters of the Han River converge with those of the Nine Bays. Upon reaching Nanxu, they flow for several thousand li."
The distance was several *li*. The number of ships could not be calculated. That they have been able to reach this place is extraordinary.

Judging by ordinary sentiments, one might think it was merely moved by the single thought of recollecting the sutra. However, Chan Master Qingliao of the Song dynasty said: "When a snail sees a sutra and does not let go of it, is it for fame?
Is it for profit? Is it for wealth? Or is it for beauty? It must surely be because it seeks to escape the cycle of birth and death."
It is so. Alas! Among the myriad things, only humans are most spiritually gifted. Yet there are those who do not hear this sutra for their entire lives;

those who hear it but do not see it; those who see it but do not believe it; and those who believe it yet allow fame, profit, wealth, and beauty to enslave their minds, unable to receive and uphold it.
Who can be called the most spiritually gifted? Reading this further adds one more whip of admonition (from the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).

Li Weiyen, the Magistrate of Jiande County during the Tang Dynasty, had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. At the end of the Tianbao era, he served as a subordinate officer (*canjun*) in the Yuyao Prefecture.

Upon completing his term, he was returning northward and passed through Wuzhang Village, where he encountered the low-lying embankments of the Shangyu River; the waters were exhausted, making travel difficult.
In the middle of the night, it was dark and gloomy; the four directions were desolate and empty. This road had long been notorious for bandits.
Since there were several hundred bolts of Wu-silk in Yan’s boat, he feared they would be seized by thieves. Consequently, he took up a sword and went before the boat to recite sutras.

After the third watch, he saw two torches on the embankment approaching from afar; when they reached a hundred paces from the boat, they turned back. He found this quite strange and redoubled his efforts.

As he recited the scriptures aloud, he further thought that the water was drying up and that he would need the aid of more water. At that time, the inner pond had dried up while the outer pond was full.
After half the night had passed, he suddenly heard the sound of flowing water at the bow of the boat. Startled, he said, "The pond is several zhang wide;

how could it have been breached? After a long while, he felt the boat floating. By dawn, the river water was already full. Facing the location of the boat, he saw a hole several chi in diameter and thus realized [the source].

It is said that both water and fire are aided by the spiritual power of the *Vajracchedikā*. Only Yan Di and Wei Yu were serving as District Vice Governors in Qianzhou when they followed their elder brother’s example and recited the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*.
Later, while traveling by boat out of the gorges, the current became so violent that the oar broke and the boat was about to sink.
They then recited the sutra with all their might. Suddenly, they saw an oar floating downstream; they were thus able to reach safety (*from the Guang yiji*).
Sūnmíng of the Tang dynasty was a native of Yángwǔ in Zhèngzhōu. His family had been poor and lowly for generations.

He worked as a tenant on a manor in Lùshì, abstaining from meat and reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty times every day. After twenty years had passed, while he was reciting with right mindfulness, he suddenly saw two officials come to summon him.
Sūnmíng took them to be local magistrates and accompanied them. After traveling about five or six li, they arrived at the gate of a government office. There he encountered...
The King went on an inspection tour. An official consequently confined Ming in an empty room, which was extremely dark. Seven days passed. When the King arrived, the official led Ming in to see him.
Ming personally stated that he had upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty years. The King said, "This is a matter of great karmic cause and effect.

He extended Ming’s lifespan by twenty years and ordered the official to escort him back home. By then, Ming’s funeral rites had already been performed; although his spirit had returned to his body, his family did not recognize it. It happened that...
A hunter passed by his coffin and heard the sound of wailing; he informed the family members, who opened the coffin and found him alive.
This was an event from the end of the Tianbao era. Mao Zongqi said: "A person of great talent may be self-deluded regarding the conscious spirit and fail to awaken to the original nature.
Ten thousand conditions entangle and disturb them as they respond to circumstances from all sides. One thought comes and one thought goes, like the wind in the sky, having no place of reliance."
It is like grass pressed down by a stone; it stops for a moment only to sprout again. How can one truly maintain the practice of recitation?

Among those who discuss sutras and expound the scriptures, there are not a few whose merit is deficient and whose conduct is impaired, clinging to appearances and destroying their very roots—this is truly to be lamented.

The guest Sun Zhuang has maintained his recitation for twenty years with single-minded faith and devotion; the fruit he plants is exceedingly deep, precisely because he remains in a state of undifferentiated wholeness (*hundun*) without carving at it. Therefore...
Miaoxi said: "If one is clever and quick-witted, one lacks the capacity for the burden [of the Dharma]. (Cited from the *Guang yiji*).
During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Yang Xun, the judicial official of Kuizhou, constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and was upright in his accumulation of merit.
When his son was twenty-three years old and about to take the imperial examinations, he suddenly dreamed at night that the Vajra Deity said: "Your son shall change his name to Yang Chun."
In the sixth round of the provincial examinations the following year, he again dreamed of the examination questions; he passed with the ninety-sixth rank.
Upon leaving for the palace examination, he dreamed again that someone said: "Your son's essay did not meet the examiner's expectations, so he has been placed in the third tier.
I shall exchange him for first place upon the imperial dais. This is due to the merit you have accumulated through reciting the sutras throughout your life."
This was the retribution for that. When the Governor of Kui heard that Xunzi had passed the metropolitan examination (dianyuan), he granted him a seat and ordered him to resign from his post.
Xunzi replied, "My family possesses no assets; we have only striven to accumulate hidden merit (yin-de). We have been able to save three bags; I beg you to open and look at them.
The first bag contained thirty-nine large coins; the second contained over four thousand medium coins; as for the third...

There were ten thousand small coins. The Governor questioned him about this, and Xu said: "Every year when the death-row prisoners are reviewed, if their circumstances and the nature of their offenses are such that they may be commuted, they are sentenced to exile;
one large coin is then cast. For those who commit crimes warranting exile, they are sentenced to penal servitude; one medium coin is cast.
For those who commit crimes warranting flogging, the punishment is assessed as light and they are released; then one small coin is cast. This is modeled after the system of the Zhou dynasty."

The *Chíxíng Tàishàng Gǎnyìng Piān* sets forth ten kinds of wholesome deeds. First, to collect abandoned infants and entrust them to others for care and nourishment, returning them to their parents once they have reached a slightly mature age.
Second, on the first day of every second winter month, to collect those who are impoverished and without support.
Those aged sixty and above, and those under fifteen, shall be supported with one *sheng* of rice daily and provided with fifteen coins.
Upon reaching the third month of spring, they shall be permitted to live according to their own convenience. Third, he provided efficacious medicinal decoctions to relieve the suffering of the sick.

Fourth, he provided coffins for families unable to afford the expenses of a funeral. Fifth, when female slaves reached adulthood, he would provide them with a portion of their value regardless of the full price.

1. He married a suitable wife. 2. He observed the precept against killing by purchasing and releasing living beings whenever he encountered them. 3. Whenever he met with years of famine, he bought grain at high prices and sold it at low prices to relieve the poor.
4. He repaired temples, monasteries, bridges, and causeways. 5. He provided financial assistance to impoverished travelers so they might return to their hometowns. 6.

When he served as a district magistrate, he always showed compassion and sympathy toward every prisoner. Now, having fortunately obtained one son who passed the examinations—perhaps this too is [the result of his merit].
"This is brought about by ten days of serving the public and practicing goodness. How could I dare so hastily resign from public office to seek my own ease?
Upon hearing these words, Shu sighed in admiration and ceased not. As the saying goes: "Even a man of but one rank, if he maintains a heart that seeks to benefit all things..."

There will surely be those who are saved; how much more so for one who practices without weariness? To attain the title of "Hall Chief" through secret merit—how can this be compared to being reduced to the status of a horse or an ox for one's descendants? (From *Jingang zhengguo*).
During the Zhenghe era of the Tang dynasty, there was an elderly stone mason named Sun in Zhenzhou who recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day.
One day, he entered the mountains with more than twenty others to quarry stone when the mountain collapsed, and they were all buried alive. Only Sun remained, trapped within a fissure in the rock.

After twelve years had passed, his descendants quarried through the stone and pierced the mountain, where they saw the elder sitting upright, his appearance unchanged from before. His sons were struck with wonder and prostrated themselves before him.
Question: "By what means did you attain birth [in this state]? The elder said, "I once recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [The boy] asked, 'Are you hungry?
He replied, 'At first I ate a single *sū* cake, and even now I am not hungry. The elder asked, 'Does the sūtra I recited in the past still remain? The boy replied, 'It still remains.'"
He returned home to fetch the scripture and examine it; on the scroll there was a circular hole, exactly the size of a cake (from the *Jingang zhengguo*).

Song Canjun of Fangzhou in the Tang dynasty was a minor official who held the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When he went to his official post, he temporarily stayed in the residence of the Director of the Office of Rites.
The house had long been ill-omened, yet every evening he would constantly recite the scripture. Suddenly, he saw a woman standing outside the door. Song asked, "Are you not a ghost? She replied:
However, he asked again, "Do you have any grievances? The woman wept and told him, "I am the wife of the former Director of the Office of Personnel.

When the Director was on an official mission, his younger brother coerced me; I refused, and he subsequently killed me. He wrapped my corpse in felt and threw it into the latrine in the northwest corner of the hall.
I have long wished to lodge a complaint, but when ordinary people see my form, they are inevitably terrified. My deep resentment is difficult to make known. The official [acted accordingly].
"Maintaining mindfulness is the merit that provides great protection for all sentient beings. Seeing how you have been defiled by such filth, how could I not feel compassion for you?
Song Yun said, "My office is lowly; I shall report this to my superiors. The next morning, they dug into the ground and the latrine, but did not find the corpse.
As Song Yun recited the sutras, the woman appeared again and said, "It is only one foot to the northwest. Following her words, they found it; inside the felt rug, only the remaining bones remained.

He moved the laundry to another location. That evening, the spirit came again to offer thanks, saying: "Your profound kindness is difficult to repay. Though we dwell in the realm of darkness, we possess awareness.

Of your two sons, the younger shall have descendants and shall attain a position of honor. He further stated that after Song’s death, his official rank would be changed and he would be appointed as a Vice Governor (Bie-jia) of Guizhou;
both of these came true. When Song asked why he had not sought revenge, the spirit replied: "His younger brother is currently still serving as an official; this is simply destiny."
"It is not yet time for death; therefore, it has not [happened]. Maozong Qi said: "A woman appeals her grievance to a military officer;
how could he begrudge this discarded shell? It is surely because she wishes to rely on the power of the sutra to pull herself from the depths of suffering.

As for the two phrases, 'Since the mandate for death has not yet arrived, it has not been reported,' they are especially capable of awakening the world. I have often seen that rebellious ministers and treacherous sons do not fail to employ evil causes."
They obtain evil fruits. Yet figures such as Cao Arman and Qin Mu-chou were so cruel and wicked that they surpassed all their contemporaries, yet they enjoyed long reigns and died natural deaths.
This causes people to doubt whether the law of cause and effect is fixed. They do not realize it was simply because their allotted lifespan had not yet run out.

Once their eyes fall to the ground, they will undergo the cycle of rebirth for kalpas, suffering the torments of hell, the calamities of the thunderous axe, and dwelling within the bellies of oxen, horses, snakes, and vipers.

One truly does not know when the retribution of karma will reach its full measure. Although the remaining bones of this woman were recovered from within a latrine, it is not certain that she will not come to demand her debt from the underworld on another day (from the *Guang yi ji*).

The late Prime Minister Zhang Yi of the Tang dynasty, whose father Qi丘 had reverently served the King of Emptiness (the Buddha), would don new clothes every morning to face the Buddha and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fifteen times.
He maintained this practice for several decades without slackening. At the beginning of the Yongtai era, he served as the Military Governor of Shuofang.
Within his headquarters, a minor general who had committed a crime feared his offense would be exposed; consequently, he incited several hundred soldiers to plot [rebellion].
In rebellion, Qi Qiu retired from the yamen. While strolling idly before the hall, several dozen soldiers suddenly burst in with blades bared.
Qi Qiu fled hastily toward the gate of his residence; after walking a few paces past the hall, he looked back and saw no one, suspecting it was a ghost.
As he neared the gate, his wife, daughters, and servants cried out in unison: "There are two armored warriors! At that moment, the yamen guards appeared atop the roof of the hall.
Upon hearing the commotion, the soldiers rushed directly to the front of the hall with their weapons drawn. They saw ten or so men standing with their hands hanging down and their mouths agape;
they cast their weapons to the ground and were immediately seized. Five or six of them were mute and unable to speak, while the others confessed, saying, "We intended to go up into the hall."
Suddenly, he saw two armored soldiers several zhang tall who glared at him with wrathful eyes and shouted. He was immediately stricken by a severe affliction.
Upon hearing of this, Qi-qiu was moved by the Buddha’s supernatural power; he subsequently renounced wine and meat and recited [the scriptures] for the rest of his life.

As for lay practitioners living at home who, on one hand, recite the sutras while on the other, engage with the world—those who ride horses in both directions, manage affairs while setting aside their minds, or even recite several times a day—[their merit is still vast].
It cannot be obtained. General Zhang recited it fifteen times every morning for several decades; the total accumulated amounted to approximately five thousand scrolls per year.
His roots of goodness were thus fully ripened. The soldiers with glaring eyes were none other than the Vajra benevolent deities who subdued him;
all else was merely incidental (from the *Gouyi*).
Lu Kangcheng of the Tang dynasty once served as a legal clerk (facao yuan) in the capital of Jingzhao. He did not shrink from confronting the powerful or the oppressive.

Once, after retiring from official duties, he suddenly saw a deceased subordinate official carrying several hundred sheets of documents and requesting his signature. Kangcheng asked, "Since you have passed away, how have you come here?
The official replied, "These are the records of the netherworld. When Kangcheng examined them, he saw only the names of people, with no other details. The official said, "They have all come..."

Regarding those who died by the blade during the year, [Kang Cheng] asked, "Is there a self? The official replied, "There is. He was greatly startled and said, "Could it be that the former official lacked compassion?
The official replied, "I have come specifically to inform you, Illustrious Lord; only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* can provide the solution. Having said this, he vanished.
Kang Cheng subsequently recited the *Vajracchedikā* several dozen times every day. The following year, Zhu Ci rebelled and appointed him as a Censor. Kang...
Kang Cheng rebuked him, saying, "A treacherous minister dares to offend a man of state! Shi Ci was struck with rage and ordered several hundred cavalrymen to surround and shoot at him.

Kang Cheng silently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the arrows could not harm him. Shi Ci said, "The Confucian's armor of loyalty and integrity is indeed true," and he then abandoned his pursuit and departed.
Kang Cheng subsequently retired to Mount Zhongnan and never again entered government service (from the *Taiping guangji*).

During the early Dali era of the Tang dynasty, when Cui Ning was stationed in Western Shu, Yang Lin rebelled. A veteran soldier named Zhang Guoying engaged him in battle and struck him in the abdomen with an arrow;
the shaft remained embedded and would not come out. A physician declared that he would certainly die within one night. His family prepared the funeral equipment.
He wept as he bid farewell to his comrades. Guo Ying habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One night, he dreamed that a foreign monk placed a pill into his mouth.
When morning came, an arrowhead was expelled, and the wound immediately closed and healed (from the *Baoying ji*).

Xu Wang of the Tang dynasty was a man of immense wealth who served as an official in the administration of Zhexi. Every night at the fifth watch, he would recite three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before entering the public offices.
Once, when a band of one hundred thieves plundered his house and bound him, shooting arrows at him, Xu said, "The Vajra-body is indestructible;
what can you do now? In an instant, he beheld a Buddha appearing in the sky, and although they loosed their arrows, not a single one struck its mark.

The bandits were startled and questioned him; realizing it was due to the power of his recitation of the sutras, they released him. All the bandits then abandoned their weapons and changed their ways.

Considering how Kang Cheng’s quills clustered upon him without causing injury, and Guo Ying survived with arrows buried in his abdomen, one knows that even in the midst of certain death there remains a swift path to preserve one's life (as recorded in the *Jingang Zhengguo*).
During the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, a horse-thief from Taiyuan falsely accused Wang Xiaolian of complicity based on an old grudge.

After ten days of interrogation and torture, he was coerced into a confession under extreme duress. However, the investigating official suspected his innocence and did not immediately finalize the case.

Wang Xiaolian devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with such intense and piteous lamentation that it never ceased day or night. Suddenly, a segment of bamboo fell from the sky, having two ends...
The joints fell into the prison. While he stood before the king, other prisoners scrambled to seize them. The jailers were startled and suspicious; they split them open for all to see.
Inside was a half-verse from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that read: "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas. The calligraphy was exceptionally fine.

The ringleader of the thieves felt sorrow and repentance, and the filial official was released. Since the prison did not allow any air to pass through, from where could these bamboo joints have come? Two.
The head has joints. From where does this sutra enter? How could it be within the reach of thought?
How could one not cause the thief to feel sorrow and repentance? (Cited from *Jiuyi*).

In the eleventh year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Zhou Boyu, the Vice Administrator of Weizhou, daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, maintaining this resolve without wavering in either public or private affairs.
One day, he suddenly saw a monk from India arrive and asked him, "Who is this venerable one? The monk replied:
"I am Subhūti from the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. You have recited the sutra for several years, yet I regret that you have not yet ceased eating meat.

If you truly seek the Buddha with a sincere heart, you must observe the perpetual fast. Thereupon, Boyu abstained from meat, recited the sutra, and subsequently attained the ability to foresee future events.
At the age of ninety, he sat in meditation and passed away (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
Ren Zixin of Tang was a native of Jiazhou. In the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he had been residing in Hunan.
He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. While crossing Lake Dongting, a strange object resembling a cloud suddenly surged over his boat;

it dispersed after a short while. Zixin then vanished from the boat, and no one knew where he had gone. After a long time, he emerged upon the waves and arrived at the Dragon Palace to pay his respects.

The King commanded them to ascend the hall to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and presented them with several items of precious jewelry. The two monks escorted each other out of the palace;
one monk entrusted a letter to be delivered to Master Shaozhen at Guanyintai on Mount Nanyue, instructing him to say, "This was sent by your Upādhyāya," and to have him recite the *Vajracchedikā*.
Upon reaching the mountain, he met Shaozhen and learned that the Upādhyāya who had entrusted the letter had already passed away.
"It has been five or six years" (from the *Taiping guangji*).

Du Chengshi, the Tang Dynasty Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, said: "In the seventeenth year of the Zhenyuan era, my late father went from Jingzhou to Shu to respond to the summons of Wei Gao, the Prince of Nan’gang.
When Wei reached his later years, he was slandered by Liu Pi; consequently, [my father] served as Acting Magistrate of Ling..."
In Chixian County, Wei Xun passed away, and Li Bie took charge as acting governor. My late father had previously been at odds with him; upon hearing this, he left the county that very night.

When he reached the eastern gate of the city, Li Bie issued a notice forbidding the officials of various counties from leaving their posts. That evening, the wind was dark and the sky was pitch black.
Having traveled two *li* beyond the outer walls, he saw two torches flanking the road for a hundred paces, serving as a guide. At first, he thought they were county clerks.

They went out to welcome him and were surprised that he did not proceed further; yet his position relative to the high and low, the distant and the near, was no more than a few inches off. Only when they reached the outskirts of the county seat did it vanish.

When they questioned the county officials, they had not yet received the official notice from the prefecture. My late father had been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for five or six years.
There has been no day without this occurring. What I have witnessed leading the way is precisely the traces recorded in the scriptures. Later, rebellious conduct gradually became manifest;

an imperial edict appointed Lord Yuan Zi as the Military Governor (Jiedushi). Chengshi’s second cousin, who had followed him into military service from his youth, was in charge of affairs at the Left Guard.

Fearing that disaster would befall him, he conspired with the military inspector to communicate with Yuan via a letter written on wax. When the plot was discovered, they were all slaughtered like fish and meat.
My late father believed the rebel knew of his plan; at that time, my late father had been reciting sutras for a long time into the night and did not notice he had fallen into a drowsy sleep.

All the doors were closed, yet he suddenly woke up and heard someone enter through a door, saying three times, "I am not afraid. It was as if something had slammed against the table with a sudden *pop*.
There was a sound; as he started up in alarm, the voice still lingered in his ears. He looked to his left and right, but the officials and servants were all fast asleep.
He ordered a candle to be lit at the four desks, but at first nothing could be seen. The door that had been locked earlier was already wide open.

My late father had recited this sutra over one hundred thousand times, and the signs of its efficacy were remarkably manifest. Chengshi has recently examined the records and biographies of successive dynasties, which provide ample evidence of such spiritual responses.

Furthermore, I previously commissioned the transcription and recitation of three fascicles on the miraculous efficacy of the Vajra [Sūtra], hoping that its transmission might reach those beyond limit.

Having gathered these accounts for circulation, they are intended to supplement deficiencies in Buddhist rites. This work is titled *Jingang Jiuyi* (Miraculous Anomalies of the Vajra). The author is Chengshi’s father.
His taboo name was Wenchang. Master Zhukong said: "In the Tang dynasty, men of talent and heroism all departed from secular life to preside over Dharma seats.
This was because at that time, internally there were demonic women and eunuchs, and externally there were rebellious vassals and haughty generals;

all held wealth and honor in their hands and used their breath to enshroud the scholars of the empire. Those scholars who lacked discernment scrambled to follow them, yet how could they have been caged?"

It is like the dragon’s cage and the elephant’s stall. Men such as Zhaozhou and Linji all possessed the talents of princes, dukes, generals, and ministers, yet they stilled their minds to take refuge in the Buddha.
With great capacity and great function, they were free in both killing and giving life; there was no need for the assistance of external studies.

For this reason, the *Record of the Karmic Retribution of the Vajra* notes that from the Jin to the Song dynasties, the Tang period alone had the most [masters], because its sovereigns included Emperor Taizong and Emperor Xuanzong.

He [the Emperor] personally annotated [the scriptures] and greatly turned the Wheel of Dharma. Consequently, among the officials and commoners of both the court and the countryside, there were none who did not follow his influence and turn toward the Way.
Although Fu Yi and Li Ao of Changli vehemently opposed and bitterly slandered it, they were like ants shaking a great tree, unable to cause even a fraction of damage. Minister of State Duang...

The literary skill and discerning power [of this work] stand as a pillar and foundation for their time. Consider the twin torches held aloft along the pathways: some shine by themselves and others extinguish themselves;
some gates open suddenly, while others are accompanied by speech and sound. These are the actual sights and sounds within the family home—how could they be mere hearsay or "eating with one's ears"?
This single volume of *Qiūyì* (Strange Tales from the Crow) is truly a golden fortress and moat of Prajñāpāramitā. (Cited from *Qiūyì*).
In the third month of the eighth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang Emperor Xianzong, Wu Shaoyang, the Regional Inspector of Henan, was on an inspection tour of the various prefectures.
While traveling by boat, he saw from afar a post-station attendant whose feet did not touch the ground. He asked for his name, and the man replied, "I am the lowly Quan Xin.
I have been conscripted as a post-station attendant by official duty. He further asked what means of livelihood they had, and the man answered, "My wife and I sell wine."
He had made a living by dealing in dried meat for over thirty years, yet he maintained a vegetarian diet and recited three volumes of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day;
whenever he found leisure, he would chant the name of the Buddha. Wu asked him, "Are you willing to sell this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that you have been reading? Xìn replied, "I can.
Wu said, "If we calculate one taël of silver per month, over thirty years I shall give you a total of three hundred and sixty taëls. How does that sound? He then took [the scripture].
Silver and the Letter. Wu examined it again. Xìn had already stepped onto the shore, his feet touching the ground.
On the fifteenth day of the intercalary month in the ninth year, Wu fell ill and was seized by authorities. Suddenly, a Vajra deity descended from heaven and rebuked the ghosts, saying:
"This man has the merit of having purchased the Prajñā Sūtra; you must not bind him with ropes. Since his lifespan has ended, you may let him go as you please. The ghost-officials knelt down.
He replied, "Yes. Upon waking, he told his wife and children: "In my life I did not observe the fasts, and thus my karmic offenses are immense.
During my travels last year, I purchased the *Complete Faith Sutra* (*Quanxin Jing*), which has reduced my sins by half. You must all diligently uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;

do not wait until the moment of death to regret this, for it will be too late. Furthermore, I entrust you with the task of inviting monks to recite it with devotion to save me from my sufferings in the netherworld."
Having finished speaking, he passed away (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
Qiang Boda was a native of Fangzhou during the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty. His family had suffered from a hereditary foul disease for two hundred years.

When Boda reached the age of twenty, he contracted leprosy. He addressed his father and elder brother, saying, "I will certainly not recover from this illness. I fear it will bring calamity upon my descendants. His father—
His elder brother packed provisions and placed them beneath a crag in an empty mountain before departing in tears.

Before long, having ceased eating, a monk happened upon him and said with pity, "If you can recite the four-line verses from within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you may perhaps escape this suffering.
Bo Da accepted the instruction and recited it without ceasing. After several days, he suddenly saw a tiger approach; terrified, he simply closed his eyes.
He recited the gāthā with utmost sincerity. The tiger licked his wounds all over; it was as cool as applying medicinal ointment, and he felt no further pain at all.
When the tiger departed, the wound gradually healed. The next morning, the monk returned to the side of the mountain, gathered a handful of green grass, and gave it to him.
He was instructed to go to a mountain stream to soak grass and wash his sores. Bo Da wept and bowed in gratitude; the monk pushed him away as he departed.
After he had left, he washed himself, and his wind-leprosy (vāta-kuṣṭha) fell away like a garment. Upon returning, he saw his father, elder brother, and kinsmen, all of whom were struck with wonder.
From then on, the contagious disease ceased entirely. (From the *Baoying ji*).

During the Yuanhe era, when Yan Siguō was serving as the Minister of Works in Jiangling, Wáng Miǎn, the Commandant of the Cényáng Garrison, was a regular reciter of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
While returning from an official investigation in Guīzhōu, his boat was wrecked at Zhàtān, and five people were drowned together.
As Miǎn entered the water, it was as if someone had handed him a bamboo pole; he followed the waves, surfacing and submerging, for over three hundred *lǐ* until he reached Xiàláozhèn.
He reached the shore alive. Looking at the object in his hand, he saw it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (as recorded in the *Jiuyi*).
Tang dynasty, Wu Kejiu, a native of Yue. In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, Kejiu resided in Chang’an and followed the Manichaean teachings.

His wife, Lady Wang, also followed him. After more than a year, his wife died suddenly. Three years later, she appeared in a dream to her husband and said, "I have become a snake due to my wrong views and am now beneath the stupa at Huangzi Pool. I shall die tomorrow morning.

I pray that you invite a monk to that place to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* so that I may escape this karmic retribution. The husband rebuked her in the dream; the wife became enraged and spat in his face.

He woke up to find his face swollen and in unbearable pain. His wife again dreamed that her husband’s elder brother said, "You should go to the garden, take some *nāgavallī* (dragon-tongue) grass, pound it, and apply it as a poultice.
Upon waking, the brother took the grass and gave it to his younger brother; he was immediately healed. The following morning, the brothers invited a monk to recite the scriptures.
A large snake emerged from within the stupa, raised its head, and gazed about everywhere; when the recitation ended, it died. Kējū.
The entire family took refuge in the Buddha and sincerely upheld this sutra. Alas! When the world is in turmoil, heterodox teachings flourish.
Today, teachings such as Longevity, Non-action, and Nirvana have the whole nation following them like madmen. According to the records, Wang Shi, the wife of Kejiu, [did so].
Having received the retribution of a snake for following the teachings of Māṇibhadra, he ultimately used what was correct to subdue the heterodox.

He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and took refuge in the Samyaksaṃbuddha as the gateway to liberation; this can also awaken those who are deluded and mistaken. (From the *Baoying ji*).

Xing Xingli of Tang was a native of Shan Prefecture. He was a merchant who could not read a single character. At the beginning of the Changqing era, he followed a virtuous friend who orally transmitted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to him;

after one year, he was finally able to recite it from memory. Once, while transporting three hundred *guan* worth of silk and cloth out of Tongzhou, he encountered bandits with drawn swords as they pursued him on a mountain pass.
Abandoning his chests and baskets, he threw himself into a deep ravine at the foot of the pass. Suddenly, he saw...
The Vajra Deity. As he walked and stood upon his fingers, he suddenly felt as though his body were above water, like treading on level ground.

His luggage weighed only fifty or sixty catties; when the bandits attempted to lift it, they could not move it. Looking at one another in astonishment, they summoned him to stand and questioned him: "What kind of magical arts do you actually possess?
He replied, "Throughout my life, I have done nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with devotion. As he entered and exited [the city],...

It did not leave his ear. When the bandits opened the bag and took out the scripture, five-colored light appeared. The multitude all joined their palms in repentance and discarded all their weapons of violence.
They offered one hundred strings of coins to request the scripture for recitation, vowing never again to commit robbery.

Among those in the world who could not read, those who recited the scripture were always superior to those who could read, because they were free from distracting thoughts. Reciting the scriptural text from memory was always superior [to reading it].

Regarding the practice of reading and reciting scriptures from a text, it is because this can concentrate the mind. For one first entering the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the essential point lies in concentrating the mind on a single object (from the *Taiping guangji*).
During the Tang dynasty, when Si-kong Gao was away from Shu, there was a commoner named Zhao An who had regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

While traveling through the countryside, he saw a bundle of clothes abandoned beside a tomb. Since it had no owner, An took it back with him. A neighbor accused Zhao of stealing property, and he was arrested and sent to the county office.
The magistrate, enraged that An would not confess, used a large gate-bar to crush his shins, breaking them into three pieces. Later, the magistrate...

When he struck his back with a staff, the staff would break each time it touched him. Suspecting that he possessed some other supernatural art, the official questioned him. He replied, "I merely recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and perform prostrations.

The official was likewise amazed by this and subsequently ruled that he be released and returned home. His wife said, "On such-and-such a day, I heard [the sound of recitation] from within the sutra case."

It thundered and split with several sounds; [the man] was so terrified that he did not dare to open it. Dao’an rushed to inspect it: the leather strap was severed, the axle was broken, and the paper was completely torn to shreds (from *Jiuyi*).

Ni Qin of the Tang dynasty was a native of Zizhou. He was renowned for his military strategy and tactics. In the fifth year of the Taihe era, he served as the administrator of the Xingjiao Granary in Fuzhou. He had long been devoted to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇī Sūtra*.
The granary possessed a hall facing the river, which was celebrated as a magnificent sight. Qin installed Buddhist images and recited the sūtra therein.

On the ninth day of the sixth month, the river waters swelled greatly, yet they did not reach the base of the hall. As Qin’s recitation became increasingly devout, by the time— (Note: The source text ends abruptly; the provided segment concludes with "洎" [and then/upon], indicating the narrative continues.)
The waters receded. Looking around for several li, walls and houses were all submerged and ruined;
only this hall and the granary remained uninjured (from the *Baoying ji*).
During the Qianfu era of the Tang dynasty, the Prefectural Commander of Yanzhou, Minister Cui, was strict and severe in his administration of the law.

Once, a military officer failed to appear for the morning audience; the Minister immediately ordered his attendants to execute him. After being executed, the officer’s facial expression did not change.

The assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement. That night at the third watch, he returned home. His wife and children suspected he was a ghost, but the officer said, "When I was first executed, it was as if I were drunk."

He dreamed that he did not know of his suffering; when he woke at night, he found his body lying upside down in the street, so he rose and returned home. After being repeatedly comforted and exhorted, [the Emperor] bestowed upon him a set of robes and one hundred scrolls of this sutra written in silver ink for his recitation and offerings. Furthermore, he ordered that [the remains] be placed outside the gate of Yanshou Temple in Yanzhou.
He depicted the place where [the culprit] was executed and an image of the *Jing* that had been cut, thereby manifesting a miraculous trace.
The military general lived to the age of one hundred and four (from the *Taiping guangji*).
Tang Ningmian was a native of Yunzhong. In his youth, he was courageous and skilled in horsemanship and archery; he was capable of grappling with fierce beasts without the use of weapons.
At that time, the Governor of Beidu admired his valor and appointed him as a commander of the guard. Subsequently, he was assigned four thousand troops and ordered to defend Feihu City.

It happened that the Governor of Jimen was arrogant and tyrannical, abandoning the laws of the Emperor; news of his rebellion reached the imperial court. Emperor Wenzong issued an edict to the north...

The Metropolitan Governor attacked from the south. Before he had even arrived, the troops at Jimen launched a night raid on Feihu. The sound of gongs and drums shook the earth, and the hearts of those within the city were filled with alarm;
everyone sought a temporary retreat. [The General] reasoned that his own forces were too few to withstand the vanguard of the Jie commander.

He intended to listen to the advice of the elders, yet feared incurring the wrath of the Son of Heaven for failing to advance; he wished to hold the fortifications and defend himself, yet remained apprehensive.
The people of the entire district were all at the hands of murderous bandits; deeply anxious, Yuanmian deliberated but could not decide on a course of action.
Suddenly, a spy reported: "The rebels have broken and scattered. Yuanmian immediately ascended the city wall to observe.

At that time, the moon was quite bright, and he saw the rebel hosts fleeing, tripping and stumbling one after another, as if a great army were pursuing them from behind. Yuanmian was overjoyed, unaware from where the relief forces had come.
[The enemy] approached from their position. [He] opened the gate and unleashed his soldiers to pursue them. He captured dozens of men alive and seized a great many abandoned armor and weapons.
Previously, Yuan Mian had been fond of the Buddhists; he had often read Buddhist scriptures and delighted in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
After defeating the commander of Jī, he arrested the rebels and interrogated them. They said: "That night, we saw four great generals atop the city wall, each two..."
He stood over ten feet tall and was fierce and formidable, inspiring dread. As he descended from the city wall brandishing a sword and driving away those he slew, the multitude fled in terror;
who would dare harbor a heart for combat? [The protagonist] urged the four generals to realize that they were actually *vajra* deities, whereupon he marveled at himself even more.
Later, he served as Censor-in-Chief and Assistant Commissioner for the Clear Barrier (from the *Xuānshì Zhì*).
Zhang Zheng of Tang was a native of Qiongzhou. On the seventh month of the third year of the Kaicheng era, he died suddenly. Initially, he saw four men come to arrest him;
after traveling for half a day, they reached a vast great river about three feet deep. Upon closer inspection, it was entirely pus and blood.

Zhang then quietly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereupon the messengers’ expressions changed. They entered the city and saw a monk over eight chi tall, who rebuked the messengers.
The monk said, "How can you recklessly seize a virtuous person? The messenger was startled and prostrated himself. When they were led before the king, the monk took the seat of honor.
He declared, "This man is merely a disciple from my own home; he has been unjustly detained. The king said, "Wait, let me briefly interrogate him. The monk’s expression grew stern with anger.
The king immediately ruled that he be released and returned home. The monk led him out of the city himself, where they no longer saw the river they had crossed.
The monk said, "I am your honored teacher Subhūti, whom you revere. Only then did [the king] realize the power of upholding the sutra; he joined his palms, prostrated, and paid homage.
The monk said, "Disciple, close your eyes. He struck him once with his staff; the man unconsciously let out a cry and revived.
He had been dead for three days, yet because only his heart remained warm, his family had not yet performed the enshrouding. (From the *Baoying ji*).

Tang Fangzhu was a man who throughout his life revered and placed his faith in the Awakened King (the Buddha). Every day he recited the name of the Buddha and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
One day he died suddenly and arrived at the Office of the Netherworld. The presiding official said to him, "According to the registers, you possess the merit of the *Prajñā* [wisdom];

furthermore, you once exhorted an elderly man to recite the Buddha's name, and that man has already been reborn in the Pure Land. By virtue of this power of merit, it is fitting that you too should attain rebirth there. Fangzhu said: "I—"
He made a vow to recite ten thousand scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā*, though it remains unfinished even now. He said, "I shall wait until the vow is fulfilled before seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.

The Master replied, "While fulfilling one's vow through the recitation of sutras is certainly a virtuous endeavor, it would be better to be reborn in the Pure Land sooner. Recognizing that his resolve was firm, [the Master consented].
[The account of] sending an official to escort [the scripture] back (from the *Jingang linying*):

Lady Lu, wife of Dou Gong of the Chen state during the Tang dynasty and elder sister of Duke Rui Kuan, was long a believer in the retribution of sin and merit and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Before she had finished, she suddenly developed a headache, which grew increasingly severe by nightfall. She thought to herself, "If I die now, I shall not be able to complete this scroll."

Struggling against his illness, he sought a candle, but all the flames were extinguished. Suddenly, he saw torches gradually ascending the hall steps and entering directly into his bedroom, hovering about three feet above the ground without anyone holding them.
The radiance was like that of day. The lady was filled with wonder and joy; she took up the scriptures and began to recite them.

After a short while, the family members produced fire by drilling wood, and the light of the candles immediately vanished. From then on, his illness was cured, and he recited [the scriptures] five times daily.
Scroll. One day, as Lord Rui was about to die, he said to his wife: "My sister recited the sutras with such devotion that the records of the underworld noted her name and increased her longevity.
She subsequently reached the age of ninety and passed away without illness" (from the *Fayuan zhulin*).
At the beginning of the Yongtai era of the Tang dynasty, there was a beacon-tower guard from Fengzhou whose mother constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

One evening, while the guard was out on duty, he was captured by the Qiang tribesmen and taken into Western Tibet to be traded for horses. The Tibetan general, the Tsenpo, ordered his shoulder bone to be pierced and a leather thong passed through it, and assigned him several hundred horses to herd.
After half a year, the number of horses had increased twofold. The Tibetan general, appreciating his diligence, rewarded him.

Using several hundred sheep hides, he gradually drew closer to the imperial tent, ordering him to hold the banner on the left or right. Whenever there was leftover meat or surplus curd, he would give it to him.
After half a year had passed, while giving him curd and meat, [the prince] wept bitterly and refused to eat. When questioned, he said, "I have an elderly mother."
He frequently saw this in his dreams. Upon hearing of it, the Tsenpo was despondent. That night, he summoned him into the tent and said, "The laws of the Tibetan people are strict;
there is no precedent for allowing you to return. I shall give you two powerful horses; release you by way of such-and-such a path, and say nothing of me.

The beacon-tower guards received the horses and galloped as fast as they could, but both horses died of exhaustion. They hid by day and traveled by night for several days, until one was wounded in the foot by a thorn.
In the midst of the inverted sandbars, a wind suddenly blew an object past him. He seized it and wrapped his feet with it; no longer in pain, he ran as before.

Upon reaching the borders of Fengzhou, he returned to see his mother. She was both sorrowful and joyful, saying, "Ever since you were abducted, I have only recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in prayer that I might see you again.
Now it has truly come to pass as I vowed. Thereupon, she took the sūtra and prostrated before it; however, several pages had been torn and lost.
It was extensive. Fengzi then recounted how he had injured his foot in the desert sands. His mother understood; she looked at what he was wrapping and found it was a sutra.
The wound subsequently healed. Generally speaking, filial piety and compassion in this world are most capable of moving the spirits of the unseen realm.

To the bond between Fengzi and his mother, the power of the *Vajra* was further added; thus, they were able to cause even the fierce poison of the Fan and Han peoples, such as the Tsenpo himself, to suddenly turn their evil ways.
He gradually turned his mind toward joy and, though he had temporarily allowed the horse to return, ultimately succeeded in the reunion of mother and child—how extraordinary!
Yet, within the Emperor’s (Zanpu) tent, those few words neither extinguished the filial affection nor violated the laws of the state;
was this not because of great roots of wisdom from past causes? (From *Jiuyi*).

During the Tang dynasty, when Liao Dengguan was serving as the magistrate of Shanhua County, there was an elderly woman who would daily recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while begging for food in the marketplace.
At night, she would return to lodge in a mountain ravine. Suddenly, after several days, she was nowhere to be seen; however, a flock of crows gathered and clamored at her usual dwelling place.

People vied with one another to go and look, only to find her lying beside a cliff, having passed away with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* held in her arms. The crows were carrying earth [to build a mound over her remains].
They covered it over, and thus it was called "Crow-Burial" (as recorded in the *Huguang Tongzhi*).
During the Tang dynasty, there was Liu Shi, the wife of He Zhen. At the age of twenty-six, she had given birth to a son who was three years old and a daughter who had just turned one.

One night, she dreamed that she entered the underworld, where a verdict was issued stating: "Your life shall end in the third month of the coming spring. Upon waking, she wept in grief. She then proceeded to paint...

The Buddha abstained from pungent roots and greens. Day and night he reverently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, praying only that he might live to the age of forty-five so that his children could marry and he might die with peace of mind.
At thirty-eight years of age he took a daughter-in-law, and at forty-three he married off his daughter.

In the winter of the fourth year of the Taihe era, he was exactly forty-five years old. Liu gave up all his clothing and wealth to provide offerings for the Buddha and informed his relatives that the time of his death had arrived.
Because Zhen did not believe in such demonic speech, he remained unconvinced. On the eve of the New Year, Liu personally requested a śramaṇa to receive the precepts;
he bathed, changed his clothes, sat cross-legged in a single room, and after reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with great devotion, he passed away in silence.

However, he passed away. Only the heat from the top of his head was felt upon touching it. Out of compassion for the monastic community, he was accorded a funeral according to the rites. His stupa is located outside the northern gate of Jingzhou.
When worldly people briefly resolve to study the Way, they soon regress again. If one investigates the causes and conditions for this, there are three kinds of burdens.
Regardless of whether they are men or women, monastics or laypeople, each is burdened by their own body, speech, kin, and household affairs, leaving them in a state of constant busyness.
One life is spent in suffering. Furthermore, due to these three burdens, one gives rise to immeasurable greed, anger, and ignorance, creating all manner of evil karma;
it is simply that one does not awaken. How could one know that this stinking skin-bag cannot be made subject to one's own will?
In the heat of midsummer, a robust man may suddenly die of a sudden illness at night; by dawn, he is already being viewed [as a corpse].
One cannot hear [the world] once one has departed; as for one's kin, who can take their place? As soon as the light of the eyes closes, each no longer recognizes the other.
One must follow whatever provisions of the household are used up; not even a single hair’s breadth can be taken along. Why not turn the mind around and study the Way with single-minded devotion?
These words—each character a drop of blood—are the sincere speech of this good spiritual friend. Liu wished to complete her marriage arrangements and held them in mind.
Jingang, this is because you are burdened by your retinue; you are not one who can suddenly empty all worldly thoughts. However, within the Buddha’s teachings, faith is the most important thing.
Therefore, although your vision is not yet clear, you have nonetheless been born in a superior realm (as recorded in the *Chingzhou Zhi*).
Tang Kangzhongqi departed for the Eastern Sea with his mother in the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era. He did not return for several years.

His mother had only this one son, and after a long time of constant longing and remembrance, she spoke to a monk who was on alms-round. The monk said, "Simply uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and your son will immediately return.
As the mother could not read characters, she requested a person to copy the sūtra for her; she then hollowed out a pillar of her house to store it.
He stored it there and applied lacquer over its surface, paying it respectful homage morning and evening. One night, a great thunderclap shook the earth, and the pillar was uprooted and carried away.

More than a month later, the boy indeed returned, bringing a massive log to his home. Seeing his mother, he wept and prostrated himself before her. His mother questioned him, and he replied: "My second cousin said..."
While at sea, they encountered a storm; their boat was wrecked and they fell into the water. Suddenly, there was a clap of thunder, and a wooden pillar was cast upon the waves.

A child clung to it and floated to the shore, whereby he was able to survive. His mother, in amazement, said, "Could this be the pillar from my own collection of scriptures? She immediately broke the pillar and recovered the sutras.

Mother and son recited them for the rest of their lives, carving out the pillar to enshrine the scriptures—an extraordinary event. That the wooden pillar was struck by thunder and cast onto the waves was a karmic retribution.
How extraordinary! An illiterate old woman excels those who are distracted by three minds and two intentions or who engage in empty quarreling by a hundredfold (from the *Baoying ji*).

Lady Yang of the Tang dynasty was a native of Jianghuai; she was the wife of Song Kan. When Kan went to Heyin County at the beginning of the Yuanhe era to take the examination for the Mingjing degree, he fell ill and abandoned his studies to become a clerk in the Salt and Iron Office, receiving a monthly salary of two thousand cash. He took Lady Yang as his wife. She was...

Xian had lived in peaceful seclusion during the summer retreat for over a year. At that time, there was one who was transporting a grain shipment through the Three Gates, and he invited Xian to go with him to oversee the accounts, offering a monthly stipend of eight thousand coins.
Xian informed his wife of this, but she dissuaded him, saying, "The Three Gates are treacherous and perilous;
the profit does not outweigh the danger. Xian did not heed her words and went anyway. He indeed encountered a violent storm, which struck and sank the fleet of ships; only...
Kǎn entered the water and felt his way until he found a bundle of millet straw. It gradually drifted toward the shore; although there were several dozen others nearby, none came to his rescue.
He then prayed, saying, "My life has been granted by this straw; I vow never to abandon it, whether I live or die. He embraced it and ran for several li.
He took lodging at an old woman’s tea shop and related his circumstances to her in detail. The woman felt pity for him and prepared some gruel for him.

The next morning, while she was spreading out clothes to dry on the south side of the house, she untied and aired some straw mats. From among them, she found a bamboo tube; upon opening it, she discovered it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
She was startled and did not understand how this had come to be. The woman said, "Since you left the house, your wife has been praying with disheveled hair, seeking [your safety]."
The man had transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and had recited it with sincere devotion; therefore, he was able to save you. Wang Kǎn wept with gratitude and took his leave.
The old woman gave him two *shèng* of rice and pointed toward a path to the southeast, saying, "From here it is two hundred *lǐ*; by the day after tomorrow, you will reach home.
Two days later, he indeed arrived at Héyīn and apologized to his wife. When his wife asked how he knew this, Wang Kǎn recounted the entire account from the beginning.

At the end, his wife was even more astonished. Yuankan then brought out the sutra and, weeping, prostrated himself before it with his wife. He further asked whether there was any record of the color [of the characters].
His wife said, "When it was being transcribed, the scribe mistakenly wrote 'luohan' (阿羅漢) instead of 'luo' (羅), and the character 'wei' (維) above was missing four strokes.
They then went to the abbot of Huguo Temple to request that these be added. The abbot was elderly and his eyesight was failing; half of the characters were black, and for ten days he had not...
He knew where they had gone. When he investigated, everything was exactly as she had said. The following day, he went to thank the old woman, but neither she nor her dwelling could be found.
He questioned the cowherds, who replied, "The waters here have risen to the horizon; who would be selling tea?

Several years later, when Minister Zheng Yin was stationed as the Imperial Resident in the Eastern Capital, he summoned Wang Kuan and questioned him about the previous events. He then conferred a military rank upon Wang Kuan’s son and provided him with a monthly stipend.

Five thousand [copies]. Because he sought this sutra, it has been venerated by the Zheng family until the present day. When the Imperial Chancellor, the Duke of Hongnong, who served as the Prefect of Yuezhou, observed these events, he subsequently recorded them.
Consider the cases of Kang’s mother and Song’s wife: one took prostration as her practice, while the other took transcription and recitation as her salvation.
That the sutra was stored within the pillar of the house was the deed of the mother; that the sutra entered the bamboo [slats] was the deed of the wife.

In whose hands does this record rest? A wooden pillar was cast upon the waves; it was thanks to the Thunder God that it survived. The water-gate was like a galloping horse—how could one have survived on mere guest-grain and straw?

Had it not been for the provision of shelter and the granting of meals, leading one step by step toward safety, one would not have died by drowning, yet would have died of hunger (as recorded in the *Yangyuan Zhiyan*).

At the end of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Mingdu whose heart was set on compassionate salvation. He diligently cultivated pure karma, making it his daily practice to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
A dove nested in a pillar of his dwelling and raised two fledglings; Mingdu would regularly feed them with the remains of his own gruel.
He further recited a mantra, saying: "By the power of my sutra, may your wings be swiftly formed. May the fledglings, having suddenly learned to fly, all perish upon falling to the ground.

After he had finished performing the funeral rites for them with compassion, more than ten days later, he dreamed of two small children who said: "We were originally born from eggs, but we were nurtured by you, Venerable One.
Through your recitation and dedication of merit, we are now fortunately reborn into the human realm. Ten *li* to the east of here, at such-and-such a household..."
Sengdu silently noted this down. After more than a year had passed, he went to the man’s house to inquire; indeed, two twin sons had been born. Sengdu therefore named them "Pigeon-children" (He'er).
The two children looked at one another and laughed, as if they were old acquaintances. (From the *Jingang lingying*).

In the first year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, the monk Mingjun died suddenly. He saw two men dressed in green robes lead him before the King of Hell, who asked what arts he had practiced throughout his life.
Mingjun replied that he had merely recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King said, "Excellent! If you recite it one hundred thousand times," [you shall attain liberation].

"In the year to come, you will surely be born in the Pure Land. As for me, your disciple, I shall not see my teacher again. Having said this, he released him and allowed him to return. Xu Jun redoubled his diligent practice.

In the third month of the second year, he passed away while seated in meditation. All present smelled a wondrous fragrance. As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings are dull and ignorant; they cannot understand through contemplation.

One need only maintain the continuity of the sound of recitation, and one will naturally attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus it was clear that the master’s diligent practice had given rise to this extraordinary fragrance.
This is so (from the *Vajracchedikā-pratītyasamutpāda-siddhi*).

During the Qiannian era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Qianhui from Guangzhou who, from his youth, had upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing, regardless of cold or heat.
Later, while traveling by sea with a dozen or so people toward the Nan'an Protectorate, a great storm arose. The boatmen...
The ship was submerged. Only Qianhui remained amidst the waves; he happened upon a thicket of reeds and grasped them tightly with his hands.
He drifted with the current for three days and three nights before reaching the shore. Upon untying and examining the reeds, he found a single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Qianhui prostrated himself, took hold of it, and continued his journey. When he reached the age of one hundred and thirty, he sat upright and passed away. The original manuscript of the sutra had spontaneously emitted fragrant smoke.
Gradually, it formed clouds of five colors and slowly ascended into the celestial realm.
The assembly of monks, the governor and his officials, and all people from near and far, both old and young, beheld this (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
The Tang Dynasty master swordsman was surnamed Zhang by secular name and styled Boying. During the Qianyuan era, he served as a soldier in Shouzhou.
Being of an exceptionally filial nature, because his father was in Yingzhou, he secretly took an official horse to visit him. Upon reaching Huaiyin, he was captured by patrol guards.
The Prefect, Cui Zhao, ordered that he be executed at the marketplace. When the executioner struck three times with the blade, it snapped each time. He then stabbed [him].
The official asked, "What skill do you possess? He replied, "When I was fifteen years old, I observed the fasts and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for over ten years.
Because the world was in turmoil, I joined the army and consequently ceased my practice. Yesterday, when I encountered this unforeseen calamity, I did nothing but recite it with utmost sincerity.

The official sent someone to open the casket; the sūtra had already been divided into three sections. Thereupon, he was released from his punishment and ordained as a monk. At that time, people called him...
Regarding the Monk Sandao, the Sūtra says: "If I were to go toward the Mountain of Blades, the Mountain of Blades would spontaneously crumble.

These words of the Buddha are clear and evident, yet his nature was one of supreme filial piety; this was his fundamental seed. If one’s mind commits an act of rebellion while one’s mouth recites the sūtras, how is this any different from steaming sand in an attempt to make rice? (Cited from the *Guang yi ji*).

At the beginning of the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Hui-zong of Jingzhou, whose secular surname was Cai. He had once been poisoned by a *gǔ* (insect venom), leaving his body emaciated until only his bones remained.

He made a vow to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to await the end of his life. When he reached five hundred recitations, he dreamed during the day that someone ordered him to open his mouth;

from within his throat, they drew out more than ten strands of hair. That night, he again dreamed of vomiting a large intestinal worm over one *zhǒu* (cubit) in length. His illness was subsequently cured. [Jingzhou]...
This mountain monk Xingjian has witnessed these matters: the tumor of Yao Chang, Prince of Hejian, was the lingering retribution of six generations;
the knee abscess of Master Wuda was the karmic debt of ten generations. These are what are called "fixed karma. One’s only concern is failing to attain the Way;
once the Way is attained, what fixedness remains? Thus, Hejian eventually met Xuansu, and Wuda ultimately encountered Huinuo.

"Kaya! The task of realizing the fundamental principle may yet be uncertain as to its success or failure; however, that you were able to neutralize this life-threatening poison shows that your faith in the Way is sufficient to overcome Māra. (From *Jiuyi*).
The monk Fǎzhèng of the Bānruò Monastery in Jīnglíng during the Táng dynasty recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty-seven times daily.

In the early years of the Chángqìng era, at the age of sixty, he fell ill and passed away. Upon arriving before the Lord of the Underworld, the King interrogated him. He replied that he had habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā*.

The King invited him onto the palace hall and ordered him to ascend the embroidered throne; as he recited the sutra seven times, the attendants all joined their palms in reverence, while those being tortured below the steps were released.

The debate was suspended, and once the recitation was finished, the king sent an official to escort him back. Descending the steps to see him off, the king said, "May you, Venerable One, live another thirty years among men;
do not neglect your reading and recitation, and strive to transcend birth and death. He followed him for several li.
He arrived at a large pit, where an official pushed him from behind as if he were falling through the air. He had been dead for seven days, yet only his face was not cold;
he has now reached an age of over eighty years. The monk Changjing of Jingzhou personally witnessed this event (from the *Jiuyi*).
The Tang dynasty monk Shi Lingyou entered the monastic order at Daxingshan Temple in the capital. In the second year of the Changqing era, he died suddenly.

Seven days before his burial, he saw two messengers lead him to an audience with the King of the Netherworld. When the King commanded him to state what he had done during his life, Lingyou replied that throughout his entire life he had constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King pressed his palms together, granted him a seat, and ordered Lingyou to recite it aloud once. [Thereby,] the various sufferings of hell...

He paused for a moment. Having finished reciting, he asked You: "There is still one chapter missing from the scripture. According to your calculations, it should have ended; now your lifespan has been extended by ten years.
Return and exhort the people of the world to receive and uphold it. The authentic copy is upon a stone tablet at Zhongli Temple in Haozhou.
When You returned to his soul, he presented a detailed memorial to the throne. By imperial decree, a palace messenger was dispatched to Haozhou, but there was no such text upon the tablet.

It may be said that this is called "preaching the Dharma later. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti arrived at the point where the Tathāgata said, "That which is not a sentient being is called a sentient being.
This is the mantra for supplementing deficiencies, transmitted together with the true text from the stone stele by one who came from the Netherworld.
Sentient beings throughout the ages have the Buddha leading them from the front and Yama whipping them from behind; only then do they begin to know.
The Buddha and Yama are both Lords of Compassionate Merit (*Kāruṇika-puṇya-adhipati*). (From the *Jinyucheng Xují*).

During the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Lu Bian whose elder brother served as the Magistrate of Hucheng. While traveling from the Eastern Capital to the provincial capital, he stayed overnight at an inn.

In a dream, he saw an official in yellow robes lead him into the underworld to meet a Judge of the Dead. Just then, a messenger arrived, and the official led him out to welcome him. [The official] led him to a...
The site had stone walls above and no beams or pillars below. Inside were placed some ten or so large grinding wheels.

Beside them stood more than a hundred women; the wheels rotated constantly by themselves. Ox-headed executioners would then hurl the women into the openings, and they would emerge from the wheels with blood and flesh dripping down, their bones pulverized.
The sound of their agonizing cries was so horrific as to be unbearable to hear. Bian saw this.

Lady Bumo of Hucheng was also among them. Startled, she asked, "For what reason do these people undergo such suffering? Lady Bumo replied, "It is because they were consumed by jealousy during their lifetimes;
thus they receive this retribution after death. She then pleaded piteously, saying, "You have long maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Recite it for me immediately; perhaps the punishment may be lessened. Because Bian recited the sutra with such sincerity, the millstone ceased to turn, and those undergoing punishment were all released.
He obtained a brief respite. Suddenly, an officer came forward and said, "Who is it that has come here to recite sutras and turn the Dharma-wheel to deliver us from calamity?

Bian replied, "I wish to save my paternal aunt. The officer said, "Report this urgently to the presiding lord. The judge then dispatched an official in yellow robes to escort Bian and his aunt back to the world of the living.
Initially, Bian had been accompanied only by a small servant boy; seeing that she had already been dead for half a day, he was struck with alarm.
He was terrified and at a loss for what to do. After reviving, he arrived at Hucheng. Upon entering the gate, he encountered his elder brother Fang performing ritual repentance and chanting sutras.
His elder sister-in-law came forward, took his hand, and said, "Had it not been for you, my remains would already have been ground to dust.
That I have now regained life is due to the power of the Mahayana transmitted to you. (From the *Guang yiji*; this case should be included among the "Good Men.")
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Wúshì lived in Bùzhèng Fāng. One evening, as he was returning home and found the gate closed, he crouched beneath a large bridge.

At midnight, several horsemen suddenly arrived at the bridge and said that one rider was going to Bùzhèng Fāng to fetch Zhāng Wúshì’s wife and an old man from the same lane, while another rider was going elsewhere to fetch several people. When Wúshì heard this, he was greatly alarmed. Shortly thereafter—

The collector arrived and said, "Everyone else has received their share; why is it that you alone have not? It is because your wife recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and a benevolent deity protects her, so she has not been obtained.
When he called out the names of those who had received their shares, they all responded; however, there was no response to the voice of the old man Wang, whom he did not know.

Just as he was about to leave, the drum suddenly stopped. He hurried back and saw his wife still sitting upright, reciting the sutra. His wife said, "I feared you would be breaking the curfew, so I recited the sutra for you."
While they were conversing, they suddenly heard the sound of weeping from the southern neighbor; it turned out that the old man Wang had died.

Taking what they had witnessed as a sign, the husband informed his wife, and the couple was struck with great fear. They subsequently made a vow to observe the long fast (*dīrgha-śīla*), reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā* forty-nine times every day, thereby attaining immortality (according to the *Jiwen*, this case should be classified among "virtuous women").
*Record of Experiences of Holding the Vajra [Sūtra]*, Upper Volume;
*Record of Experiences of Holding the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Throughout Successive Dynasties*, Lower Volume.
Compiled by Zhou Kefu Zhonglang of Jingxi; proofread by his son, Zhou Shi.

In the second year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, Chen Jisheng Huangs, a man of the Huang clan from Wu Commandery, served as a military aide (*canjun*). He resided in Huating County, Xiuzhou, holding the rank of Song Chengxin. He suffered from the ailment of "upside-down stomach" (*fanwei*) for several years, yet none of the hundred medicines were effective.
Suddenly, one night he dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to him: "You have karmic grievances from past lives; you are suffering this in your present life."

Regarding the suffering of illness: whenever men or women of the world suffer from wind-stroke, consumption, abdominal dropsy, blindness, deafness, or muteness, and with their bodies entangled by disease for years on end, lie prostrate upon their pillows and mats unable to seek death, their spirits are mostly summoned into the Office of the Shades.

There they are interrogated regarding the evil deeds committed in their previous lives and the present life. If one can reverently offer the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or personally transcribe it or have another do so...

He transcribed [the scripture]. Having either maintained it throughout his life or merely brought it to mind, he immediately caused the officials of the underworld to first release his soul and allow it to reanimate his body, after which he encountered a skilled physician and his illness was cured. Upon regaining consciousness, he was filled with faith and attained realization.

The following morning, he instructed his wife to burn incense and make a vow to donate one thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and he further resolved to maintain it with a sincere heart, as had been manifested in his dream.
The Spirit of Firmness bestowed a single pill of medicine and commanded him to swallow it. On the following day, his illness diminished; after more than a month, he was completely cured.

All who saw or heard of this joined their palms in praise and admiration. Indeed, since beginningless time, sentient beings have given rise to various forms of ignorance and committed various sinful karmas.
Through the six sense faculties, they produce the three poisons; by committing a thousand evils, they invite a thousand calamities, planting all manner of seeds for rebirth in the hells.

Roots, fetters, enmities, and knots—how could there ever be one who plants bitter *yuan-chen* (Picrorhiza) and does not experience bitterness? Receive this with faith and uphold it with all your heart;
as consciousness is eliminated, wisdom will grow. Bestowing thousands of scrolls of this sutra, transgressions will be extinguished and blessings will arise.
Prajñā is the excellent medicine, and the Tathāgata is the Great King of Physicians. Do not let such an opportunity pass you by face-to-face. (From the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).
There was a Zhu, a Jinshi (licentiate), of Suzhou during the Song dynasty. Throughout his life, he had studied for the civil service examinations and had never heard of the Buddha-dharma.

One day, while visiting Tiger Hill Temple, he happened to hear Master Foyin lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When he reached the four lines concerning "all conditioned phenomena," he experienced a joy he had never known before.

Consequently, he desired to investigate the meaning and intent of the entire scripture. One day, while taking a midday nap, he dreamed that five men were being driven along by a man in blue robes; Zhu followed them.
Afterwards, having walked about two *li*, he reached a major street and entered through the gate of an alley. There was a household with a blue cloth curtain hanging at its entrance;

he went into their kitchen, where there was hot water in a bucket. The five men all drank from it, and Zhu was about to drink as well when a man in green clothing shouted, "Those who listen to the Dharma may not drink this!
He was startled awake by this. Thereupon, he proceeded on foot to the main street and entered the alley, where indeed [he found...]
The account matched his dream exactly. Zhu knocked on the door and entered; the host explained that in the kitchen six puppies had been born, one of whom was dead.
Zhu was struck with terror and broke into a sweat, thinking to himself, "Had I not heard the Buddha-dharma, I would have entered the womb of a dog."
Because he had single-mindedly upheld and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his lifespan reached eighty-nine years.
