On the full moon day of the eighth month, he invited all his friends and fellow practitioners from the various mountains for a final farewell. He climbed onto a branch in the rear garden and spoke this verse: "Eighty-nine years of life, Master Zhu."
With both hands he split asunder the void; with his feet he crushed the floating clouds to pieces. Standing before the Bodhi tree, he immediately passed away. Mao Zongqi said:
"In the five turbidities of human life, throughout several decades, within the twelve hours of a single day, every thought and every movement involves committing evil and creating karma.
In a mere instant, one does not know how many such acts have been committed. Roughly speaking, throughout a single lifetime, one leaves behind..."
The karma accumulated over many lifetimes—when such karma becomes increasingly heavy, the kalpas one must endure become increasingly deep.

If Master Zhu were to falter even once, when his karmic debt is fully repaid, one knows not what form he would again be reborn as. As the saying goes: "Once lost is the human body; ten thousand kalpas may pass before it is regained. And again:
"If this body is not used to cross over in this life, toward what other birth shall we turn to save this body? That Master Zhu has had the opportunity to hear the Buddha-dharma is [a rare blessing].

Having heard that the Buddha-prince [Foyin] lectured on the sutras, it is said that the Tathāgata most highly values preaching the Dharma for others (as recorded in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* regarding the realization of the fruit).

In the first year of the Chūnxī era of the Song dynasty, Zhou Xing, a subordinate official of Yangzhou Prefecture, had recited one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* daily since childhood.
The Prefect, Mo Hao, dispatched him to the capital with over a thousand strings of silk as tribute to present to the high officials of the court. Upon arriving at Guazhou...
He crossed over and stayed overnight at Yusan Inn. There, he conspired with his elder brother, Yuer, to murder him for the sake of wealth; they buried him by the roadside five *li* from the inn.

Because Xing had exceeded his travel deadline, his wife and children were confined and reprimanded for one year. When the Governor was summoned to the imperial capital, he was about to reach Guazhou when he suddenly saw a single lotus flower by the roadside.

He ordered his attendants to pluck it, but as they struck it— (Note: The original text ends abruptly with "斫之" [zhé zhī], meaning "he struck it," likely indicating the beginning of a miracle narrative regarding the lotus.)
It did not cease. He dug the earth four or five feet deep and saw flowers emerging from the mouth of the deceased man;

his eyes were still able to move. Upon looking closely at him, it was found to be Xing. They supported him back home. Only on the following day was he able to speak, recounting in detail how he had been murdered at the guesthouse and buried in the ground for eighteen months.
When the Prefect asked why he had neither died nor suffered hunger, he replied: "I was intended to be killed and was buried; I was unconscious."
Deluded as if in a dream, he saw a Vajra deity insert a lotus flower into his mouth, after which he fell into a deep sleep that has lasted until now.
The Prefect sighed and said: "I have often heard that this sutra possesses inconceivable merit; I am ashamed that I have forbidden my wife and children from reciting it.

Furthermore, I wonder if the legal cases I have adjudicated in my daily duties have not been entirely free of injustice. He immediately issued a formal document to the official of Yangzhou Prefecture to release him.
He brought his wife and children into prosperity, yet the two brothers, Juyou and Juer, were imprisoned. Upon reporting the matter to the throne, Juer and Juesan were executed.

Observing this, although they were buried in the earth, lotus flowers still grew within their mouths. If one who upholds the sutras with such single-minded devotion can have a body seated upon a lotus pedestal even in death, how could there be any doubt? (From the *Jingang Zhengguo*).
Guo Cheng'en, a resident of Shaoxing Prefecture during the Song dynasty, was about to take up his post as a military aide (*canjun*) in Wenzhou.

He visited Tianning Temple to burn incense and make a vow that, upon arriving at his post, he would diligently practice expedient means by prohibiting the slaughter of oxen while awaiting the completion of his term of office.

Once he returned home, he transcribed one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in gold ink and respectfully enshrined it in the Buddha hall for offerings. This [act] was comparable to three... [etc.].
When his term of office had expired, he purchased a boat with his colleague, Yuan Zhen, the Judicial Officer, to travel by sea back to his hometown.
The member of the staff’s family was in the forward cabin, while the Judicial Officer occupied the rear cabin. Upon reaching the borders of Shaoxing Prefecture, a great tempest arose;

the four directions were shrouded in darkness, and they beheld gods and spirits within the sea. The boat was split in two: the forward cabin reached the shore with a favorable wind, while the rear cabin sank.
They were submerged in the sea. This was because the Magistrate had accepted bribes and yielded to private interests, whereas the Military Commissioner served the public interest and upheld the law;

it was also due to the power of the Vajra. Once the principles of retribution are established, good and evil are distinguished, and calamity and fortune are instantly adjudicated; thus, a single ship was split into two pieces.
This is even more extraordinary. General Guo made three vows upon taking office; truly, they were like a great Dharma-ship amidst wind and waves (as recorded in the *Ganying ji*).
Lord Wen Zheng of the Song dynasty was originally from Chengdu in Sichuan, but while serving as the Governor of Suzhou, he came to reside there.

Twenty-one days after his mother’s death, he dreamed that she wept and told him: "Because I committed karmic offenses during my life in the world of the living, I have been detained by the Lord of Mount Tai.
Day and night I suffer hardships that are beyond description. My son has always been filial and obedient;

I beg you to recite one *zhàng* (one hundred thousand scrolls) of the *Gongde jing* (Sutra of Merit) to rescue me from my transgressions. Do not hesitate, lest I once enter hell and never again attain rebirth."

As he was leaving, [the monk] looked back and instructed him, saying, "The Sutra of Merit is none other than the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. At dawn the next day, the official woke up in a state of startled weeping;
he immediately bathed and observed the precepts of purification, then personally went to the Chan monastery at Xuanmu to invite monks to recite the sutra for seven days.
On the night of the sixth day, she again dreamed that her mother said: "Because of your sincere repentance, the Great Being Pāṇḍaravāsini descended to the human realm.
You have recited half a scroll of the scripture; thus, not only have your sins been extinguished, but you shall also attain rebirth in heaven—all through the power of the Buddha."

The following morning, the boy entered the sutra hall; upon inquiry, he knew it himself. When the public officials and nobles completed the religious service, they prepared generous offerings as a reward for the assembly of monks.
Thereupon, he asked about those who had recited the sutras on the sixth day, and found that among them were some who had only held half a scroll. The entire assembly turned pale with dismay.
The respondent replied, "The scriptures being venerated are all complete in their respective numbers; how could there be such a thing as holding only half a scroll?
A monk standing nearby spoke calmly, saying, "Yesterday, when the assembly was reciting the sutras, this mountain monk stood leaning against the wall watching in silence.

When we reached the sixteenth fascicle, suddenly the Great Master arrived to offer incense, whereupon I returned to the kitchen to perform my duties. Now that I have received your question, I dare speak with straightforward honesty."
The Duke responded, "Yes. He immediately prostrated himself with his head to the ground. The monk said, "Mo mo" (Do not, do not), and suddenly ascended into the air until he vanished from sight.
Among both the monastics and the laity, there was none who did not gaze up in reverence. Consequently, the Duke established the "Mo Mo" Meditation Hall to commemorate this miraculous event;
it remains intact to this day (as recorded in the *Lingshan Shengji*).
Deputy Censor Feng of the Song dynasty daily recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When he reached the age of twenty-eight, he submitted a memorial regarding a certain matter. That night at the fourth watch, he suddenly saw two messengers escorting him into the underworld.

The King said, "Your lifespan was destined to reach seventy-nine, and your rank would have reached the Council of State (*shufu*). However, because your memorial harmed the people, your emoluments must be cut off and your years of life subtracted. Feng—
Startled, he said, "Since my allotted lifespan in the world of the living has not yet ended, I beg you to grant me rebirth.

I swear that for the rest of my life I shall uphold the sutras and diligently practice deeds of merit. The King admonished him, saying, "Whenever you hold authority, you must maintain a register. Record all the deeds performed during the day."
One must record these deeds every night. If they cannot be recorded, then one must certainly not have performed them; this is the art of prolonging one's years.

The moment a virtuous thought arises—such as benefiting the people or showing compassion toward all creatures—one’s fortune and lifespan will surely increase. Yet, if one harbors even the slightest intent to exploit or oppress others, the Supreme Deity will immediately mete out severe retribution.
Having been restored to life, Feng’s hidden virtue became increasingly manifest; he lived to the age of ninety-eight and was appointed as Prime Minister.
One day, while lying ill, his ninth son, who was then eleven years old, went out before the hall and saw countless figures with ox heads and horse faces.
Startled, he asked where they were coming from. The ghost officials replied, "We have come specifically to welcome the Son of Heaven, Yama.
He reported what he had seen to his father. His father smiled and said, "To be a Chief Pillar of State while alive and to become King Yama after death—this is my destined office.

He spoke in verse: "Cease using the pen of litigation to display your literary brilliance; Turn instead toward the King of Emptiness and find joy in leaving the home-life. Having already made this resolve..."
The mind returns to the Great Way; there is no need for the six thieves to laboriously obstruct it. To rejoice with one's wife and concubines ultimately leads to illness;
to reach the rank of high official is like a flower that must fade. From this point on in his later years, he relied upon the sword of wisdom, wishing to entrust his name to Danxia.

He requested a bath, changed into his court robes, and sat in meditation until his passing. He further composed a verse, saying: "Beating the drum within the vast ocean, The sound is heard atop Mount Sumeru."
The bell! When the karma-mirror is brought forth, it shatters into brilliance; turning the body over, one penetrates through empty space.
For Lord Feng to treat the Minister of Justice as Yama is indeed his primary retribution (*vipāka*), yet it is not the ultimate fruit.

Nevertheless, his daily recitation of three volumes of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* could not withstand even a single memorial of his regarding the harming of the people. Alas! How terrifying this is! (From *Jingang zhengguo*).
Chai Zhu of the Song dynasty was a native of Qingzhou. He served as the Judicial Administrator of Shouchun Commandery.
While investigating a case involving a plot to commit murder, a prisoner confessed: "Thirty *li* from the city, I made my living by lodging travelers.
Whenever a guest arrived with heavy luggage and stayed alone, I would kill him at midnight and cast his corpse into the Baisha River. I have done this countless times; I only spared one old woman."
"It must not be done. He asked the reason for this. The prisoner said, "This was an elderly woman who came alone seeking lodging. My brothers and I saw that her belongings were not meager.
When it grew deep in the night, I sent my eldest son to push against the door; he returned after a long time saying that someone was pressing against the door and it could not be opened.
I did not believe him, so I took a knife and went there myself. Upon reaching the door, I bored a hole in the wall to look inside, and I saw—"
Within a red light stood a large figure, about the same height as the room itself, standing with its back to the door. Startled and terrified, I let out a cry and nearly fell over.
When dawn was approaching, the door finally opened. The old woman continued to comb her hair and recite sutras without ceasing. I asked, "What sutra is this?"

He said, "It is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thus he knew that the divine being from last night was indeed Vajra (the Vajra-being). (From the *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Vajra*).

During the Bingzi year of the Deyou era of the Song dynasty, at Huajia Mountain in Chongzheng, there was a man named Hua You who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and experienced many miraculous responses.
In that year, the cavalry of the Great Yuan arrived. To avoid the danger, You secretly prayed to the Buddha. That night, the Vajra...
A deity appeared in a dream and said: "In a previous life, you killed a person whose debt remains unpaid.
That person has now been reborn in Leliang in Hezhou, with the surname Wang and the given name Er. He is currently in the army; you shall die at his hands.
No amount of merit can save you, and there is no benefit in fleeing. On the following day, Yu sat upright and recited sutras without ceasing. Near noon, two men entered and bound Yu.
He cried out, "Wang Er, Official of the Second Rank! I shall die at your hands; I do not contest my death.
Allow me to finish reciting the sutra, and then I shall submit to execution. The soldier asked, "How do you know my name? Yu told him of his dream.

Wang Er said, "Since the Vajra deity has entrusted this to me in a dream, how about I release you from your karmic enmity? He then left, parting with his clothes. Yu then proceeded to recite [the sutra].

After reading several fascicles of the sutra, he suddenly passed away while sitting upright without illness. Alas! When the great destiny is already fixed, even though the grudges and resentments of past karmic bonds have been extinguished, one cannot escape death.
Yet, to avoid losing one's life and to pass away peacefully while seated—could this not be the merit of the protection of benevolent deities?
(From *The Miraculous Responses of the Vajra*).

South of the city of Huzhou in the Song dynasty, there was a butcher named Old Man Lu. When he was twenty-three years old, he encountered a wandering monk who claimed to be there to convert those with whom he had a karmic affinity.
Lu did not understand this. The monk said, "You have slaughtered countless pigs and sheep;

why do you not change your occupation? Lu replied, "I am following my ancestral profession; it would be difficult to abandon it so abruptly. The monk said, "If you do not change, then in future lives you will surely..."

"You have fallen into this category. Considering that you possess roots of goodness from past lives, why do you not uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* to eliminate your evil karma?
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished. Lu was then awakened to realization and vowed never to slaughter living beings again.

He became a vegetarian and took refuge with his teacher. He painted a single scroll of the Master’s portrait and daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before the Buddha to repent, praying only that the sentient beings he had killed might be quickly reborn in the Pure Land. Before five years had passed, he was able to recite it from memory.
At the age of eighty-one, he foreknew the day of his death; having bathed and sat upright, he composed a verse and passed away. The verse says: "Over sixty years..."
Devoted to the karma of killing, one carries a blade in hand and scales life while practicing in secret. This morning, one has reached the path to Bodhi;
the lotus flower blooms within the water and within the fire. In human life, there is nothing but good or evil; there is no other path that can allow for a mixture of the two.
Among our own kind, we often live according to our own ease and convenience, acting with mere expediency and evasion.

If one considers this to be free from great transgression, it is sufficient to lead one directly into the path of delusion. Thus, those who are stubborn and evil may brandish their knives and claim to have realized the fruit;
because their power is easily inverted and their habitual tendencies are fully matured, they are neither dark nor light—neither dreaming nor awake—and are cut in two by a single stroke.
Lifan Nan (from *Jingang zhengguo*).
Daughter of Li Xuanzong of Jiangling County, Jingzhou, during the Song dynasty. At the age of thirteen, she dreamed of a Brahman monk who said to her:

"You possess roots of goodness; why do you not recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? He further said, "If good sons and good daughters of the world can daily recite one fascicle with a pure mind, their lifespan will increase in this world, and at the end of life, they will be reborn in the celestial realms.
If they can fully master the *Prajñā*, they will reach the other shore of *nirvāṇa*. Even if they have not yet grasped the meaning of the sūtra, when they die, their *antarābhava*..."
The Prefectural Office was likewise unable to detain her. She was destined to be born into a wealthy and noble family and receive various superior karmic rewards.

Empress Xuanzong believed this and consequently recited three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day. At the age of twenty-four, she had no desire for marriage; suddenly, she contracted a case of *shanghan* (febrile illness).
She died on the third day. King Yama examined her and found no fault. Upon seeing the Buddha manifest upon the woman’s head, the King said, "This woman possesses the merit of *prajñā*.
I shall release her and restore her soul. As he was about to release her, the King cautioned her:

"Your father committed karmic offenses, which have already reduced his lifespan by two *yuga* (twenty-four years). Before long, he will be summoned here for interrogation. This is because your father was fond of taking life."
He was slicing raw fish for a meal. At that moment, there were over seven thousand fish, which pleaded for their lives. He returned home and questioned his father, who said:
"Every night I dream of falling into a net, and during the day my head aches; these fish are seeking retribution. The daughter returned to life and informed her father.

Startled and at a loss for what to do, he went with his daughter to Tianning Temple, where they provided a vegetarian feast for a hundred monks, abstained from meat and wine, and personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When the copying of the forty-nine fascicles of the sutra was completed, Emperor Xuanzong suddenly dreamed of several thousand youths dressed in blue robes.
They bowed toward him and said, "We were slaughtered by you and have come to appeal our grievances and seek our lives.

Now, through the merit of your transcription of the sutras, we have all relied upon this power of goodness to escape the miserable realms and be reborn in the happy paths. Since you have released us from our grievances, your own life span shall also be extended. Thereafter, Emperor Xuanzong...
From then on, her recitation of the mantra became increasingly devout. She lived to the age of one hundred and twenty without illness, passing away while sitting upright after bathing.
A girl of only thirteen was able to believe the words spoken in her dream and maintained them with single-minded devotion, refusing to marry.

Compared to this, even robust men and elderly sages who had personally heard the Dharma preached from the seat of teaching still gave rise to doubt and slander; how vast, then, is the difference between them, like that between clouds and mud!

This was the Scripture of the Emperor Xuanzong’s Confession of Faults. Not only were the karmic offenses of his excessive consumption of minced fish and meat instantly extinguished, but his diminished life span was restored;
furthermore, those with whom he had formed grievances were all reborn in the good realms, and he himself attained a long life ending in a virtuous death.
This, moreover, demonstrates the vast power of the filial daughter to deliver herself, her parents, and all sentient beings (as recorded in the *Jingang zhengguo*).
Wang Didong’s wife was a native of Song; she recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily and was sincerely devoted to the good.
Wang Didong, however, delighted in falconry and hunting, taking the lives of many creatures. One day, after returning home from a hunt, he happened upon his wife reciting the sutra.

He then urged her to recite the fifteenth fascicle of the "Merit" section together with him. Before the scroll had even been finished, Wang Didong went straight to the kitchen to prepare roasted meat.
After five years of indulging in food and drink, Dijing suffered a stroke and lay bedridden for a year. One day, he saw two messengers who summoned him, and he passed away.
Upon meeting King Yama, the King rebuked him in anger, saying: "Having received rank and emolument, why did you not cultivate further merit?

Instead, you delighted in killing living beings; thus your lifespan was shortened and your fortune cut off. He then ordered the prison officials to drive him into the cauldron of boiling water. The ghost-officials...

The official examined the registers and informed the King: "Although this person's karmic offenses from killing are grave, during his lifetime he once recited one section of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* together with his wife.

Though it was but a fragment of paper, its merit is as heavy as a mountain; therefore, he should be exempted from punishment and released. The King then ordered that he be placed within the cauldron of boiling water.

He took a ladle of hot broth and poured it over his back to make him aware of the need for vigilance, whereby he was able to live again. Later, he suffered from a carbuncle on his back that became suppurated and painful;
though treated with a hundred medicines, it could not be cured. He summoned his wife before a Buddha image and made a vow, vowing never again to harm living beings.

Furthermore, he wished to hand-copy the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and maintain its practice through vegetarian fasting. That night, Di Gong dreamed of a monk who rubbed his back three times with his hand.
After one circuit, at dawn, the abscess was immediately healed. Maitreya Buddha said: "One may cut the flesh from the bodies of sentient beings to add fatness to one's own face;
even if you were given ten million taels of gold, who would be willing to take a knife and cut their own skin?"
Although King Digu had the virtuous cause of reciting half a chapter of the sutra, he could not take a female believer as his wife;
how then could he have escaped from the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons? (Cited from the *Vajracchedikā-pramāṇa-phala-sūtra*).

In the ninth year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, there was a woman of the Wang family in Mingzhou who daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. She had been pregnant for twenty-eight months;

she was frequently ill and emaciated, and was deeply anxious that she would have difficulty giving birth. While she happened to be leaning against her gate, a strange monk appeared and said to her, "You possess roots of goodness.

Why do you not print and distribute one thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā*? The Wang family printed and distributed the scriptures according to the number requested, and further held a vegetarian feast.
She recited the *Vajra-sūtra* one thousand times for a thousand monks. At the third watch of the night, she saw a Vajra deity point his mace at Wang Shi’s abdomen.
When she awoke, two sons had already been born upon her bed; their features were perfect and full, causing people to admire them with joy.
Wang Shi thereafter maintained her vegetarian fast and her practice without ceasing. When she reached the age of sixty-one, she passed away without illness. She then saw two messengers.

He was led before the King of the Underworld. He personally reported that he had maintained the recitation of the *Vajra* since childhood, whereupon the King bestowed upon him a golden throne and commanded him to sit beside the hall.
As he chanted it once aloud, the bitter sufferings of hell ceased instantly. The King asked again, "Why did you not recite the mantra?
He replied, "There were no copies in the world. The King then ordered his ghost-officials to retrieve a copy of the mantra from the treasury and deliver it to the Wang family.
He instructed her, saying: "When you return to the world of the living, propagate this widely and do not let it fall into neglect.
After your life ends, you shall go directly to the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) and will never return to this place again. The Wang family’s daughter returned to life after fourteen days.
Later, at the age of ninety-one, she passed away peacefully while sitting upright, free from illness. The mantra for the *Pūrvapraśamana* (Supplementing Deficiency) is: Oṃ hulu hulu śa.
Ye. Mukte Svāhā. First dedication: May the true mind accord with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). Second dedication:
May the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi be perfected in every thought-moment. Third dedication: May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm be reborn together in the Pure Land.
Alas for the people of this world! When the light of their two eyes falls to the ground, it is just like searching for a needle in the vast ocean. Part three.
The breath returns for but a moment in the narrow throat; as before, the west wind passes over the donkey’s ears.

How could one attain such diligence as Wang Shi, who upheld the sutra without ceasing and did not fail the transmission of the true mantra, so that it has circulated down to the present day? (As recorded in the *Vajracchedikā-sūtra-pratītyasamutpāda-phala*).
Master Jiang of the Song dynasty was a native of Jianghua County. He was born on the twenty-seventh day of the second month in the Jia-yin year of the Xining era.

His residence was near the shrine of Emperor Shun; from childhood, he considered it a blessing to be in close proximity to the Sage’s countenance, and whenever he passed by, he would pay his respects with the utmost sincerity. Upon reaching adulthood, he...

He was filial toward his parents and harmonious with his brothers. Daily he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the fifth month of the year Kwei-mei (1103) of the Ch’ung-ning era, he attained sudden enlightenment.

Thereupon, he took leave of his parents and wife and children to establish a dharma platform at Lang-seok Temple to expound the teachings. After more than a year, he looked back toward his home village;

seven days prior to the appointed time, he completely abstained from all food containing fire (vegetarian diet). Ascending to Ch’a Rock, he sat cross-legged and passed away. His disciples established [a memorial] at the temple.

Stupa. To this day, his true body remains undecayed. Mao Zongqi said: "The Great Master Jiang, through his supreme nature of filial piety and fraternal affection, achieved an adamantine, indestructible true body.
Compared to those who hold biased views of emptiness and achieve the mark of annihilation, he is far superior" (from the *Huguang Tongzhi*).
Chan Master Daoning of the Song dynasty was a monk of Kaifu Temple in Tanzhou. In his youth, he became a practitioner of the Way and served as the bath attendant at Chongguo Temple.
One day, while about to wash his feet, he happened to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until he reached this passage:

"One who can give rise to a mind of faith and take this as reality will, consequently, forget all that they have learned. Suddenly, as he lowered his feet into the boiling water, he experienced a state of realization. Later, he received the tonsure at Jiangshan.
Shan resided with the venerable Chan Master Liang of Xuedou for one year, traveling extensively through various monastic communities (*conglin*) and studying under many renowned masters.

Later, he arrived at Bailian Temple, where, upon hearing the informal sermon (*xiaocan*) of Wuzu, he was suddenly enlightened to the source of the Dharma through the kōans of National Teacher Huizhong’s "Ancient Buddha’s Pure Vase" and Zhaozhou’s "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature.
During the Daguan era, Xi Gong Zhen, the military governor of Tan, invited him to reside at Kaifu Temple. [He was a] patch-robed monk (*nà*).

His disciple Jingcong, on the fourth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Zhenghe era, shaved his head and bathed. On the following day, after the midday meal, he gave a small discourse (*xiao can*) to exhort the assembly to practice the Way;

his words were sincere and earnest. He initially intended to pass away on the seventh day. When that day arrived at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), he sat in the full lotus posture (*kaḍu*) and passed away.
Upon cremation, five-colored *śarīra* relics were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa. Master Lianchi said: "He was one who had attained the Way."

Knowing in advance that the time had arrived—namely, that the conditions for the Sahā world were exhausted and the conditions for the Pure Land were ripened—the sacred realm naturally manifested in a hidden manner.
This is exemplified by Master Huiyuan’s seven days and Master Jingguan’s twenty-seven days. Worldly people, lacking genuine virtue in life, desire to imitate such examples at death;
they contort and embellish their remains, only to be ridiculed by those with discernment. In extreme cases, they even burn the living body while still alive, [merely] to attach [a false reputation].
Possessed by demons and flowing into the evil destinies, they are especially worthy of compassion. Among those who attained rebirth in the past, there were none whose bodies were burned while alive.
I pray that the wise will proclaim this widely to the world to save these ignorant people. (From *The Fruits of Recitation and Retention*).

Song Songmingjiao traveled to Mount Kang and took up residence at Kuangguang Temple. The presiding master of the Dharma assembly, noting that Song was young and keenly devoted to literature, appointed him as secretary.
Songmingjiao laughed and said, "Would I do this for the sake of your single cup of ginger-and-apricot broth?
He left and lived by West Lake in Hangzhou for thirty years, keeping his door closed and never engaging in frivolous socializing. During the Jiayou era, he composed the *Fuzi*...

He compiled the *Jiaobian* (Compilation of Teachings), the *Dingzutú* (Chart of the Fixed Patriarchs), and the *Zhengzongji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage), which he presented to the imperial court.
Wang Gong Su of the Hanlin Academy, serving as Acting Governor of Kaifeng, further submitted a memorial recommending him to the throne. Emperor Renzong sent these works down to the Secretariat;

Prime Minister Han Gong and State Councilor Ouyang Gong read his writings and praised them greatly. The Emperor decreed that they be entered into the Imperial Canon, whereupon his fame spread throughout the world. In his later years, he resided at...
Lingyin. Every clear morning he recited the *Vajracchedikā* without ceasing; at midnight he recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
At the time of his death, he sat upright with a smile and requested paper to compose a verse, saying: "The moon is bright in the late night; I shall go forth alone.
I do not emulate the old man of Damei, who still craved the cries of the flying squirrel. (Recorded in the *Jingang lingying ji*).

The Song dynasty monk Shi Qingxu was by nature stern and decisive, and his actions were often contrary to conventional norms. Suddenly, he turned his mind toward the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, practicing it without any slackening.
Once, while he was chanting in the mountains and forests, seven deer became tame and submissive at his side, departing only when his voice fell silent.
Furthermore, when a neighboring house caught fire, the connected pillars were reduced to ashes, yet the empty room alone was passed over by the flying flames without being scorched at all.
In the second year of the Chang’an era, he visited the northern courtyard of Wuzhen Temple in Lantian; it previously had no well or spring, so water had to be fetched from a distant stream.

The endeavor was extremely arduous. At that time, the Great Master of the Avataṃsaka, Fazang, having heard of the spiritual efficacy of Xuchi’s recitation of the sutra, went to the spring to pray for rain.
He immediately entered the Maitreya Pavilion and recited the *Vajracchedikā* throughout the night without ceasing.

After three days had passed, he suddenly saw three jade maidens on the western slope of the mountain within the pavilion using knives to mark the ground. Xuchi carefully noted the location and dug there.
He subsequently obtained sweet spring water. In the fourth year, he sat in summer retreat at Shaolin Temple. On the mountain peak there was a Buddha chamber that was extremely spacious;
no one dared to go there, as it was said to be the dwelling of spirits and ghosts. A Vinaya master, relying on his own observance of the precepts, went there at night to recite the Vinaya.
He saw a giant who pierced him with a spear, causing him to flee down the mountain in distress. There was also another monk who maintained the *Vajrapāṇi-agnimukha-mantra*.
At that time, he was highly esteemed by the public. He was asked to carry incense and a lamp, enter the hall, and sit there chanting mantras.

Suddenly, a spirit emerged, seized his feet with its hands, and threw him down into a mountain stream. He remained silent for seven days. Hearing this from afar, [the Emperor] said: "The creatures of the lower realms have committed such evil as this.
Thereupon, he went to that place and recited the mantra of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara. At night, he heard a very fierce sound coming from the east of the hall. Furthermore—
It was as if two oxen were fighting; the Buddha image trembled throughout. Since the incantations proved ineffective, he returned to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

In a brief moment, all disturbances ceased. From then on, those dwelling there suffered no further afflictions. In the second year of the Shenglong era, an imperial edict summoned him to the palace to pray for rain.
For seven days, rain fell across a thousand li, filling all the ditches and canals and submerging houses and walls; yet the water reached the temple courtyard and immediately receded.
These various miraculous signs cannot be fully described (as recorded in the *Jingang Lingying*).

The Chan Master Wumen Cong was a native of Mount Xiangshan by the Ru River. In the first year of the Zhizhi era (the Xin-si year), the Elder Wu’ai of Zifu Temple requested that the Master provide a commentary on the thirty-two sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At that time, purple clouds covered the temple.
Upon its completion, several stalks of five-colored numinous mushrooms grew consecutively before the Dharma seat in the courtyard. The commentary on the sūtra was subsequently circulated.
To this day, whenever Master Cōng provides his commentaries on the various sections, he appends verses that open the eyes of humans and devas and penetrate the Diamond Mountains.

It is fitting that there should be auspicious responses such as purple clouds and divine mushrooms. Furthermore, among those who have carved the scriptures, there are instances where śarīra relics emerge from within the printing blocks;
these are all people of wisdom who have personally cultivated the fruits of wisdom. They do not manifest supernatural powers because they are Buddhas or Bodhisattvas. (Cited from *Shou*)
[This was] to maintain the karmic fruit.
During the Yongle era, thirty *li* north of the city of Rugao County in Yangzhou, there was a man named Sun Gong’er.
He maintained a lifelong fast and established a hermitage, where he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty fascicles morning and evening. He continued in this manner for forty years.
The times were in their chaotic infancy. The village bordered the sea and lacked city walls; jackals and wolves caused great harm, occasionally roaming through the hamlets.

Yet, whenever they heard the sound of him reciting the sutras, they would immediately lower their heads and depart. Once, when a violent typhoon struck and all the neighboring houses were swept away and destroyed, the Master continued his recitation as usual;
the hermitage stood tall and unharmed. His room had no locks or keys, and it was filled with the rice, grain, money, and silk bestowed upon him by various donors.

Regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople, whenever anyone encountered him in need, he would distribute his provisions to them all; thus, he profoundly realized the meaning of non-abiding generosity (*apratiṣṭhita-dāna*).

After his passing, the local people established a shrine specifically for his worship. For over two hundred years, whenever the spring and autumn sacrifices were held, the shamans and ritualists invariably recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to appease his spirit.
The post station known today as Sūngōng-po (Mr. Sun’s Inn) is his legacy.
[This is] the "Zhi" (The Feet) [section] (concerning the karmic retribution of receiving and upholding [the teachings]).

During the Xuande era of the Ming dynasty, there was a Daoist priest named Chen Ruxuan from Heguan in Western Sichuan. He sought longevity with a resolute will, contemplating diligently day and night and praying to the deities for the transmission of the Dharma.
One night he dreamed of a person whose appearance was unlike any he had ever seen, who called himself the Vajrapāṇi Spirit (*Jīngāngshén*). He said:

Xuán said, "If you seek long life, go quickly to Mount Mín and pay homage to Master Zhìróng; he shall transmit the Dharma to you. Xuán followed these words and went there to earnestly request instruction.
Zhìróng said, "Have you not seen the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says: 'All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow;
they are like dew and also like lightning. One should view them in this way'? Xuán asked, "Since they are like a dream..."
"An illusion. "What is meant by 'long life'? Huirong replied, "If one sees that all marks are no-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. It is also said:
'That which is not the Tathāgata is called the Tathāgata. Upon hearing these words, Huan attained great enlightenment and subsequently took his leave to live in seclusion on Mount Wagu.
Hujüyan did not cease his profound cultivation; he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day until he had completed several entire collections (*piṭakas*).

He lived to the age of ninety-eight. One day, he gathered the recluses living nearby and told them, "I originally sought the immortality of the immortals (*xian*), but now, by great fortune, I have attained the Buddha’s immortality.
Looking at the gentlemen, he said, "May you obtain what I have obtained. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes and passed away.

There are several hundred households near the mountain who have collectively built a shrine and fashioned an image to worship Xuan, asserting that he attained both the Way of the Immortals and the Fruit of the Buddha.
Xu Guan of Zhaoyang served as the Inspector of Sichuan and personally recorded these events (from the *Jinyu cheng xují*).
Mingyan Jiang was a leatherworker from Xiangcheng. In his middle years, he abandoned his trade and began carrying offerings of vegetarian meals to Buddhist temples.

On the road, he single-mindedly upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while simultaneously reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, his voice never ceasing. At over sixty years of age, he suddenly ceased eating grain and drank only water for one month.
He then declared, "I shall depart on such-and-such a day at such-and-such a time. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed.
He changed his robes and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Upon cremation, several *he* (measures) of *śarīra* relics were obtained;

his tongue was as hard as metal or stone, and when struck, it produced a resonant sound. This event took place in the thirteenth year of the Zhengde era. Nothing is more supple than the tongue, yet if the mind is firm, the tongue becomes firm.
This is a concrete proof of the indestructibility of the Vajra. (Recorded in the *Xiangcheng Zhi*).

During the Ming Zhenghe and Jiajing eras, there was a man from Duan-nan named Zhou Tingzhang, whose style name was Chufeng. He was simple and honest by nature and took refuge in the Buddha’s vehicle. In his life, he had never known the use of scales or measures;

in managing his household, he did not calculate whether his resources were abundant or lacking, yet he was refined in his fondness for charity. Whenever he had something, he would immediately distribute it to the poor.
People who spoke with him often laughed at him, or mocked him, or even went so far as to insult and revile him, yet he would simply smile. Every morning when he arose...

He invariably recited one scroll each of the *Vajra*, the *Amitābha*, and the *Avalokiteśvara* sūtras. At times, he would say with joyful self-assurance: "How could I rely on these as provisions for my practice?
I do not depart from daily life, nor do I involve myself in greed and attachment; it is simply a matter of being thus.

Once, while he was ill and napping during the day, a monk of Central Asian (Hu) appearance entered his room, joined his palms in salutation, and vanished in an instant. His family members were filled with anxiety.
He said, "I am about to depart. Suddenly, his illness was cured. At the age of eighty-seven, on the Qingming festival, he went to the grave to bid farewell to his ancestors.
Upon returning, he said to his wife, Lady Tang: "Amitābha is welcoming me; Avalokiteśvara and Śrī also have arrived. On the following day, he said:
"Avalokiteśvara gave me a taro to eat and told me not to consume meat. I have been observing the five-day fast."
The sun may travel to the west; from that time on, he ate only one gruel and one vegetable dish daily.

When the appointed hour arrived, he bathed and donned his cap, ordered his disciples to recite the names of the Seven-Jeweled Tathāgata, and after reciting the sutra himself, sat upright and passed away.
On the following day, his body was fragrant and pure as if alive (as recorded in the *Jingang Lingying*).

During the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, when the Grand Guardian Qi Jiguang served as Deputy Commander-in-Chief, he was leading troops to defend the Three Rivers against the chaos caused by the Japanese pirates.
He had long been devoted to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, never ceasing even while on the battlefield. One night, he dreamed of a soldier who had perished in combat, who said:
"Tomorrow, I shall send my wife to you to beg that you recite one volume of the *Vajracchedikā* for her sake."
The soldier’s wife came to seek deliverance on the following morning, exactly as she had spoken in her dream.

The next day, after the official had completed the recitation of sutras while observing a vegetarian fast, that night the soldier’s wife dreamed that her husband said to her: "I am grateful that the commander has recited the sutras for me;
however, because the recitation was interspersed with the word 'not used' (bù yòng), the merit is incomplete, and I have not yet escaped from suffering. The next morning, the soldier’s wife...
At dawn, he again appealed to the deity in a dream. The Duke was greatly astonished. He then recalled that while he was reciting the sutras, his wife had sent a maidservant to deliver tea and cakes;
the Duke saw her from afar and waved his hand to dismiss her. Although he did not speak aloud, his inner thought was, "I do not need these.
The Duke spoke of this matter to his attendants at the time, and the story subsequently spread. Master Dian Cheyong said: "While I was ill, I had a dream."
A divine being held a register and said, "This is a record of the transgressions of those who recite the sutras while harboring miscellaneous worldly thoughts. I took it and examined it;
all the names and transgressions of those who intermingled vulgar thoughts with their recitation were written therein. My own name was also listed at the end of the volume.
Having read it, I was struck with awe. He further said to me, "If one scroll of a sutra is interspersed with two different states of mind, try..."
Reflecting on the sutras one has recited throughout a lifetime, one should interweave them with various thoughts. Suddenly awakening from a dream, sweat poured down one’s back. Alas!
This is the luminous precept for both monastics and laity regarding the upholding of sutras. Tu Changqing said:

"Gu Yangqian, the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review in Tongzhou, was a man of lofty talent and unconventional spirit. His wife passed away first; he extensively performed Buddhist rites for her. Several years later—"
The Duke had a concubine who died suddenly. After one night, she revived and wept incessantly.

When the Duke questioned her, she replied, "After I died, I entered the underworld and saw my mistress shut me up in a dark chamber, saying, 'I am suffering here beyond description; you must quickly perform meritorious deeds to save me.
I asked, 'After my mistress passed away, the Master performed great acts of goodness—was all that of no benefit? My mistress said:"

He said, "In the performance of sutra recitations and repentance rites for the sake of the deceased, it is only when the presiding master maintains fasting and the utmost sincerity that sins can be extinguished and blessings increased.

Previously, while the śramaṇas were chanting in the hall, you, Excellency, were drinking and playing chess in your private chamber; what benefit could there have been in that? Upon hearing this, the official also wept bitterly.

He then selected and engaged renowned monks of virtuous precepts who were pure and solemn to establish a *dharmadhātu* (meditation hall) for three days and nights. This was [the beginning of] his long...
"You, who have witnessed this with your own eyes and recorded it in writing, would find even gambling and chess unacceptable; how much more so, then, alcohol and meat?
Recently, a monk named Jizhou from Juefeng Temple in Beijing was visited one day by a person in blue robes who said, 'I am the Unchang (Yama) of the Underworld.
A certain old woman is suffering the torments of hell and cannot escape. Because she made offerings to you, Master, during her lifetime, she now entrusts herself to you for rescue.'"
She vowed to recite one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, she knelt before the Buddha and chanted the *Lotus Sūtra*.
When she reached the fifth fascicle, she became extremely thirsty; unable to find tea, she found cold wine in the kitchen and drank several mouthfuls.
She then returned to the Buddha and completed the third fascicle. On the sixteenth day, Death came again and said, "The old woman..."
Relying on the power of his teacher’s recitation of the sutra, the golden light had already reached the underworld.

Just as it was about to leave the hells, suddenly from within the five volumes of the scripture, the entire hell became filled with the stench of wine, and [the light] could not emerge. When Zhongzhou heard this, his hair stood on end and his skin crept.

With utmost sincerity, he made a vow to recite the scripture on their behalf. Thus, to drink wine and eat meat while holding a scripture only serves to increase one's karmic burden (from the *Xin yi lu*).
During the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, a servant named Feng Qin from Mao Lumen of Guian consulted a diviner regarding his destiny.
He asked an elderly monk how he might extend his years. The old monk said, "As you are a person of low station, you lack the power to accumulate merit;

however, if you merely collect discarded paper with characters written upon it and recite the *Juxing jing* (Sutra for Prolonging Life), you may perhaps avoid an early death. Qin asked about the *Juxing jing*, and the old monk replied: "It is..."

He possessed a *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as well as a pair of bamboo tweezers and a bamboo basket. During the day, he would traverse every street and alleyway, plucking up all scraps of defiled or discarded paper and placing them into the basket.
He would wash them with scented water, dry them in the sun, burn them to ashes, and wrap the remains to cast them into a clear stream.

He did not dare to neglect even a single character. At night, upon returning home, he would kneel and recite one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to dedicate the merit. He maintained this practice for years.

He once tasted [the world]. Later, he gradually learned to read and became proficient in the meaning of texts. The people of Lumén treated him with courtesy. His household was prosperous and well-off; he had two sons and four grandsons.

He lived to the age of ninety-five and passed away without illness. As for written characters, they unify culture and facilitate universal communication and ease. Among the scriptures of the Three Teachings, there is none that does not rely upon them.
Those who treat them with contempt will surely receive an evil retribution, while those who respect and cherish them will naturally obtain the causes for merit. — By Lǎo [Zǐ].
The monk instructed Feng Qin to recite the *Sheshi* (拾) character as a means to prolong his life. There was no other method besides this;
its principle was truly earnest and its practice an especially swift path (from the *Xin yi lu*).

Yan Guangyu was a man of clear character who had inherited his family’s tradition of Confucian scholarship. One day, together with local gentry and elders, he attended a *Vajra* assembly to listen to the sutras and engage in discussion.
Returning home at dusk, he was filled with joy and admiration, desiring to investigate its profound meaning; however, as he was occupied with his official appointment, he found no leisure to do so.
Later, while serving as the magistrate of Tàihé County, he suddenly fell ill. He dreamed that two men dressed in green led him into the underworld;
the scene was dark and gloomy, solemn and horrific. After a short while, he saw the King. An official holding a register said, "Guāngyù’s allotted lifespan has already ended.

During his life, his karma was heavy due to his fondness for killing; he indulged in roasting and grilling, and moreover, he enjoyed eating oxen and dogs. There are now countless living beings [to be accounted for] before you."

The executioners seized him by the neck and led him away. The King sentenced him to be cast into boiling oil for smelting and refining. As the Ox-head Yama entered the seething cauldron, he saw a lotus flower shielding his body; the boiling liquid became clear and calm.
The ghost-judge reported this to the King, and with palms joined, requested an audience, asking: "By what merit was this karmic retribution transformed? Please examine the register of his good deeds.
It was found that he had performed the work of upholding the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra for a single day; having planted this golden [seed], [he was thus delivered].

"The body is of an indestructible diamond nature. The King said, "Excellent! May your lifespan and fortune be extended, and may you return to life. I shall universally exhort all people of the world to uphold [this teaching].
After he had returned to life for seven days, he never ceased his recitation and chanting thereafter, carving and distributing six thousand scrolls of the *Vajra* [Sūtra].
He served in official capacity as a Grand Councilor (Dàcān). At the age of seventy, upon his death, the fragrance of incense wafted through the village lanes.
He earnestly exhorted his descendants to uphold the most supreme scriptures from generation to generation. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
This was the sixty-sixth descendant of Yanzi; recorded by Dr. Bo Lian (*Konggang Lingying*).
Zhou Shaoyue of Kunshan, whose given name was Zhicheng, lost his sight at the age of fifty. His pupils turned inward and became the color of azure;
by day it was as if it were night. He considered himself useless to the world and devoted his whole heart to taking refuge in the Buddha to extinguish his past transgressions.
Every morning at dawn, he would solemnly recite three fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When reciting, he would chant aloud with great fervor. Even when guests arrived...
He did not perform ritual prostrations. Fifteen years passed, when suddenly one day he saw objects vividly before him; they appeared and then vanished.
Startled and uncertain, he ordered his family members to look, and they saw that the pupil of his left eye was flickering, revealing a single strand of light.

After two months and some days, his azure pupils gradually shifted, and the clear luster of both eyes was fully restored. Compared to his youth, he could now see even further into the distance. Little... [text fragment ends]

Yak was moved by the spiritual power of Vajrapāṇi, and his recitation of the sutras became increasingly devout. He passed away at the age of eighty. His ancestor, a man of one hundred and sixteen years known as Suye, possessed many hidden virtues.
King Taejo summoned him to the private audience hall and issued an edict for the practice of the *xiangyin* (local banquet) rite throughout the realm, beginning with this elder.

Yeol-sok was his eighth-generation descendant. His lineage flourished daily. [Note: The character "百" (bai) at the end of the final sentence appears to be a scribal error or an abbreviation; it is likely intended to mean "hundred" or refers to the number of generations.]
Bai Zhi paid his respects and said to Gu Bonian: "This is a recent event within my own district that I have heard about since childhood.

Now, because I am compiling these miraculous responses, I fear my account may be incomplete. Therefore, I have personally visited its direct descendant, Song Longfu, who produced this for me and bestowed it upon me."
Included here to transmit the account of this miracle (from the *Jingang Lingying*).

Ming Chen Mingyuan was a native of Xinghua Commandery who had formerly participated in the jinshi examinations. While traveling through Sizhou, he visited Puzhao Monastery and saw an elderly monk in tattered robes leaning against a tree reading a document on blue paper.
A light radiated from the book for some hundred paces; as he approached to look at it, [he saw...]
This is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with the verses of Fu Dashi from the Liang dynasty. The monk Gu Mingyuan said, "Do you also delight in this?
and subsequently bestowed it upon him. The following year, while serving as an official in Hailang under his father, he suddenly fell ill and died.

As the body was being prepared for the grand enshrouding, it became warm again; after a short while, he revived. He said that he saw four soldiers with deep-set eyes and tiger-like muzzles, who drove him toward the northwest with great violence.
The terrain they traversed was all vast wilderness, and dust covered his face as if he were in the midst of a mist.

As they drew near the great river, the government offices were strictly guarded. Three soldiers entered first, while one remained to guard Mingyuan. In a short while, a monk arrived, traveling through the air;
he was the same one who had bestowed the scriptures upon him at Sizhou. The Governor hurried out to meet him, casting a sidelong glance at Mingyuan.
The monk called Mingyuan forward and compelled him to repent. The Governor then ordered his officials to release him, and the monk led the way ahead.

I strolled along the two corridors and saw several hundred prisoners in confinement. Furthermore, there were various birds, beasts, and insects, all of whom could speak human language and engage in debate with the prisoners.
There were also five or six seated śramaṇas before whom were lined up dozens of jars of spoiled food and drink.

What I encountered on the road further showed that the local authorities, who had previously been so formidable and imposing, were now reduced to states of utter distress and disarray upon reaching this place.

Soon they reached the vast wilderness they had previously passed through, where the mountain stream was swollen to a great height. The monk grasped the handle of his staff and handed the end to Mingyuan, who took hold of it and they waded across together.
At first the water was shallow, but midway it suddenly became very deep; Mingyuan cried out in alarm and revived (from the *Mingyuan zai sheng zhuan*).
Li Shiying of Qiantang was a native of Ming. He served as the Magistrate of Qin Prefecture in Nanhai. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra*.

In the Dingmao year of the Longqing era, while serving as an assistant examiner, he died within the examination hall after three days. Initially, he saw a deity clad in golden armor who intended to take him away to see the Lord of Mount Tai.
The City God and the Local Deity were both present; however, because Li had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra*, the Local Deity [intervened].

Sengjian refused to sign his name. The deity in golden armor grew enraged; drawing a fire-nail from his sleeve that was over three feet long, he drove it through the crown of the local tutelary spirit’s head.
Immediately, the spirit was seen to be completely consumed by flames. In an instant, the deity returned to his original form. Sengjian remained stubborn and continued as before not to sign.

The deity in golden armor said, "I shall lock you up together and take you to Mount Tai. Suddenly, several ghosts appeared, crying out in grievance and demanding their lives. At that moment, [the deity] rebuked them.
In his previous life, Ying served as the Magistrate of Jiujiang. He accepted bribes and committed murder. In a moment of extreme panic, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Suddenly, he saw Master Lü descending from the clouds. The ghosts all fled in haste. At that time, Ying prostrated himself on the ground and begged for mercy.
Master Lü said, "Give me back my Lord Lao’s elixir! He stared intently at him and said, "Heavy karma! Heavy karma! It is a pity that the elixir has been completely ruined."
"It is all over. Recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and seek salvation from the Sixth Patriarch. Suddenly, the Sixth Patriarch arrived.
Seeing Shiying prostrate on the ground, he also said, "Heavy karma, heavy karma! I shall wait until I have consulted with the Fifth Patriarch. Shiying then reached out one hand.

He dragged the cassock of the Sixth Patriarch, and every fragment flew with golden light. After a short while, suddenly a wondrous fragrance filled his nostrils, and he heard the Fifth and Sixth Patriarchs commanding from the air:
"Let the reciter of the sutra go back. Immediately, he saw the previously mentioned god in golden armor arrive once more.

When Shi Tingying threw [the image] once, sweat fell like rain and he revived. Tingying then left the monastic compound and returned to Jingci Temple in Hunan, where he devoted himself to ascetic practice.
Every morning he would invariably recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to deliver deceased spirits from their grievances. He passed away without illness (as recorded in the *Xin yi lu*).
In the early years of the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Minister Zhong Gongfuxiu and Minister Xu Gongzunsou both resided in Luojia Lane in the capital.

They devoted themselves to the Buddha and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In a separate courtyard, they occupied several clean rooms where the two ministers sat side by side to chant and maintain their practice.

Zhong’s household had two white geese that, upon hearing the sutra and the recitation of the Buddha’s name, would follow behind the two ministers, walking along while making sounds as they went. They followed them wherever they went.
They did not depart. They held their heads high as if listening, following the sound of the wooden fish gong whether walking or stationary.

After several years, the two geese stood side by side before the scripture table and passed away. The two masters buried them on the grounds behind Jingye Temple, naming the site the "Tomb of the Geese Listening to the Sūtras."
Formerly, the venerable old śramaṇa Huiyuan of Jingying Temple was originally in his native village, where he raised a goose that followed him about to listen to the sutras.
When Huiyuan entered the capital, the goose remained in the temple, crying out loudly day and night. His disciples sent it into the capital and released it at the temple gate.

It was able to know when [the master] was in his private quarters; once he entered, it would become tame and familiar. Whenever he lectured on a sutra, it would enter the room and listen intently with bowed head.

When he spoke of other matters, it would flap its wings and fly out. Considering both cases together, the spiritual intelligence of this goose was like this, whereas that student reciting the sutra harbored distracted thoughts.
"To hear the sutras as if they were merely filling one's ears is truly worse than being among the beasts" (from the *Xin yi lu*).
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Sheng Zhide of Fengqiao in Suzhou received the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from the lecturer Xuanming.
He died suddenly of illness and was summoned to the underworld. There, he was subjected to severe torture by vengeful spirits and brought before the City God (Chenghuang) for interrogation.

His virtue and reasoning were upright; thus, he was permitted to observe the hells of the netherworld. Upon his release and return to the world, he saw the City God descend from his steps and address him, saying:
"In my previous life, I was a man of Jingzhou, surnamed Cao. Since ascending to the divine registers, my mother, Lady Zhang, has been reborn three times."

"Indeed, my female body has been barren. If you would act on my behalf to earnestly entreat the Illustrious Master to reverently recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Candrottarādārikāparipṛcchā Sūtra* five hundred times each, it is certain that I shall be transformed from a woman into a man. I shall be reborn with virtue; I respectfully request the Illustrious Master to undertake this."
The recitation was completed and the record was submitted; Guan Dongming composed a preface to commemorate it. The verse of Maitreya says:
"The parents present right now are none other than Śākyamuni and Maitreya. If one can make offerings to them, what need is there to seek merit elsewhere?
Thus, the Bodhisattva Śyāmaka gouged out his own eyes to save his parents, and their chronic illness was immediately cured. The Compassionate Youth made a vow to take their suffering upon himself.
The fire-wheel was instantly extinguished. The story of Huangmei supporting his mother has been recorded in the various regional records (*fangce*). Master Lianchi said:

"There are three kinds of filial piety in the mundane world, and one kind of filial piety that transcends the world. Although the City God had already ascended to the divine rank, [Huangmei] nevertheless sought to deliver his mother and transform her into a male.
If a filial son wishes to repay his parents' labors, why not take refuge in the Great Way? (From the *Xiaojiao zhai xují*).
Ming Wang Pan was a native of Shanyin and a jinshi of the Wanshi Jiaxu year. Once, while his uncle was playing with an infant at the gate, the child’s silver bracelet suddenly went missing.
At that time, Wang Pan’s father happened to be nearby and suspected it had been stolen by him. Pan—
His father was dissatisfied. He invoked the divine spirits with an oath, took the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and stepped upon it with his feet, causing it to split into various fragments.
Although he repeatedly ranked high in the examinations, he did not obtain a degree. One day at dawn, as he was going outside the city, he saw two white-bearded elders who said to one another:

Wang Pan, a distinguished scholar from Daxiansi Temple, was destined for the highest honors in the imperial examinations. However, because he had defiled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his name was now struck from the official registers.
Unaware of the reason, Pan returned home to question his father; his father told him of the previous matter, and Pan was greatly shocked.
He performed repentance before the Buddha and personally transcribed one scroll of a sutra. In that same year, he passed the provincial examination (xian-shu).

Upon returning home, he intended to transcribe another scroll, but before it was finished, he was dismissed from the Ministry of Education (Shang Chun-guan). Reaching the Jiashu year, he completed the transcription of the sutra and only then attained his degree.
Tu Long of Chishui witnessed this and recorded the account (from the *Jinyucheng Xují*).

During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Mr. Tu Long of Siming was widely recognized for his extraordinary talent. While serving as the Magistrate of Qingpu County, he suddenly encountered a malevolent ghost within the prison that threw the prisoners into chaos;
some of the prisoners even died as a result. When the prison officials reported this to him, Mr. Tu composed a written address to exhort the spirit of the prison, saying:
"If you are a god, how can you be a ghost? If there are those who died unjustly in this prison, it is the fault of the official; what has the prisoner done?"
Furthermore, Yu burned incense within the courtyard and secretly cremated a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

While he sat in prison, by the time of midnight, the next day he asked the jailers and guards, and the ghosts had vanished; their traces were completely gone. Mao Zongqi said: "The prisoner is a ghost that has not yet died;
the ghost is a prisoner who has already died. The ghost then kills the prisoner—this is creating karma within karma, and it is truly a source of confusion."
This is to manipulate [the spirit] in its place of movement, secretly incinerating the Vajra; yet it is in its place of immobility that it is subdued.

The ghost vanishes, and the prisoner remains unharmed. Both the hidden and the manifest are delivered. Were it not for the Red Water, how could one possess such eminent insight? (From *The Fruits of Recitation and Retention*).
Ming Dynasty: A fisherman from Haiyan named Zhang Yuan, along with his younger brother Zhen, returned home at night after casting their nets.

Upon reaching Qingsong Tang, they saw an extraordinary light upon the water’s surface that eclipsed the stars and moon. Suspecting there might be pearl oysters beneath, they dove into the water to retrieve it and found a stone casket.
Opening it, they discovered the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in gold; its radiance was unlike anything they had ever seen. Yuan placed it in his home.
In the hall, he dreamed at night of a deity clad in golden armor who said to him, "In your previous life, you were a laborer for the lecture platform of Dharma Master Changshui.
Because you lacked the aspiration for the Way, you have fallen back to this state. However, your past affinity has not been extinguished; I shall bestow upon you the Great Dharma.
You must maintain it with diligent recitation. Yuan initially declined on the grounds that he was illiterate, but the deity commanded him to open his mouth and cast a golden pellet into it.
A fragrant warmth entered his belly, whereupon he was startled awake. At dawn the next morning, he began reciting the scripture; it came as fluently as if he had practiced it for a long time.

At that time, in the year Jiashen of the Wanli era, Yuan went to visit the Great Master Daguan and related these events in detail. The Master further encouraged him to continue reciting the sutras and to dedicate the merit toward rebirth in the Western Paradise.
In the seventh month of the Dingchou year, Yuan said to his relatives and acquaintances: "My karmic burden of killing has been eliminated; my lotus pedestal..."

He manifested [his passing] without illness; sitting upright, he passed away. For those in this world who possess the proper capacity, awakening is easy to attain and it is easy to be roused from delusion.
It is like using millet to make rice; how could the timing of the fire be difficult? Furthermore, regarding those who have attained the Way since ancient times:
It is mostly found among those who are dull-witted and simple; conversely, those who are clever and sharp often lose it.
As for the brothers Zhang Yuan, their mastery lay in their illiteracy (from the *Jinyu cheng xují*).
The late Minister of Justice, Lord Jiang Bao, was a native of Danyang County. While he was in his study, he was suddenly pursued by two messengers and led into the underworld.
There, an official—wearing a towering crown and wide sashes, with a formidable retinue of guards—questioned him regarding the deeds performed by Jiang during his lifetime.

Before Bao could respond, another official stepped forward from the side and replied, "This man’s evils were many and his virtues few; he shall become a creature of a different species. The ghost-messenger then [led him away].
He then took a cowhide to drape over his body; though he draped it three times, he could not cover himself three times. The King marveled at this.

The official replied, "This man has heard nothing but the title of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and possesses no other wholesome karma. Jiang pleaded piteously for his release, saying that if he were to return to the world of the living, [he would repay the favor].
He maintained the recitation of the sutra for the rest of his life. The King, moved by his repentance and awakening, subsequently released him back into the world of the living.
From that time on, Bao observed the fasts and recited the sutras, humbled himself before the monastic community, and investigated the profound meaning of the *Vajracchedikā*.

He tirelessly expounded it to others. One day, he told his relatives, "At noon tomorrow, I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, he indeed heard celestial music and a wondrous fragrance; with palms joined, he passed away.

Recorded by the Layman Pu-men, Cao Feng, in the Wuli戊子 year. Whenever an ordinary person recites the scriptures, if they harbor even a single thought of distraction or a single thought of indolence, they will be unable to gain mastery for the rest of their lives.

After Master Jiang was awakened from his fall into decline, his chanting, upholding, and expositions of the teachings necessarily surpassed those of ordinary people; thus, it is not merely that he was free from ignorance.
His karmic offenses were extinguished, and he even foreknew his own passing into peace. Fragrant music came to welcome him;
how marvelous was the spiritual response of Prajñā! (From the *Jinyu cheng xují*).
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, when the Duke Wang Fanglu of Jintan was gravely ill, he became restless and agitated.

His son, Kentang, stepped forward and said, "Father, it is precisely at such moments that the power of your lifelong practice of mental cultivation can be most effectively applied. I pray you will clear your mind and listen as I recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Wang Fanglu nodded his head in agreement and gave the order to fetch the scripture. As the son recited it aloud, they reached the passage on the "mark of selflessness" (*anātman-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the four lines on the mark of non-self, he would suddenly laugh and say, "Afflictions are fundamentally non-existent; who would cling to a self-mark? He then joined his palms and passed away. An ancient worthy once said:

"The person of ultimate attainment possesses meditative concentration and wisdom in every thought-moment; how could they be disturbed at the moment of death? Ordinary people possess scattered and distracted thoughts in every moment;
how could they attain stability at the moment of death? Master Fanglu was long renowned for his cultivation; even when his illness was grave, he still—
Although he could not entirely avoid agitation, he was able to turn [his mind] with a single stroke; from this, one can discern the power of his prior consciousness.
When Master Sun’an reached the point of his final illness, he remained entirely unperturbed and composed, calmly exhorting his parents to listen to the sutras.
His conduct at the time of death was a supreme filial piety that far transcended worldly sentiments; it serves as a model for all sons. Formerly, Wen Zhong...
When Ou-yang Hsiu was about to die, he called his disciples and instructed them, saying: "In my youth, I was renowned for my literary works and strove to denounce the Buddhists.
Lately, however, I have suddenly heard their profound doctrines and was just beginning to investigate the true fruits of the path. I did not expect to pass away with my aspirations unfulfilled."
"You all must exert yourselves; do not tread the path of regret. Thus he spoke, and the veteran monk borrowed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from a nearby temple.

Having recited it to the eighth fascicle, he passed away while sitting peacefully. Furthermore, Yuan Gong Zongdao, in his later years, deeply repented that what he had studied and practiced was unrelated to birth and death.

He consequently focused solely on the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land to demonstrate to others. These two gentlemen may be said to have finally attained awakening at the end.
This is an account of Ming Shen Jihuan (from *The Fruits of Upholding and Retaining*).
He resided at Beiliqiao in Jiaxing and operated a green fruit shop. Every morning he would rise and invariably recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Whenever he went out, he would place the scripture in a small bag and suspend it from his chest, never failing in his recitation. [The year was] the Gui year of the Wanli era...
In the winter, I went to Mount Dongting to sell tangerines. Midway across Lake Tai, I was suddenly struck by a dragon-wind;

the surface of the lake turned pitch black, and my boat was tossed about like a leaf. My oars and paddles were completely lost, and massive waves rose like houses, surging more than ten feet above the vessel.
They had already sunk beneath the surface of the water. Amidst their cries for help, a sudden great force lifted the boat and pulled it out from amidst the waves, carrying it along as if flying.

In an instant, they reached the mouth of Wengjia. Upon landing, those on the shore all saw two deities in golden armor walking through the water, supporting the boat on either side as they approached. Those inside the boat knew that these were the Vajrapāṇis who had rescued them.

Jiù was moved by Shen’s profound virtue and came to be known as "Qingguo (Green Fruit) Shen of the Buddha Family. Chāngzōng rose and said, "What honeyed fruit is there upon the branches of the *huángbò* tree?
Old man Shen has cultivated the fruit and realized its fruition; he has saved himself and saved others—he is truly no mere man who seeks only his own liberation" (from the *Xīnyìlù*).
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Shen Guanghua of Jiahe once served as the Salt and Iron Commissioner for the two Huai regions.

On the day he retired to his estate, while sitting idly with his fellow countyman, Wu Song, the Director of Transport, they conversed at ease, each asking the other what he had been doing during the day. Shen said:
For twenty years, Shen had observed the vegetarian fast at dawn and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* more than twice through its two volumes.

Wu, however, had left it aside with indifference. Not long after, Wu suddenly rose one morning and hurried to see Shen, congratulating him by saying, "The young master will certainly pass the examination at the Southern Gate.
When Shen asked for his evidence, Wu replied, "Last night I dreamed that a deity said, 'A scholar-official in this commandery, because he has maintained..."
Regarding the merit of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, his son Yingde was destined for success. Upon waking, Master Jue recalled that Master Gong should fulfill this dream.
That autumn, Shen’s son Yingming indeed passed the provincial examination for the Imperial Academy (*Yingtian Xiangjian*).

It was widely heard that Master Shen upheld the *Vajracchedikā* with extreme devotion, never ceasing whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. He often traveled to the home of Ji Zi in the Eastern Suburb, maintaining single-minded concentration throughout the journey.
He maintained his recitations and, with a mind free from the four marks (*catur-nimitta*), cultivated all wholesome dharmas.

Having accumulated merit over successive lifetimes, his descendants have held their positions in the imperial examinations in continuous succession, making them the preeminent clan in Hezhou (from the *Xin yi lu*).

During the Ming dynasty, Mo Qinghong of Jiaxing encountered a man from Jinling at a sutra shop who requested scriptures. The man was muttering the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* under his breath.
Observing his facial features, [Mo] found him quite terrifying. He therefore asked the man, "For what reason are you reciting the sutra while on the road?
The man replied, "I am skilled with the pen and brush and have long served as a scribe. One day I died of illness and arrived before King Yama."

At the royal court, he was interrogated regarding his transgressions and evils committed during his lifetime; yet, employing his eloquence, he refused to submit. The King ordered the jailers to bring all his accusers and adversaries before him.
