He questioned them, saying, "These people have been driven to their deaths by your accusations. What further words do you have?

Seeing that there was nothing left to defend himself with, he then recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in a loud voice. The King stood up in solemn reverence; as the man continued to chant without ceasing, the King’s devotion grew even deeper.
The King immediately ordered that they be released for the time being. Their adversaries all cried out, "We have suffered this grievance for many years with no way to seek retribution.
Now that you have pursued us here, you must not let us go. The King said, "Their lifespan has not yet run its course; they were brought here because they committed evil deeds."
"Now you recite the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle with a loud voice; how can the Netherworld dispose of such a case? For now, let him return to life.

He is an evil man, and it will not be too late to pursue his debt and take your life once his transgressions have reached their full measure. Because of these circumstances, he has changed his ways and followed the good;
fearing that he might ultimately meet his karmic retribution, he recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily and dedicates the merit toward your deliverance."
Autumn, the ninth month of the Gengzi year of the Wanli era. *Qinghong Biji* (Notes from the Rainbow in Clear Skies). The harm caused by litigation and lawsuits is no small matter;

the profession of the scribe and the pen is the greatest. In this world, many trivial affairs become discordant; a single word that offends or irritates leads both parties to harbor resentment and feel unjustly aggrieved.

Fortunately, if one encounters a good person who mediates from within, the anger and hatred will immediately vanish. Or, if one falls into the hands of those who specialize in filing petitions or carrying lawsuits... [text continues].
You deceive Heaven and spread falsehoods, hoping to establish a standard for fees and appointing mediators to reap profit therefrom.

You disregard the original documents and the ruin of families, causing litigation upon litigation that entangles you for years on end. You sell your wife and children, yet cannot bring the matter to a close;
your life will end because of this, and by then, regret will be of no avail. Such is the cruel and poisonous nature of the calamities instigated by litigating attorneys.
The laws of yin and yang allow for no negligence or leniency. This letter was written on behalf of a person from Jinling, who was fortunate enough to be reborn through the recitation of sutras.
Had he not turned his heart toward the good, could the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* have served as a constant protective talisman? (From the *Xinyilù*).

Zou Yue of Kunshan was born with a simple and honest nature. He had never learned to read characters; although he made his living through small-scale business, he delighted in practicing expedient means.
Whenever he encountered hungry people or those with disabilities, he would joyfully give them a bowl of rice or a few coins without begrudging anything.

One day, while on the road, he met a wandering mendicant reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Yue set down his load of rotten wood to listen, and he memorized the passage: "No mark of self... [and so forth].
The four lines—"the mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, no mark of a life-span"—were never forgotten as he entered and exited [meditation].

One day, he fell ill and invited a monk to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. His younger brother, Zhen, was exceptionally brilliant in his studies and possessed a reputation for literary talent;

however, he was dissolute and did not believe in ghosts or spirits, and his conduct was often harsh and cruel. On this day, he was compelled to perform the ritual repentance on behalf of his elder brother. As he listened to the recitation...

When the scripture reached the fifteenth fascicle, his mind suddenly attained awakening. He joined his palms in reverence and offered praise, saying, "Our Confucian tradition has never known such a thing.

From then on, he placed his faith in the Triple Gem. On the tenth day of the tenth month in the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he was stricken by a seasonal epidemic and fell into a stupor, losing consciousness for over ten days. Only his chest remained warm; then, suddenly upon his bed, he awoke with a start.
He arose and told his family members: "I was escorted by the minions of the underworld outside the Chang Gate. Li Zuofang’s household has become an ox, its body entirely white.
I saw a deity clad in golden armor who said: 'Zhen has heard the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle and possesses great faith.'"

"How could I have entered this animal womb? With a single strike of his precious vajra upon [Wu]zhen’s head, he was awakened; Zhen turned back toward the realm of the living. He still felt an intense pain at the crown of his head.
Thereupon, he and his elder brother observed the fast and recited sutras day and night for over thirteen years. Wu Zhen passed away first without illness;
seven days later, Wu Yü suddenly said to his family, "At noon tomorrow, a sage will welcome me to the Western Land."
The following day, by noon, a rare fragrance filled the air. He bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away.

This case differs slightly from the version recorded by Zongqi and Wang Zaisheng due to errors in oral transmission; I have verified it against the *Lingying benji* (Record of Miraculous Responses) by Gu Bonian.
In the *xinchou* year of the Wanli era, Zhang Ai, an eunuch of the Shuncheng Gate, recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in his later years.

When he reached the point of death and was about to change his bedding, his family members instructed him, saying, "Do not forget your intention to maintain the recitation of the sutra. Zhang Ai took these words to heart; though he could not respond verbally, he remained focused on them.

He saw two green-clad youths pressing him down and saying, "You must go to the east of the mountains to take rebirth. His movement was like flying, and by noon he had already arrived in the eastern mountains.
There he beheld the mountains and waters of that land, as well as his parents who would receive him into birth; he loved them with a single mind and focused solely on upholding the sutra.
They were led along until they reached a palace hall; he suspected it was that of the Eastern Peak (Mount Tai), yet there were no ox-headed jailers present.
A person atop the hall, wearing a flat-topped crown, came forward to meet Ai-shi and said, "It is fitting for you to arrive at this place to take rebirth.

Ai replied, "I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* throughout my life; I only wish to be reborn in the Pure Land, I do not wish to take rebirth here. The crowned one said, "As for your recitation of the sutra..."
"His merit was small," [the monk] Ai said. "I have heard that even ten recitations can bring accomplishment; how much more so for one who has been upholding this sutra for several years?

The man wearing the cap then looked at his two green-clad attendants and said, "For now, send him back to uphold the sutra. Ai had already been dead for nine days, yet his heart remained warm and he had not yet been encoffined.

He subsequently revived and left his home to dwell at Biyun Temple on the Western Mountain, where he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This was the eleventh [instance].
In his later years, one day he gathered the assembly and said, "By the power of my upholding this sutra, I shall now depart for the West. He sat upright and passed away.
The Buddha can know the natures of all beings and exhaustively understand the events of billions of kalpas; yet, he cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic affinity.

Zhang Jian upheld the sutra with the vow to be reborn in the Pure Land and, upon his death, succeeded in departing for the West. This was certainly due to the mutual support of his vow-power, as well as the fulfillment of causes and conditions (from the *Xin yi lu*).
In the Ming dynasty, in the Baozhong Ward of Jiaxing Prefecture, there was a servant of the Fan family whose name has been lost to memory.
When the layman Wang Zaisheng was young, he saw this man daily carrying a shoulder-pole of vegetables through the marketplace, chanting incessantly under his breath.

Hearing that he rose early to attend to his work, he would invariably first burn incense before a Buddha image and kneel to recite several scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before departing; at evening, he would likewise do so.

He proceeded to the Buddha Hall of Kimmyeongsa Temple. After prostrating before the Buddha and dedicating the merit, he returned home. Along the way, whenever he encountered living beings, he would reduce his own expenses to purchase them and set them free.
Whenever he met beggars or the sick, he would diminish his own food to give it to them. When the head of the household gave him permission, his wife was unwilling;
however, he eventually consented to leave the household life. He went to Master Daejeong of Samtasa Temple, shaved his hair, and became a disciple. For several years, he worked with diligent effort.

He devoted himself to his duties; all the arduous labors of the meditation hall, he undertook personally, never once complaining of weariness. One day, he manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying:
"In a previous life, I was negligent in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and for this I was punished by being made a human slave.

Now my term has ended, and I shall go to a good realm to take birth. He then suddenly closed his eyes and passed away. Whenever one recites a sutra, one must strictly maintain purity and solemnity, burning incense and focusing the mind with single-minded devotion.
When reciting and upholding [the scriptures], and when making offerings to the sutras, one must use brocade cloths and jade cases. The altar and desk must be kept clean and pure;

no meat, alcohol, or miscellaneous items shall be placed there. Furthermore, they must not be carried into the chambers of women. The sin of such sacrilege is most severe according to the laws of the underworld.

Because Fan Pu was negligent toward the Vajra [deity] and was punished by being made a laborer, it is evident that he must have possessed roots of goodness from a previous life, which enabled him [to encounter this teaching].

Throughout one's life, by performing recitations and liturgies, replacing indolence with diligence and laxity with reverence, one will be reborn in a virtuous realm; that such a response occurs is a truth not to be doubted.

Furthermore, I have often seen ordinary people suddenly struck by lightning or executed by divine punishment, where not only do bystanders fail to understand the cause, but even their own families remain ignorant of the nature of their transgressions.
One must realize that these are all brought about by the influence of past karma. Or...
Question: "If these are the results of past karma, why were they not manifested as retribution in that very lifetime, but instead deferred until a future one?

In that case, it would be 'A acts and B receives,' which would be utterly disconnected from the original cause. How can this be? Answer: "Rebirth in the present life is the flower; rebirth in a future life is the fruit.

It may be that the karmic reward has not yet been exhausted and the force of the karma is still delayed; or it may be that the retribution of the present life is difficult to fully atone for, resulting in punishment being endured life after life. This is like the cases of Bai Qi and Li Linfu."

This refers to those such as Fu. To know [the truth] is itself not-knowing; yet when one undergoes [retribution], one truly undergoes it. Though the physical form is changed, the spirit-consciousness does not alter.
Thus, in the underworld, there is certainly no distinction between "A" and "B," or "self" and "other" (from the *Xinyi lu*).
During the Xinhai year of the Wanli era, there was a wealthy merchant from Huainan named Hu Ran, a native of Guanzhong. His wife, née Wu, was forty years old;

she was fond of doing good but had no children. A monk exhorted her, saying, "If you can carve copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and bestow a complete set [of the Tripitaka] as alms, you will certainly give birth to a son as rare as a qilin. Ran was moved by these words and acted accordingly, further donating a coffin.
He buried [the remains] and covered those skeletons that had been exposed. In this manner, over more than ten years, his meritorious practice was perfected.

He invited a community of forty-nine monks and established a seven-day and seven-night *dharmapūjā* site. Suddenly, he dreamed of a divine being who told him: "Do not worry about the delay of your son.
The Supreme Deity has minutely examined whether your vow is sincere and whether your mindfulness has remained unchanging from beginning to end. He is about to select..."
Those whose fortune and longevity were both complete were elevated. After one year had passed, his concubines successively gave birth to three sons, all of whom were intelligent and precocious.

When the couple exceeded seventy years of age, their household prosperity flourished even further. Among those in the world who cultivate goodness, the most feared are regression and leakage [of merit].
Although Lord Hu’s power of aspiration was vast, the Supreme Deity still strictly scrutinized him. Because his virtuous deeds were pure and enduring, he naturally obtained such results.
Mental merit is the cause [of such results] (*from the Jinyu Cheng Xují*).
Formerly known as Xiang Dexin, Vice Minister of Rites Xiang Hixian dreamed that he had been selected in the provincial examination of the Xinmao year;

however, because he had defiled two young maidservants, his name and record were removed from the divine registry. Thereupon, he diligently practiced deeds of sowing virtue and donated his wealth to entreat his friends [to assist him].
Gāosōng was skilled at calligraphy and carved woodblocks for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, distributing them annually for over ten years.

Once, he dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where he saw a name on the eighth position on a yellow paper scroll. The surname was Háng; the middle character was blurred, though the final character appeared to be Yuán.
A person standing beside him said, "Examine this closely; this is your rank on the Celestial Register. Consequently, he changed his name to Mèngyuán in the *Renzi* year of the Wanli era.
In the provincial examination of Shuntian, he ranked twenty-ninth; in the metropolitan examination of Jiwu, he was second. Everyone wondered why his rankings did not correspond.

It was only when he reached the palace examination that he was placed fifth in the second rank (di'ermen), whereupon it became clear that his positions were consistent with the numerical sequence of the top three ranks (dingjia).

Coincidentally, the placards for both the provincial and metropolitan examinations were white, while the palace examination placard alone was yellow—this was truly a matter of divine ordination. According to Mr. Mao Zongqi: [End of Excerpt]

In the *Wanli* era, the year of *Bingwu*, at the age of seventeen, he already believed in and upheld the *Daoshang Ganying Pian*. He would recite it with solemnity on the first and fifteenth days of every month without fail.

In the year of *Wu-wu*, when he sat for the examinations, he suffered from a carbuncle that nearly proved fatal. Upon entering the examination hall, he was in a state of profound stupor as if dreaming;

at night, though he lit a candle, his eyes were so blurred by the scrolls and grids that he did not know where to begin writing. After leaving the hall, he lay in bed all day long, unable to remember a single word.

After the announcement of the results, it was customary to go to the Academy to submit a personal affidavit. The characters on my ink-written scroll were so upright and precise that they did not resemble my usual handwriting when my mind was clouded;
truly, this must have been divine assistance! In the year Jiwu (1759), after failing the examinations, I first made a vow to add annotations to the *Ganying Pian* (Treatise on Retribution).

As I finished annotating each section, I would have it printed and then burn the manuscript before the deity. Reflecting upon this, I considered that lust damages one's virtue more severely than anything else, and thus I specifically addressed those instances where scholars had willfully committed such offenses.
Furthermore, regarding the section on "conceiving a private desire upon seeing the beauty of another's form," the retributions are detailed therein to assist in vigorous self-reflection.
On that day, the transcription was prepared by Luo Xianyue of Nanchang, who served as the tutor at the academy of Mr. Bijing.
In the *xin-you* year, I returned to the academy. It had been eight years since we parted. On the second day of the first month of the *wu-chen* year, during the night, I dreamed of three immortals.
An old man with a weathered face and yellow robes stood in the center, flanked by two youths wearing purple garments who attended him on his left and right.
The elder produced a volume and, looking toward the left, said, "Read this. The youth standing to the left recited it aloud, whereupon the elder said, "It is appropriate."
Turning back, he looked at the one standing to his right and said, "Try composing a poem. The man immediately responded with these words:

"Greedy for plucking the cassia in the Palace of Cold Radiance, How could he have known that the three thousand colors are empty? Having seen through the deluded eyes of the world, The moment the flower appears on the placard, the whole city turns crimson.
The old man smiled and departed. Luo eavesdropped and learned that this was from the *Sōshō Ōkanpō* (The Responsive Manifestations of Mount Song).
The two lines regarding "seeing another’s beauty" are a commentary. Xing wrote a letter to Bijing; when the examination results were posted, Gong indeed passed.

However, he did not understand the meaning of the term "banner-flower" (*bǎnghuā*). Upon consulting a lexicographical compendium, it states that during the Tang Dynasty’s Dazhong era, those with rare surnames who appeared on the examination list were called "banner-flowers.
Now, considering the case of Lord Xiang, one begins to believe that the granting or withholding of fame and office all depends upon the gateway of physical appearance.
One must be most careful in making such distinctions. Generally speaking, among the three grave offenses of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the root of lust is the most difficult to uproot.

When a sharp blade is held before one, even those with flesh upon their chests feel compassion; yet when it comes to breaking into homes or climbing over walls—acts that fall within the same category—one considers them minor and does not refrain from them.

Once one is submerged in the waves of the ocean of desire, one sinks to the very bottom and accepts it with a willing heart. Even if one possesses a beautiful countenance or white hair, such affections are as fleeting as dew, and as for those who have broken...
It ruins one's reputation; it causes decline in youth and illness in middle age. Regret comes too late, and such instances are not few. It is most easily where one loses one's footing:

when the soul is startled and the spirit flies away at that single, sudden moment when the object of passion stands before one—a moment so abrupt that it is difficult to restrain. Within this single moment...
The laws of the state do not reach him; the clear judgment of public opinion is not enough to inspire fear; his reputation and integrity need not be considered.

There is only the two words "cause and effect" that might perhaps suffice to restrain him. Within the realm of cause and effect, moreover, there is but the single path of fame and achievement sufficient to divert him.
It requires nothing more than a momentary resolve to maintain it, and one can thereby move the response of the Lord of Heaven—when compared to a lifetime spent with yellow scrolls and green pages.
Lamp! To others, it serves as a path for accumulating benevolence and merit, achieving double the result with half the effort.

How can one who is not utterly foolish fail to feel deep remorse and exert themselves? Otherwise, they will claim to possess unique elegance and call themselves "plants of emotion," yet by this they diminish their fortune, by this they steal their lifespan, by this they bring about their own death, and by this they fall into kalpas of suffering. Why, then, suffer for the sake of a moment’s pleasure?

Consider the calamities and harms of birth and death! Since the retribution for lust is so grave, the merit of guarding against lust and the karma of inciting it must both result in no light retribution.

Recent cases, such as those of the concubines in the *Yīnshǐ* (History of Lasciviousness) who early ascended the registers of ghosts, and the accounts in the *Jīnpíng* (Golden Pitcher) which clearly describe their punishments, are manifest facts that are deeply sufficient to cause people to reflect with trepidation. (Cited from the *Shòuchí Guǒbào*).
Wen Borin of Wufeng in Mingzhou was skilled in poetry and painting; he was a court attendant and the nephew of Zheng Ming.

Once, while lodging at a commoner’s house after reporting a runaway servant to the county office, he dreamed that two men dressed in green arrested him, whom he took to be county officials. He followed them along.
He arrived at a public office whose halls and buildings were so vast and grand that they seemed not of this world. At first he was terrified, thinking there was a sovereign above him.
The Sovereign rebuked him, saying, "Many have brought lawsuits against you; what will you do? Wen pleaded his lifelong life as a scholar, claiming he was innocent.

The Sovereign laughed and said, "I have forgotten. He then ordered an official to rub a blue pellet over Wen's crown. A coldness pierced through to his heart, and he suddenly realized his former life.
During the Zhengtong era, Wang served as a eunuch in charge of the Changling Mausoleum. In winter, he excavated a pond and killed over a hundred hibernating snakes.
Suddenly, a swarm of snakes gathered and bit him. Wang then looked at an official and said, "This is but one man; how can he possibly repay the debt for these countless lives?
When examining his many past lives, could there not have been even a single act of goodness? The official produced several volumes of records; Wang read them.

After a long silence, he said, "There is such a person. During the Yongle era, he once painted two arhats on the corridors of Mount Jiuming and transcribed one copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King said, 'That will suffice,' and instructed him: 'Your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted;
return at once to transcribe scriptures to expiate your sins and deliver sentient beings. He then awoke. Wufeng had previously lacked faith in Buddhism, but from that time forward, he made a vow."

He transcribed scriptures and recited the Buddha’s name, never flagging despite the cold or heat. Feng Jiqu carried his account in the *Kuài Xuě Táng jí* (Collected Works from the Hall of Swift Snow).
Gu Bóniàn remarked: "Wǔfēng transcribed only a single scroll of scripture, and that was several generations ago; yet even several generations later, he still relied upon it for rebirth.
The Sūtra says, 'The retribution of karma is inconceivable. It is thus, it is thus" (*Quotation from the *Jīngāng Língyìng*).
In the second month of the Jia-yin year of the Wanli era, Wu Yide of the local school in Huizhou accompanied his uncle Ansheng to study at Lindang Temple.

There, he sought instruction from Master Pumen and attained a realization. He made a vow to observe a vegetarian diet and transcribed thirty copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to distribute as gifts.
Having just finished copying three copies, on the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month, while bathing casually in Qinxī Creek, he suddenly fell ill. One—

At night, his breath ceased. Because his mind was burning with fever, his family members did not dare to place him in the coffin. Anmo (Anmo) recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for him. After eight days had passed, he suddenly revived.
He rose and supported himself by clutching his waist, crying out repeatedly that his back was in unbearable pain. Gradually his breathing steadied; when questioned, he said:
He said, "Yesterday, while bathing in a stream, I suddenly saw two men in blue robes escorting me away toward a place of deep gloom.

There were many fellow sinners traveling with me, and the infernal guards each held iron clubs and struck them on their backs. Only because I had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* during my life did I not receive such blows.
We gradually reached the shore of the Black Sea; within the sea were beings resembling humans and animals, possessing strange and monstrous forms."
The manifestation: emerging from and submerging into one’s head, a state of terror and unprecedented experience. One enters a city;

within the city, fences line the perimeter, and those who have committed offenses are all inside the enclosures, looking out with upturned faces. There, one encounters deceased brothers and sisters, all coming to borrow silver to divide among themselves for use.
He further requested one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying, "My family has come to recite the scripture for my elder brother and will bring silver.

Shortly thereafter, they indeed arrived, and he distributed it to them. Two green-clad youths urged me forward, and we entered another small city. Looking outside the walls, the scene was even more chaotic;
the instruments of execution, such as knives and saws, were of a kind not found in the human world. In a brief moment, we reached the hall before Lord Yama. The hall...
On the left was the Office of the Four Births; on the right was the Office of the Four Deaths. Suddenly, more than one hundred and eighty people appeared, demanding my life.
Utterly bewildered and unconscious, the ghost-judges led me to the Clear Water Pool. They washed my chest with water until all five internal organs were visible;
only then did I realize that I had been mistakenly killed by a general in a previous life. I was then brought before the Hall for adjudication, where it was stated that [I had died] in battle.
I mistakenly killed [him]. How could I possibly repay this? Lord Yama was struck with rage and summoned me for the ultimate punishment.
Suddenly, the earth split open, and a being with a fiery face and a green body leaped forth from within, holding a great cauldron of boiling oil and binding me to cast me into it.
Just then, I heard the sound of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* being recited; a single beam of golden light shone up to the Senla Palace, and the ghosts—
The judge commanded him to kneel and said, "You have arrived from the West. Lord Yama came out to welcome him and saw two giants in the air raising hammers to strike them into cauldrons;

in both cases, golden lotuses welled up in boiling water. [The deceased] made this vow: "If I am permitted to return to life, I shall fulfill my pledge to copy the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
Furthermore, beyond the thirty scrolls he had previously produced, he transcribed another one hundred and eighty scrolls to deliver to his karmic creditors.

He heard a voice from above calling for two men wearing yellow turbans to escort him back. The path they traveled was entirely different from the previous route; they gradually reached a place of radiant light.

Suddenly, as they crossed a steep ridge, the two men in yellow turbans pushed him down. He felt himself fall and suffered great pain in his waist before rising. From that time on, his virtue flourished.
The entire family observed the vegetarian precepts. [This was] written by Shi Jingang. The account by Vice Minister Wu is as recorded above.
Wang Zaisheng’s *Record of New and Strange Things* differs slightly from Tang Yizhi’s *Jinyucheng*. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*:

"If a person uses paper and ink to have others transcribe, or transcribes for themselves the True Canon of the Tathāgata, and bestows it upon others for recitation and reading, this is called the Dharma..."
Generosity. Wu Yi-de made a vow to transcribe this scripture and immediately obtained deliverance from the suffering of the oil cauldron in the Western Realm.
This is what is meant by "merit is never in vain. Some may ask: "How can one possibly repay for every instance of accidental killing on the battlefield?

In the past, a Chan Master, having accidentally injured an earthworm in a previous life, joyfully offered his own life as retribution when the worm reached maturity. When a great army passes through, [the merit protects] Yu...
Even stones are consumed by fire; yet a single thought of compassion can divide their heads. A movement that concerns the lives of thousands and tens of thousands—be cautious of it, reflect upon it!
(From *Jinyu cheng xují*).
Wang Liguo of Tiantai, whose courtesy name was Bemu, passed the provincial examination in the *bingwu* year of the Wanli era.

He dreamed that his father, the Grand Councilor (Dazhongcheng) Wang Shixing, instructed him that he had a period of "five deaths" spanning ten years. Subsequently, events occurred that somewhat corroborated this.

He composed a poem recording the dream and then, before the Three Treasures of Jiahe, vowed to observe a lifelong fast and receive the Tiantai precepts against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

He violated the four precepts regarding falsehood. Later, while serving as the Magistrate of Xingan County in Jiangxi, these matters were all abandoned. In the year Wumu, he went to the imperial court for an audience.
On the evening of his departure, he again dreamed of his father, who admonished and instructed him earnestly; his heart was filled with great anxiety.

One day, while his boat was moored at Digang, after the second watch had passed, two men in green robes suddenly appeared holding talismans and escorted him to a certain place, which was magnificent and majestic like that of a sovereign.
There resided several thousand people under a single jurisdiction, filling the courtyard. Some were bound in shackles; others wore official caps and robes.

The presiding official sat upright upon his throne with the ceremonial crown and pendants, while two ministers sat to his left and right, each leaning against a desk. The attendants standing nearby were of extremely fierce and hideous appearance.

The official called out the king’s name and rebuked him in a stern voice, saying, "If your allotted lifespan were to end according to the manifest destiny, it would have been in the eighth month of the Bingchen year.
That it has been extended until now is due to the power of your fasting and purification. Why then do you abandon it? He ordered the registers to be brought and showed them;

beneath the king's name, the years and months were all annotated, yet from the eighth month of the Bingchen year onward, the space was blank. After Guo had finished reading, he prostrated himself and said, "While holding office, I relied on my power..."

"It cannot be helped," the official said. "It is indeed so. But what can be done when one's lifespan is exhausted? He ordered him driven into prison. Immediately, fierce-looking demons arrived, appearing as if they were dragging and binding him.
To his left sat a presiding official who stood up and requested, "Let us examine the records concerning his transgressions after he broke the precepts.

In a moment, an attendant arrived carrying two large baskets on his shoulders; these were all the sealed scrolls of the case files. Altogether, there was one— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.)
He displayed a letter, along with various casual writings from his daily life; even the slips of paper no larger than a square inch were all present.
Each of these emitted a vapor: some black, some blue, some reddish-white. The presiding official ordered that each be examined separately.
First, he examined the black and blue ones, which formed a mass; next, he examined the white mass and the red mass. After a while, the blue vapor gradually faded, and the black vapor shrank.

It was like a pair of chopsticks; the red one stood out conspicuously. As he looked around the assembly from beside the hub, he saw that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Hao-sheng-bian*, and the *She-cang* (Community Granary) scrolls were all present.
After the presiding official had finished reading them, his voice softened slightly, and he turned to the subordinate officer, saying, "This man still knows how to cultivate virtue.
Would it not be right to sacrifice five of his senses to preserve his life? Thereupon, he ordered the fierce guards to step forward.
He died. They gouged out his eyes and placed them atop a pillar in the palace hall; they emitted a brilliant, shimmering light.
As Guo thought to himself that his eyes had been gouged out and he could no longer see, suddenly everything grew dark, and neither the palace officials nor the guards could see anything.
He only felt someone patting his back, saying, "Go quickly! Go quickly! After a short while, he stumbled and woke up; it was already cockcrow, and he heard his family members gathered around him.

Jiusheng heard a commotion and questioned them; they said it had been since the second watch. Consequently, he fell into a deathly sleep and did not wake. To this day, his hands and feet are ice-cold, and his mouth and teeth remain tightly clenched.
The physician diagnosed him with "chill-induced collapse" (zhong han jue) and administered medicinal enemas seven times.

When Guo opened his eyes, he saw the lamps and candles as if they were piercing needles; he was utterly unable to open them. The next day, the physician administered eye-opening medicine. That night, he dreamed that someone again...
The nails were driven into his eyes, and the pain became so intense that he finally rejected medical treatment.

Resolving to resign from office and return to his hometown, he later recited the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtras*, renouncing his home to cultivate the Pure Land practice. One night in the year Gengshen (1800), he dreamed that Avalokiteśvara applied willow-branch nectar to his eyes.
Rising at dawn to perform prostrations and repentance, he suddenly saw objects clearly; both eyes were restored to sight. Thus it passed.
He traveled to the gates of Yunqi and Boshan. Twelve years later, he was reborn and named Master Biri. Mo Zongqi said:
"This single case serves as a warning in three respects: first, one knows that breaking the precepts will inevitably result in retribution;

second, one knows that planting roots of goodness can prolong one's life; and third, one knows that for those in office, every word and every movement is observed by the officials of the netherworld."
It is recorded that one must constantly keep in mind the blue, black, red, and white vapors (as noted in the *Huisheng zijì*).

In the Ming dynasty, there was a commoner named Long Yi from Langzhou who supported himself by manual labor. Once, while visiting his parents who were ill, he happened to see someone copying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Without cause, Yi reviled and rejected it; suddenly, he became mute and unable to speak. Neither medical treatment nor prayers brought any result. Later, he again heard a neighbor...
There was one who, upon recollecting this sutra, reproached himself bitterly, saying: "In the past, I slandered this sutra and incurred this disease of muteness.

Now, repenting my transgressions, I vow to honor and uphold it for the rest of my life; I do not know if I shall yet be able to speak again. From then on, whenever he heard the sound of the sutra being recited, he would lean against the wall and listen.
For more than a month, he focused his mind single-mindedly on this. One day, he entered a temple and encountered an elderly monk, whom he greeted with reverence. The monk asked him:

"Where have you come from? [The monk] meant this to refer to the man's mute condition. The monk said, "I shall treat it for you," and after cutting under the tongue several times with a blade, the man was able to speak.
He then recited the scriptures with him, and his voice was no different from that of a neighbor. When he went to visit him again later, he did not find him there.
On the wall was a painted image that was remarkably lifelike. A monk of the temple said, "This is Subhūti. Only then did Yi realize it was a manifest response of the Bodhisattva.
He subsequently made a vow to uphold the Mahāyāna for the rest of his life and prostrated before the painted image (from *Bimyeong*).
Ming Cai Huaiting was a native of Chu. While serving as Magistrate of Jiaxing, he maintained personal integrity and loved the people. He observed a lifelong fast and devoted himself to the Buddha;

during his leisure time, he would recite only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Within his official residence, there were no superfluous possessions. The Magistrate’s constitution had always been frail; he himself said that when he was still a common scholar (*zhusheng*),...
I encountered a grave illness; being poor, I lacked medicine. Facing death at my side, I made a vow to recite and uphold this sutra for the remainder of my life.
Gradually I recovered, passed the imperial examinations, and now serve as an official with my remaining years. I have vowed to bring this sutra with me here.

He also took this sutra with him when he departed. Thus, he ultimately fulfilled his duty, never fearing those who were powerful or oppressive. He regarded the people as if they were wounded; for food, he ate only spoiled vegetables and never purchased meat.

For clothing, he wore only cloth robes and never purchased silk. He frequently used this sutra, along with texts on the prohibition of killing, to publish and propagate for the purpose of exhortation and transformation.
Indeed, while a scholar is immersed in his studies at the snowy desk, he must resolve to purify himself and love the people.
It is so. Once one enters official service, one immediately falls into the midst of social obligations, bribery, and corruption.
When those above have needs, one is compelled by circumstances to take from those below. Greed is coupled with cruelty; desire renders one lacking in integrity.

The resulting lashes and cries of distress exhaust the people’s meager funds—money obtained from selling wives and children—yet it can never purchase the favor or a smile from those in power. This is truly pitiable; this is truly lamentable.
Furthermore, Lord Cai possessed no superfluous belongings; thus, he was able to regard the people as if they were his own wounds and did not fear powerful oppressors.

This is truly sufficient as a model for later generations serving in office. From the time he took up his post until he left it, he carried with him nothing more than a single volume of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*, which he regarded as accompanying him like a zither or a crane—far surpassing those who merely provide themselves with entertainment, as this constitutes a truly practical course of conduct (from the *Xin yi lu*).
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Mr. Wang Keshou of Huangmei was performing the Lianghuang Sūtra Repentance on a boat.
On the fifth day, at midnight, a stone casket struck the vessel. A crew member reported this to Mr. Wang, who took it and opened it to inspect its contents.

Inside were thirty-two copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, each written in a different style of seal script (*zhuàn*) such as he had never before seen. Mr. Wang carried them with him to the Northern Capital.
On the day of Wumu, [the inscription] was engraved upon the wall of Mahānanda. Following each section, a passage in regular script (zhengshu) was appended;
all were by famous calligraphers of the time, such as Huang Shunxuan, Jiao Ruohou, Dong Sibai, Mi Youshi, and Xing Ziyuan.

The exquisite calligraphy was so finely engraved that it reached the pinnacle of magnificence. Scholars and gentlemen visited the site daily to strike their seals upon it, until the stele eventually became blurred and worn.
The resident monk of the hermitage raised funds to procure new stone slabs, intending to solicit famous calligraphers to engrave it anew.

In the ninth month of the Taichang era, Li Tengfang, a Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Instructor to the *Shuji* (Graduate Scholars), suddenly dreamed one night that the deity of the monastery said: "In Mahā Hermitage, there is a Vajra..."
The scripture was completed through the superior conditions provided by Lord Qi and his disciples.
On the following day, Lord Li visited the hermitage and saw twenty slabs of fine stone already ground and polished within the meditation hall.
At that time, thirty-two people were residing in the guest quarters, including Hou Mengze, He Xianggang, Liu Pengxuan, Chen Juyi, Yao Mengchang, Gu Jiuchou, and Kong Yuheng.

The various gentlemen of Qiutao were all skilled calligraphers. The Master specifically spoke of his dream to them, and each of them transcribed one portion in stone using the *kaishu* (regular script).
They contributed their stipends to recruit master craftsmen to complete the carving and installed it between the walls, thereby restoring the site to its former splendor.

Formerly, Dongpo inscribed a colophon for Kou Xindao’s transcription of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, stating: "From the year Yisi until now, twenty-eight years have passed; thirty [copies] of the scripture have been transcribed."
Of the two, more than one-third have passed away. Yet, the merit of their single-minded devotion remains unblemished through kalpas.

Furthermore, my younger son Guo has transcribed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* to assist his mother’s rebirth in the Pure Land. He wept and said to Dongpo: "The labor of copying this scripture is but slight; yet I dare hope for a bountiful reward.
I must recite it with my mouth and master it with my mind, and write it with my hand and embody it in my conduct. Only then—
They are able to move the Buddhas and Patriarchs and deliver those in the dark realms of the netherworld; all of these are those who have grasped the great meaning of copying the scriptures.
It is essential that we, too, understand this (as recorded in the "Fruits and Rewards of Receiving and Maintaining").
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, there was Wen Xiang Nan Yu-fa, a native of Changzhou who served as the Governor of the two prefectures of Wei and Hui.

By nature he was upright and straightforward, and he did not believe in the teachings of Śākyamuni. Later, while ill, he dreamed of traveling to the underworld and first realized that the hells were no mere fiction;

he subsequently turned his attention to the Buddhist scriptures and came to place particular faith in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Every morning, he would rise early and recite it with solemnity once through. His family members would wait for him to finish his recitation.
After twenty *fen* [of the day], they would immediately take their meal; this was their constant practice.

Together with his old friend, the Duke of Honggang, they would sit beneath the trees and, whenever they gathered, would recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* back-to-back. If they missed a single character, they were fined one *liang* of silver.

Consequently, the two gentlemen became extremely proficient in their recitation, sometimes completing dozens of scrolls in a single day. Later, his elder brother, Lord Zhanchi Gong Zhenmeng, became the Grand Champion (*Da Kui*) of the imperial examinations.

He had also once personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā* in clerical script for carving onto stone. There was a man from Jiading named Wu who, one day while lying in his guest chamber, dreamed that he entered the realm of the underworld.
Terrified and at a loss for what to do, he was suddenly led by someone through a small gate.

Inside, he saw a majestic and magnificent hall containing a Dragon Treasury (*nāgagarbha*), guarded on its sides by armored soldiers. Upon opening and inspecting the sacred volumes, they were seen to be solemnly adorned, with each scroll clearly labeled.
Wen Yuanfa mentioned his name, and when Wen was questioned about it, he replied, "These are all the passages I have been reciting in my daily life.
Upon waking, Wen recounted his dream to Mr. Wen of the same academy, who was the elder brother of [Wen] Xiangnan. Only then did he believe in such spiritual wonders.
From that time on, both Wu and Wen continued their recitations without ceasing. Wu Yusheng said, "The person with the utmost faith in the world must surely..."

It begins with a lack of faith. Generally, those of great capacity turn [from delusion] upon a single nudge and never again fall back, as was the case with Xiangnan (as recorded in Wu Yusheng’s *The Karmic Retribution of the Diamond Sutra*).

During the Ming dynasty, when Lord Zhu Gongjing of Wumen was living as a private citizen, there was a wandering monk who came to beg for food. For his single meal, he received only one *dou* of grain.

On this particular day, the monk received three sets of alms in succession, which startled the people in the market. When word of this reached the Lord, he invited the monk in to converse with him. The monk was skilled at discussing the law of cause and effect.
The Lord asked, "I do not know whether those of our class can escape [karmic retribution]. The monk replied, "Retribution in the afterlife does not distinguish between the noble and the lowly."

The wise despise the foolish, yet they bestow their gifts impartially. If you, my lord, wish to know the causes and effects of the afterlife, you should pray to the spirits in whom you have faith to seek a dream as an omen.
You, my lord, invited a monk to stay overnight; following these instructions, there was a miraculous sign. At dawn, you rose and informed the monk.

The monk said, "You must recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before it can be explained. Thereupon, the gentleman diligently recited this sūtra without ceasing, and it frequently manifested miraculous efficacy.
A few days before he changed his bedding [i.e., passed away], he told his relatives, "I have received great benefit from the *Vajracchedikā*;

now, as I depart, I shall be reborn spontaneously among the nobility. This was recorded by the eighty-one-year-old Luchuan Cao Yinru (*Record of Miraculous Responses of the Vajracchedikā*). (Cited from the *Jingang Lingying*).

Deng Shaofeng of the Ming dynasty was a native of Jiangxi. He was born in the Jiāyīng (1529) year. Whenever he consulted those who cast his horoscope, they all predicted that he would have few sons and a short lifespan.
Consequently, he resolved to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, praying for longevity as well as progeny.
He passed away at the age of ninety-five in the Rénwǔ (1642) year of the Chóngzhēn era, having fathered thirteen sons and thirty-six grandsons (as recorded in the *Fruit of Recitation*).

During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, there was Wu Junping of Tongxiang. From his childhood, he had been filial; having lost both parents early on, he took up residence in the Taoguang Hall of Lingyin Temple.
Although he repeatedly failed the imperial examinations, he constantly reflected that the kindness of his parents was difficult to repay, weeping with unending grief.

A monk told him that for a son who wishes to repay his parents' kindness, copying the sutras is the supreme method. Junping then resolved to abstain from meat and observe a vegetarian fast for four months.
On the nineteenth day, he drew blood to transcribe one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He made eleven incisions in total across his two arms and chest.

Monastics and laypeople gathered together to witness the "Blood Scripture," all of whom sighed in admiration, saying: "The Master’s sincere heart and ascetic practice are such that no Buddha fails to perceive their fragrance.
To repay the boundless debt of gratitude with this is a hundred thousand times more magnificent than the glorification of fame and official rank. However, [the wounds] were merely...
The mantra for the *Guanzizai* (Avalokiteśvara) was not yet transcribed. Junping once again drew a blade across his chest;
having finished writing, he immediately dreamed that at night his parents were in the clouds, saying to him: "We rely upon you drawing blood to transcribe this scripture.
Your filial piety has moved us, and we two have been reborn in the Pure Land. Originally you had no son, but the Buddha has sent a virtuous youth to continue your lineage. Its...
In his later years, he fathered a son. A few months later, when the boy was tested with meat, he closed his mouth and would not eat.

Jūnping also vowed to observe the fast and recite the scriptures for the rest of his life; the scars from the knife wounds upon his body were still clearly visible (as recorded in the *Lingyin Si Jishi*).
Ji Zhongwei of Zhide Township in Wu County during the Ming dynasty was descended from an ancient lineage. From his youth, his aspirations transcended the mundane world.
At the age of twelve, when his father sought to arrange a marriage for him, he resolutely declined; at seventeen, when a date was chosen for the wedding, he again fled into the mountains.
There he applied himself to arduous cultivation, faithfully upholding the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (the Diamond Sutra). His parents, having no other recourse, relinquished the betrothal gifts.

Tuchin. Wei then obeyed his parents' command and returned home. All alone, he built a dwelling to enshrine the Buddha and devoted himself solely to the recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras for over thirty years.
In the *Renchen* year of the Shunzhi era, a notorious local villain named Li Yuwu fabricated a charge of murder and falsely accused Wei.
The magistrate erred in judgment and sentenced him to strangulation; those who heard of it considered it a grievous injustice. During the trial, Wei appeared as if deaf and dazed.
He did not utter a single word in response. The next day, his relatives entered the prison to inquire about the matter.

He said, "At that time, I was completely unaware that there was a formal trial taking place in the hall. They asked again, "Did you feel the pain from the flogging? He replied, "I was entirely unconscious of any suffering or pain.
When the crowd looked at his feet, they found no injury whatsoever; however, the two characters for "Vajra" (金剛) were faintly visible upon them. There was no one who did not [marvel at this].
I praise the power of his recitation of the sutras. Li Senxian was directly exonerated upon investigation; his mother’s grievance was vindicated, while Yu Wu was wrongly convicted and died in prison.
He has now authored a commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is currently being prepared for publication (recorded by Xu Duming of Zhejiang).
Ming Tai Cang Gao Gui resided in Dao Guan Lane, where he was engaged in the trade of backing hard linings and operated a shoe-making shop.
In the sixth month of the fifth year of the Tianqi era, a lining he had backed made a sudden sound like tearing silk against the wall and flew into mid-air.
Onlookers gathered like a wall. It gradually descended, and several more pieces were seen drifting directly toward the Pútóng Pagoda outside the northern city wall.
As he was first descending, the monks took them to examine; they were all sheets of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

It appears that because this man was noble but illiterate, he collected miscellaneous paper and old cloth without distinguishing between what was pure and impure, using them as underlays for his feet.

In seeking profit, he did not realize he was committing a grave offense; thus, the heavenly deity manifested such a warning. Nowadays, people follow the instruction to revere written characters. [End of] Wumen.
Within the temple compound, efforts were made to perform restoration work; yet those who cherished it were few, while those who treated it with irreverence and negligence were many.

Amidst ditches, drains, and piles of refuse, things were discarded in utter disorder, yet this was neither considered strange nor deemed a transgression. Should a person of some discernment behold such a sight, [they would surely be moved].
Both my heart and mind were deeply moved. My father once composed "Ten Exhortations" to guide the world; I shall now provide an abbreviated version of its text.
First, I exhort families with the means to study: by providing resources for teachers and the practice of learning, the rewards of the Classics and Histories will be manifold and easily attained.
According to one's capacity, gather those of like mind to collect discarded items for cremation. The expenditure will not be great, yet the merit accumulated will be immense.
First, I exhort families who lack the means for their children to study: poverty and low station are the common lot of scholars. One should endure hardship in pursuit of advancement;
whenever one encounters discarded texts—whether encountered along the road or abandoned in filth—one should collect them daily and store them in a container. Do not neglect them.
One might face a loss by missing the opportunity. When a vessel is full, cast it into a fierce flame; throw the ashes into a clear stream—this is what is called "merit without expense.
First, I urge those from the gentry class who have already entered the registers of office:

since the fragrance of your books and the blessings of your lineage have already flowed on for generations, you must cherish the characters of the written word and block the source [of waste]. You should donate funds to purchase discarded books and scattered volumes, ensuring that they do not...
This will lead the foolish to ruin and they will surely meet with calamity. First, I urge those families currently holding official posts:

since petitions, memorials, and official documents are already numerous, and the submission of reports and correspondence even more extensive, you must strictly instruct your scribes and clerks everywhere not to allow a single character to be carelessly discarded or altered in any draft.
Furthermore, all examination scrolls, once the task is completed, shall be immediately cast into a blazing fire; do not keep them.
People secretly steal [the works of] Shi Jing, yet they instead pity those whose bellies are filled with books; this is especially true for those of great virtue.
One might advise officials in public offices to transcribe [such works] at home, while another might manage to enlist them in service; even half such a command can bring honor to one’s person.

Those who handle detailed case records may find their libraries so vast that they exhaust oxen and fill their halls, yet through such abuse, they ultimately suffer heavenly retribution. Shi Jing, however, daily accumulated hidden merit (*guìgōng*) through his reverence [for learning], wishing to benefit himself.
Those who plan for their descendants should remain constantly vigilant and alert. First, I exhort families that teach students:

whether one attains the heights of high minister or prime minister through this Way, or remains in obscurity as a teacher or friend through this Way, the principles of righteousness are truly the lifeblood of the Way, and written characters are likewise the representative words of the Sages.
Yet, even those within the inner chambers of your own households do not yet know to cherish them; how then can you [expect otherwise]?
Should one not hold those wandering travelers on the distant road accountable? One must wipe down tables and mats and polish the writing tablets and vessels, strictly instructing one's disciples.

First, one should exhort the companions who practice the Way of Śākyamuni; second, the teachings established by the two traditions are doubly venerable, and one must be even more diligent in preserving their circulation through even a single sheet of paper.

The scriptures, repentance rituals, talismans, and records originate from the Dharma-treasures of the Western Regions; the sacred hymns of the Most High are not to be opened, read, or held without solemnity and the burning of incense.

Yet, you treat them with such negligence as to allow them to be devoured by insects and gnawed by rats, showing no concern for them at all. While you claim to maintain strict and refined observance of the precepts, your laxity in this regard is already extreme.
As for practitioners and those on the Way who beg for food according to their conditions, it would be better for them to practice *huashen* (transformative alchemy) than to act thus.

The multitude has contributed funds to collect discarded characters; thus, both individuals and themselves shall equally partake in the benefits of merit. First, I exhort all sutra publishers, bookstores, and shopkeepers:
while seeking profit may allow one to establish a family, it is only through the accumulation of virtue that one can ensure prosperity for future generations.

I have often observed sutra publishers wrapping their scriptures in discarded texts, and bookstores packing their books using waste paper. To use such paper to wrap goods—save for items such as southern produce and medicinal herbs—is truly a great pity.
This is especially egregious. Furthermore, there are those who manufacture firecrackers, plastering windows and covering jars with them, causing them to fall into foul mud;

how much money is saved, while the karma created is so grave! I also exhort those who carve woodblocks and print books: since their livelihood depends on these works, they ought to protect their spirits as well.
Yet often, once the carved blocks or manuscript drafts have been used, they are discarded like refuse; errors are patched over, and the materials are trampled underfoot.

There is no restraint. Printed woodblocks are cast haphazardly upon the defiled ground; ancient manuscripts have long been discarded to rot. People rely on these for their livelihood yet do not think to cherish them.
When questioned of their hearts, how can they bear such cruelty? How can they hope to escape the retribution of their karma?

I urge the potters of Shu Mountain in Jingde to produce vessels to serve the world’s needs, ensuring they are sturdy and fine rather than seeking mere superficiality. Recently produced ceramic wares feature flowers and birds painted both inside and out.

This does not end with the depiction of human figures; it further includes the inclusion of reign titles and the names of meditation retreats (*zhāi*). There are also those who collect and record verses of praise for the Buddha’s blessings and longevity.
At times, they carve and engrave poetic lines onto jars with even greater refinement, or inscribe the *Heart Sūtra* upon sand bowls as objects of aesthetic appreciation.

After days have passed, these are discarded and ruined, resulting in eternal sacrilege. How can one not be cautious? Now, observing the warning regarding the *bèikǎn* (backing-offerings) of the Gao family, this serves as a prior admonition.

This is indeed detailed; yet it still does not reach the full extent of the matter. It further reveals that the world’s performance of good is inexhaustible, and the creation of karma is likewise inexhaustible.

This is why the Great Man of this house has tirelessly supervised the collation and carving of the *Tongshan lu* (Record of Shared Goodness) and its precepts, earnestly inquiring into the ways of the world.
Male Stone Inscription (Recorded from the *Vajra-Pratibhāsa*).

Li Shengzhi of the Jiading era of the Ming dynasty, courtesy name Shoubai, was the son of the Palace Counselor Yu Hai. He had long observed the vegetarian fast and maintained devout faith in the King of Emptiness (*Śūnyatā-rāja*).
Daily, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and maintained the *Cundī-dhāraṇī* without slackening. [This occurred] in the ninth month of the Xinwei year of the Chongzhen era.
On the twenty-second day, I accompanied my friend Wang Zhongqi on a stroll along a small path in the city.

Suddenly we encountered a man carrying a large axe who came up to us, throttled our throats, and struck us with the axe dozens of times before fleeing. Fortunately, both I and my friend emerged unharmed.
There were merely two shallow marks on his left arm. At that time, Zhongqi and the residents along the path all witnessed this in astonishment.

A short while later, the household servants gathered and bound the man, bringing him before the authorities; it was the estate servant Gan Chong. Having incurred a debt of a hundred taels of gold for taxes and rents, and realizing he could not repay them, he had plotted to kill [the master].
When the Magistrate of the district, Mr. Lai Fangwei of Xiaoshan, interrogated him in court, he asked:
Zhang Chong asked, "Why did you not simply strike off his head? [The Master] replied, "At that time, I saw only several lotus flowers; I did not see his head.
Though I struck repeatedly, I did not hit the flowers, so I had to cut their stalks. I do not know if I merely wounded my own arm. (From the *Jingang lingying*).
In the Jue-li Street of Jiaxing Prefecture during the Ming Dynasty, there lived Shi Yi-yang. He was a close friend with the monk You-heng of Dong-ta Temple.
At sixty-five years of age, although old and ill, Yi-yang would kneel and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* several scrolls daily as his regular practice.
On the eighth day of the first month of the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era, he suddenly passed away while still kneeling and before he had finished a scroll. His family...
During the mourning period for his father’s funeral, while the coffin was about to be nailed shut three days after the rites had begun, Yi Yang suddenly returned in spirit and spoke, saying:

"Since my death, I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. By the power of this recitation, I did not pass through the realm of the King of Hell, but remained instead in the presence of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Recently, the Bodhisattva told me that I had one scroll of the sūtra left unfinished; he has sent me back so that I may complete it quickly and then return here. Yi Yang—
Yang Qi’s breath was faint and his strength failed him so that he could no longer recite for himself. He spoke to his family, saying, "I must request the Venerable Youheng to recite on my behalf;
others will be of no benefit. It happened that Youheng had gone elsewhere at the invitation of another, so they waited for him for a day.
When Youheng arrived, Yang Zhi struggled up and listened until the scroll was finished. Once he had raised his hand in thanks to Youheng, he passed away with a smile (from the *Xin yi lu*).
Ming was a native of Hangzhou named Zhang Shoucheng, whose courtesy name was Buyi. Day and night he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with devotion.

Whenever he went out or returned, he would place the scripture in a pouch and suspend it from his chest. In the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, while traveling north on business with companions, they encountered a band of "ringing horse" robbers.
His companions were wounded; Zhang was struck by an arrow that hit him squarely in the chest, right upon the scripture pouch, yet it did not penetrate through.
Because of this "Heart" talisman, his life was preserved. This "Yellow Heart Talisman" was spoken by the military officer Sae-bu-am, the monk Hye-u.

As for the "Heart Talisman," the Chan master known as Dingtong was its first name. In his youth, he studied the books of the Three Teachings; though his outward station was that of a merchant or a government official, he remained devoted to the Way.
For over twenty years, he practiced the cultivation of meditation in his later life. Throughout his lifetime, he maintained the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Having encountered numerous great perils and contracted dangerous illnesses, he was in every instance delivered through transformation (as recorded in the "Fruits and Rewards of Recitation and Maintenance").
Zhu Shouzeng, styled Shugao, was a lieutenant-general of the Suzhou Guard. He upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it daily without interruption.
While transporting grain into the Yellow River, a sorcerer declared that he must sacrifice livestock to appease the river deity; otherwise, there would be divine retribution.
Shouzeng refused, insisting only on reciting the sūtra daily and dedicating the merit to the river deity. One day, amidst a great storm and rain, dragons fought.
In mid-air, the masts, sails, reed mats, and awnings were all blown away; ten thousand vessels tossed about, beyond control. Shouzeng burned incense and recited sutras with increasing devotion.
In a mere moment, the wind ceased and the rain cleared. He inspected his fleet, and among the hundreds of ships, not a single one was leaking or damaged.
Upon arriving at his lodging in Tongzhou, after every meal, he would invariably retire to sleep soundly in his room. One day, however, he did not.

He fell asleep; as he was just stepping out, the beam collapsed and his bed also shattered. Shouzeng frequently told others, "This is proof of my recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."

Ming Tang Yizhi, whose courtesy name was Shi, was a native of Huzhou. Having attained the degree of Mingjing (Exemplary Classics), he served as a Beijia (Vice-Commissioner) in Shouyang and subsequently assisted in the governance of Xiangguo.
On the second day of the second month in the Xinsi year of the Chongzhen era, when the rebel Li Zicheng broke into Xiangyang, Yizhi threw himself into a well to the left of the Duanli Gate.

His family members pulled him out, and though his breath had ceased, he revived. He privately lamented that the policies of military suppression and conciliation had brought ruin to the state, and he bore this pain [in silence].
He submitted a memorial, consisting of several thousand words of eloquent discourse. At that time, Lord Xu Baomo of Yintai, because the text exceeded the prescribed limit, ordered it to be abridged;
thus, his original intent was not fully expressed, leading to a formal inquiry. This matter fell to me for adjudication. I maintained that the case of Fuguo was different from that of Shoujiang.
Not long after the reduction [of the city], the three imperial palaces submitted successive memorials, all of which exonerated Yizhi.

He petitioned for leniency under the broad statutes of the law, and accordingly requested leave to return to his home village; however, on the fifth day of the last month of winter, Xiangyang fell once again.

This was because Yizhi had mastered the *Prajñāpāramitā*, realized the fruit of non-duality, and his entire family and kinsmen were able to recite from memory the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Samantamukha-parivarta*. By day...
Each of them maintained [the precepts]. At night, they gathered together before the Buddha, their virtuous energy permeating and penetrating both the hidden and the manifest.
First, they did not die by the hands of bandits; next, they did not die in a well; and in the end, they did not die according to the Dharma.
How can this be conceived? Recorded by Maozongqi (extracted from "The Fruits of Receiving and Maintaining").

Ming Ru was originally named Gao Maogqi; his courtesy name was Zongqi. He was a jinshi graduate of the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era. While still a youth enrolled as a scholar, he took great pleasure in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In the Xinsi year, he was transferred to serve in Xiangyang, at a time when the city lay in ruins following the devastation caused by the rebel Xiongnu.

Enemy troops have descended upon our very flanks and inner sanctuaries; arrogant generals harbor their ambitions at our very core. Military dispatches issue daily as warnings, and we do not loosen our girdles even at night.

Zongqi himself recognized that he would ultimately perish in this desolate place; nevertheless, he compiled and carved this record of the karmic rewards for upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā*.
Thus, with his failing and sickly bones, he sustained himself for three hundred and sixty days. Having nearly died four times, he has fortunately survived.

It had been barely three months since he untied his official sash when Xiangyang fell once again. Among those who shared his service at that time, some were smeared with fat upon the edges of blades, while others were the "sack-headed" victims of the legal authorities.
You alone managed to escape with your life and return to your village; was this not surely due to the compassionate protection of Vajrapāṇi?
I have compiled the *Chiyàn jì* (Records of Verified Accounts); having read Master Sōngshào’s own narrative, I have included it here in this collection.
Ming Dynasty high school student Gao Xiaozuan of Jiangdu, courtesy name Zige, style name Shenbo.

In the year of Yiyou, when the Qing troops broke through Yangzhou and Minister of State Shi [Kai] perished in the disaster, Zige composedly donned his scholar’s cap and robe and hanged himself in the Great Achievement Hall (Dacheng Dian).
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year of Shunzhi, his fellow student Huang Zhongjin was returning from a night’s drinking at the West Gate when he passed by...
Before the lesson, Huang happened to see a man emerging from the school, preceded by two red silk lanterns. Huang greeted him with a bow and spoke with him;
he was unmistakably dressed in the scholar’s attire of the Ming period. At first, Huang coveted the lanterns and walked along with him.

Subsequently, however, he wondered how one could wear such bright garments during the Qing dynasty and felt a pang of anxiety. He took his leave twice, but the man would not permit it. Huang then asked him, "Your Honored Father..."
"Are you at peace? Huang asked. An replied, "I have been very cordial in recounting my life. Once Huang had entered the gate, he inquired after his name.
