The spiritual response was indeed so manifest! He subsequently bestowed three hundred taels of silver to fulfill the monk’s vow to build the hermitage.
After receiving this gift, the monk never again set foot upon the open ground. In the eighth year of the Xinti (辛酉) era of the Tianqi period, he took his leave and entered Mount Lu;
his ultimate end remains unknown. (From the *Jinyucheng Xují*).
During the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, there was a monk named Zhou Jingshan at Pudu Monastery north of Rugao County. He had observed the vegetarian fast since birth and had no desire to marry.
Morning and evening, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with the utmost sincerity and faith. At that time, he was only twenty years old and lived with his elder brother.
When his brother’s illness reached its terminal stage, he entrusted him with the care of his younger widow and two infants still in swaddling clothes. Thereupon, [Jingshan] reflected upon his own...

Li became resentful and, seizing a knife, severed his own male organ; more than a *dou* of blood flowed out, yet he died and was restored to life. When his elder brother heard of this, he wept with such grief that he passed away.

Jingshan personally farmed the land to support his sister-in-law and nephews for twenty years. By the time both nephews had reached maturity and established their own households, the mother and children were somewhat settled.
Thereupon, he shaved his head to enter the monastic life, built a thatched hut, and began expounding the teachings for others.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* had a distinct interpretation [of its meaning], which people esteemed all the more. In the year of Gengchen, a great famine occurred;
as the rebels gathered their multitudes to plunder fields and hearths, they passed through his location and all said, "Do not alarm our Zhou master.

Those in the neighboring areas who fled the soldiers and took refuge in the hermitage were all preserved. At the age of seventy-five, he passed away while sitting upright. His breath ceased... for a long time.
For a long time, his neck bone remained upright and did not collapse. The layman Yan-geng of Lan-an recorded this in detail. Mo Zongqi said:
"To protect his younger brother's orphaned child while distancing himself from him due to the taboo—such power has already penetrated the great meaning of the Vajra.

To don restrictive robes, mutilate one’s form, extinguish one’s nature, avoid one’s elder brother, and leave one’s mother—this must mean that within worldly laws there is no Buddha-dharma. It is like being separated from—"
To seek water from a wave is certainly illogical (as stated in the *Fruit of Upholding [the Precepts]*).
During the Wanli era, outside the city walls of Guide Prefecture, there was an old nun at Shuijing An (Crystal Nunnery) who was nicknamed the "One-Eyed Vajra Nun.
She earned this name because she had once lost an eye while working as a *vajra* (a ritual implement). By nature she was simple and austere, living on coarse food herself.
Aside from his coarse clothing, whatever others left him, he would entirely distribute to provide for those among the monks and nuns who lacked necessities.

Whenever he convened assemblies to lecture, faithful believers gathered in circles around him. A certain scholar asked, "Why does the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consist of thirty-two sections?
He replied, "To unify all through one—this is true of both Confucianism and Buddhism; how could there be so many distinct segments? He then spoke this verse:
The Buddha taught that the Vajra is wondrously beyond all comparison; through a single word, one realizes awakening and transcends the Śrāvakas.
If there is someone who can understand the purport of this Golden Sūtra, why need they laboriously divide it into forty-eight sections? A monk asked: "Why is it called 'Vajra'? He replied: "..."
"Vajras exist within all people; why ask such a question? He spoke a verse, saying: "The Vajra-fruit is truly the Vajra; Forged a hundred times, struck a thousand blows, it is never harmed.
To shatter empty space would be but a trifle; Right now, there is only seen the Buddha’s radiance. Another person asked:
"Master, you are thoroughly versed in the meaning of the Buddhadharma; why do you not manifest in a male body? He replied: "Form..."

There were men and women; by nature, there was no distinction between self and other. Do not harbor views of inequality. A verse was spoken: "Why need one distinguish between male and female as false or true?
Who is this person appearing as Guanyin? When the skin-sack is cast off, it is entirely useless. Let us ask: is the male body the female body?
Responding to every question with immediate and extraordinary agility, those who took refuge from near and far were beyond counting. Her years exceeded...
Seventy [years old]. He announced the time of his passing in advance. A flame appeared at the tip of his nose; sitting upright and with eyes closed, he passed away. He left behind a verse which said:
"Once cremated, I depart forever to return to emptiness. Wherever one seeks emptiness, it is not empty. My going and my coming remain as 'I';
Like lightning and bubbles, they are all the same. The monk Xiangguang of Henan described what he witnessed and spoke of it to the layman.

As for the remainder of the *Geng* [chapter]: according to the Sixth Patriarch, upon hearing the single phrase "give rise to the mind where there is nowhere to dwell," he attained sudden and great enlightenment, saying:

"This is the wondrous existence of the Dharma-nature within true emptiness. When the First Patriarch [Bodhidharma] was with Huike, while his mind was still in turmoil, he feared that various conditions had not yet ceased;
yet when those conditions were just beginning to cease, he feared they would suddenly become annihilated. To cease all conditions is non-existence."
That which dwells is non-interruption; this gives rise to the mind. Non-dwelling is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the arising of the mind is wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*).

When the Sixth Patriarch realized this, what further matter remained? The four verses of the nun Dumen had already penetrated the essential principle of the midnight transmission (as recorded in the *Shouchi Guobao*).

The nun Huizhen of Changzhou was the daughter of an official family. From childhood, her speech and actions were never frivolous, and she wished to leave the household life; her parents granted her request.
She was sent to Lengqia Hermitage, where she subsequently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* morning and evening.

A fellow nun in the same hermitage fell into disgrace due to impure conduct, and the scandal implicated Huizhen. At that time, she happened to be suffering from an eye ailment; out of indignation and resentment, both her eyes became blind. This continued for three years.
He continued reciting the sutras as before. One night, he dreamed that the Vajrapāṇi deity said to him, "Your practice has been without flaw;

I shall restore your sight to you. At dawn, he arose and his two eyes suddenly opened. He lived to the age of ninety, passing away peacefully while sitting in meditation without illness. Formerly, there was Minister Cui Qun.
A questioner asked, as Master Huihui had said: "By what did you attain it? The Master replied, "I attained it by seeing into one's nature. At that time, the Master was suffering from an eye ailment.
The questioner pressed him, saying, "If you say you attained it by seeing into one's nature, what then of your eyes? The Master replied, "Seeing into one's nature is not dependent on the eyes;

how could an eye ailment cause any harm? Subsequently, the nun’s double pupils became bright once more. This specifically clarifies the verification of the principle, which is unfailing. However, if we speak of attaining the Way, it does not depend on having eyes.
*The Miraculous Response of the Vajra (from the *Vajra-lingying*).
By Yu Shuyan, a filial and upright scholar of the Jintan Academy during the Great Qing. His family lineage has long been devoted to loyalty and filial piety;

the entire household reveres the Buddha. He lives as a solitary mendicant, indifferent to worldly affairs. As his daily practice, he recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every day and performs the *Mahākaruṇā-pūjā*. In the year Dingyou...*
In winter, he was arrested and sent to Jinling on false charges brought by his enemies. Among the common people, there was none who did not feel resentment for him;

many of those who escorted him wept aloud, losing their voices. Yet Shuyuan’s countenance and spirit remained serene as ever; he merely recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in silence without ceasing. Once he had entered the prison, [he continued as before].
Having endured every form of bitter suffering, he hoped his countenance would appear as if he had entered meditative absorption;

yet he saw only the lictors struggling before him, exerting all their strength to strip the flesh from his thighs and shins, yet ultimately inflicting no injury. There were only several black marks, as hard as solid rock.
He was subsequently cleared of the charges. Shu Yan constantly copied the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and exhorted others to recite it to escape the calamities of this kalpa.

When he was arrested, some people doubted that the worship of the Buddha was efficacious; how could they have known that his sincerity had penetrated so deeply that he ultimately attained a body of indestructible diamond throughout his life?
Zi Shan practiced profound filial piety; every night, he would pray to the Northern Dipper while naked and exposed to the elements for a period of time.

Frost solidifies and ice forms; this process ceases only after it has been resolved. If the Buddha-dharma were not a reliable basis, then even Shanxiu would have sufficed for the practice of filial piety through death;
how much more so, then, for those like Shuyan?

Zhou De-wen, courtesy name Jun-sheng, of Wu County during the Great Qing, was a man of supreme filial piety. Even after he had passed the age of fifty, he still cut flesh from his thigh to save his parents.

After his mother passed away, he was so consumed by grief that he wasted away; he maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for three years, intending to complete a certain number of recitations.

He performed rituals and repentance with dedication, exerting himself day and night. At one point, he suffered from a painful eye ailment to the point that he could hardly see. When he was about to complete [the required number of] recitations...
At the end, his vision suddenly cleared and he was restored to sight. People considered this a result of filial piety, yet it was also due to the power of the sutras.

He had a rosary that he had lost several beads of on the road; missing them, he thought of it constantly until he suddenly found them picked up from the floor of his own home. They were exactly the same old beads.
He wrote a record of the returned beads, feeling even more moved by the divine protection bestowed upon him, and thus he continued his recitations without interruption.
Da Qing Wang was a man of integrity from Changmen in Suzhou. He had long been simple and sincere in his conduct and daily recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

By the year Gengyin of the Shunzhi era, he had already accumulated twenty-two years of this practice. In the autumn of that year, he served as a guest in the military headquarters of General Wang Xing.

He had long been acquainted with Yi, who took pity on his poverty and recommended that he lead a sandalwood ship to explore the seas; in reality, this was for the purpose of trading with various foreign nations.
On the twentieth day of the eighth month, as they were departing from Lousha Port, they suddenly saw white cloth fluttering in the air over the sea.
Turning the sails to investigate, they found it was a vessel that had capsized due to a storm, with five or six people still clinging to the mast.

The boat was on the verge of capsizing; we rescued it and reached the shore. Entering the great ocean, we traveled for seven days, covering more than three thousand seven hundred *li*, until we reached the borders of Japan at a place called Chōki.
There, we sold our goods to obtain provisions. We did not return until the tenth day of the second month of the following year.
When we set out with the oars, the weather was clear and mild. Over the course of six or seven days, we covered approximately two thousand *li*. However...
On the eighth day, a sudden west wind arose with great force. The waves surged like mountains, and all the masts—large and small—along with the rudder were lost.
A section of the stern broke off and was carried away. Fifty-six people were drowned and swept away. At that time, Yizheng was sitting on the stern;
suddenly, as if someone had lifted him up, he was brought into the hold. Before long, the wind and waves subsided slightly. The company then wove bamboo mats to serve as sails and rowed with oars.
Only after adjusting the rudder did we finally gain entrance to the harbor. On the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the Renchen year, we again passed Changqi.

On the first day of the ninth month, as our returning sails drew near Putuo, the assembly wished to ascend the mountain to perform repentance rites; however, due to favorable winds from the southeast, their purpose was not yet fulfilled.
As we traveled further toward Yangshan, they beheld a white vapor rising from the mountain for several li in length. Everyone was filled with wonder and lingering doubt, when suddenly—
A typhoon arose, tossing the sails and timber about like birds. Miao Lian was swept away by the waves; in an instant, the ship broke apart.
One hundred and eighty-three people drowned, while only three—Yi, a man surnamed Xu, and a man surnamed Chen—survived.
Clinging to a white rattan vine, they were driven by the waves onto Xiaoyang Mountain. On the following morning, they happened upon a wooden chest floating by, inside of which were...
There were two items—a fire-starting flint and a knife—and a bundle each of incense-smoke and moxa. On the third day, another half of a broken cauldron floated to the surface.
The three men wished to boil water in it to drink, but the water tasted as salty as the bitter sea and was unfit for use. Beside them, they saw within a cleft of a mountain rock...

Xiaoquan’s food became increasingly sparse and simple. Gradually, he took boiled *lu-gen* (sedge roots) as his sustenance; for several days, he relied on this to avoid hunger. However, his bowels were constipated and his abdomen distended. Seeing some grass by the water’s edge with long and large leaves, he dug it up; its root was like a radish. He gathered it and made a soup that was quite delicious. After eating it, his stomach rumbled and he had a bowel movement, feeling a refreshing sense of well-being. He remarked slowly: [The remainder of the passage follows: "Truly, when one eats what is appropriate to the time and place, even if it be coarse, it will nourish the body and sustain life. But if one eats what is not appropriate, even if it be fine, it will cause illness and death. This is why the ancients said: 'The wise man does not eat what is not right. He then sighed and said: "I have now been away from home for over three years. My family must be suffering greatly. I fear they may have already passed away. I wish to return home immediately. Having spoken thus, he wept bitterly. At that moment, a monk approached him and asked, "What is your intention? Xiaoquan replied, "My intention is to return home. The monk said, "If you truly wish to return home, you must first repent your transgressions. Only then can you go. Xiaoquan said, "I am a man of humble virtue who has committed many offenses. I do not know how to repent. The monk said, "If you wish to repent, you must first receive the precepts. Xiaoquan said, "I have no one to rely upon. The monk said, "I shall act as your preceptor. Xiaoquan then knelt and received the full precepts. Having received them, he felt a profound sense of joy and immediately set out for home. On the road, he encountered a tiger. He thought to himself, "I have now received the precepts; even if the tiger were to devour me, I would still attain rebirth in heaven. The tiger then left him unharmed. Continuing on his way, he reached a mountain pass where he met a band of robbers. They seized him and bound his hands behind his back. One robber said, "This man has a fine appearance; let us kill him and take his flesh. Another said, "Let us wait until he dies naturally, then take his flesh. They then released him. Xiaoquan thanked them and continued on his way. Upon reaching home, he found his family alive and well. His parents embraced him and wept. His wife and children also wept. They all said, "We have been searching for you for years, fearing you might have perished. We never imagined you could return alive. Xiaoquan then related the details of his journey. His family members were filled with joy and disbelief. From that day forward, the entire household lived in peace and prosperity. Xiaoquan lived out his years and attained a peaceful end. Thus, it is said: "The Way is near at hand; it is not far off. It depends entirely on whether one believes or doubts. This is why the Buddha said: "Faith is the seed of the Way. How true these words are! Therefore, one should always maintain faith and never harbor doubt. Only then can one attain liberation. This is the meaning of the story. This was none other than Du Dahuang of my own village. Together they gathered firewood and raised smoke, hoping someone would see them and come to their rescue.
Half a month later, they encountered the patrol boat of Zhang Mingzheng, who learned of their situation from a foreign merchant and sent them ashore at Laosha Port.

The three men were thus preserved and returned home in gratitude for the spiritual power of Vajrapāṇi. They redoubled their recitation of the sutras morning and night. Indeed, drifting upon the open sea is tantamount to death.
This is where life returns. There is a principle that those who are fundamentally sincere and earnest would not venture into such danger.
Had it not been for the rescue by the Vajra [deities], they would certainly have died among the one hundred and eighty-three people, rather than among the fifty-six.
It is likely that Xu Chen and the other two possessed roots of goodness, which is why they escaped this great peril. (Recorded in the Jihai year)

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was requested from me by him. He recounted his own past experiences, and having inquired into the details of their beginning and end, I have recorded them here.
Yuan Yinghe of Wulin during the Great Qing dynasty is a descendant of Master Liaofan;

he resides at the northwest foot of Mount Wu, is sixty-one years of age, has maintained the vegetarian fast for eight years, and has daily recited the *Vajracchedikā* without interruption. This was written in the fifth month of the Xinchou year of the Shunzhi era.

On the night of the thirteenth day at the hour of the rat, a fire broke out in the home of a man surnamed Chen. A fierce northwest wind blew, and within a few moments the flames had spread to more than one hundred and sixty houses.
As the fire was about to reach Yuan’s residence, his mother, who was over eighty years old, sat upright in the upper story reciting the Buddha’s name.
Yinghe hurriedly carried her downstairs; knowing she could not escape, he simply chanted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* aloud with a clear voice. At that time—
There was a man named Chen Jianyang who was a person of great sincerity and integrity.

While taking shelter from a fire in the corner of Yuan’s wall, he saw a patch of red light, shaped like a curtain or canopy, descending from the sky and shielding Yuan’s wall. It vanished in an instant. Suddenly, the wind shifted to the southeast;
the fire blazed up to the heavens, yet not a single spark was to be seen on any of the four sides. Thus, he escaped the disaster. This was in response to the Monk.

Having knelt long in the courtyard, he finished reciting the sutra. After a short while, people began to offer their congratulations. Yang specifically recounted what he had witnessed, and the assembly was all struck with awe.
From that time on, everyone’s devotion to recitation became even more steadfast. Xu Douming of Kuaiji visited Hangzhou and personally witnessed this marvel;
he has thus related it and recorded it as such.
